The trajectory Poincaré inequality will control this fluctuation once we bound the gradient of $F_s$. Set $c_i=v_iB_i$; the exact product rule gives $$d_jF_s=\sum_i c_i(x^j)d_jp_{s,i}
                   +\sum_i p_{s,i}(x)d_jc_i.$$ The columns of $B$ have entries bounded by $C_B/\sqrt n$, and the matrix $(d_jc_i)_{ij}$ has operator norm at most $C_B/\sqrt n$. For the first term, mixed-gradient symmetry changes $d_jp_{s,i}$ to $d_ip_{s,j}$. Also $v_i(x^j)\le e^{C|J_{ij}|}v_i(x)$ and $v_i\le2w_i$, so $$\sum_i\frac{c_i(x^j)^2}{w_i(x)}\le C_B.$$ Cauchy–Schwarz, followed by summation over $j$, proves <a id="eq:cutoff-coefficient-derivative"></a>$$\mathbb E\left\lVert dF_s\right\rVert^2
 \le C_B\left(
   \mathbb E\sum_iw_i\left\lVert d_ip_s\right\rVert^2+n^{-1}\mathbb E\left\lVert p_s\right\rVert^2\right)
 \le C_B.
 \label{eq:cutoff-coefficient-derivative}$$ The same estimate applies to every one of the finitely many columns.

Before choosing these recipes or $D$, freeze once and for all a moderate-rate instance of [eq:cutoff-propagation](#eq:cutoff-propagation), say with $\rho_0=\lambda/2$, and its constant $C_{\rho_0}$. The Poincaré bound at time $a$, this instance of propagation applied to the scalar function $F_s$, and [eq:cutoff-coefficient-derivative](#eq:cutoff-coefficient-derivative) give <a id="eq:cutoff-coefficient-fluctuation"></a>$$\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}\bigl(\mathbb E[F_s(X_s)\mid X_a]\bigr)
 \le C_P C_{\rho_0}C_B e^{-2\rho_0(s-a)}+o(1).
 \label{eq:cutoff-coefficient-fluctuation}$$ The coefficient approximation costs $C\delta$ in $L^2$ before transport. By [eq:cutoff-slow-transport](#eq:cutoff-slow-transport), both this error and the square root of [eq:cutoff-coefficient-fluctuation](#eq:cutoff-coefficient-fluctuation) carry the factor $e^{-\lambda(s-a)}$. Relative to $e^{-\lambda D}$, their cost is bounded by $$C\delta+C(C_PC_{\rho_0}C_B)^{1/2}e^{-\rho_0(D-1)}.$$ In particular the approximation error does not acquire a factor $e^{\lambda D}$.

The hidden part and the exact fast complement, propagated from $s$, cost at most $C e^{-(\lambda+\kappa)(D-1)}$ for some $\kappa>0$, by [thm:hidden-propagation](#thm:hidden-propagation), [prop:exact-isolation](#prop:exact-isolation), [lem:exact-upgrade](#lem:exact-upgrade). The latter also applies when the visible vector is only in $\mathcal H$ with weighted image in the fast part of $\mathcal X_v$. After division by $e^{-\lambda D}$, this fast-sector error is bounded by $C e^{\lambda+\kappa}e^{-\kappa D}$. First choose $\delta$ sufficiently small in terms of $\eta$ and $C_E$, and fix the coarse recipes and $C_B$. Now choose $D$ large so that both normalized exponential errors, $$C(C_PC_{\rho_0}C_B)^{1/2}e^{-\rho_0(D-1)}
 \quad\text{and}\quad C e^{\lambda+\kappa}e^{-\kappa D},$$ are smaller than the required fixed fraction of $\eta$. Restoring the common factor $e^{-\lambda D}$ proves the limiting mean and fluctuation estimate with exact slow coefficients and reconstruction.

The block length is now fixed, so we may choose the finer recipes $\widetilde E$ without altering the fluctuation estimate. At this $D$, an accuracy smaller than $c\eta e^{-(\lambda+C)D}$ makes all changes in the reported $A_a$, $A_b$, and the reconstruction smaller than the remaining fraction of $\eta e^{-\lambda D}$. Here $e^{CD}$ is a rough bound for any endpoint norm needed in this comparison. The finer derivative constants have not replaced $C_B$ in [eq:cutoff-coefficient-fluctuation](#eq:cutoff-coefficient-fluctuation).

Finally use strict slack, the deterministic good-disorder selection in the proof of [prop:cutoff-block](#prop:cutoff-block), and normalization by $N_b$. The condition $N_b\ge n^{-Q}$ preserves a fixed polynomial envelope; choose every Poincaré and propagation remainder with an exponent larger than $2Q+H+2$ before using it. For a violating sequence, perform the one-block or two-block restart above before extraction. The normalized gradients, actual conditional laws, common Poincaré bound, and endpoint ratio meet the same hypotheses at the prescribed relative endpoints; any parameter selected from the family is fixed conditional on the disorder before the path is sampled. The resulting fixed-interval sequence would contradict the limiting estimate. Returning by [eq:cutoff-restart](#eq:cutoff-restart) proves [eq:cutoff-alignment](#eq:cutoff-alignment) uniformly at the original block positions, without a rate for any fixed-time $o(1)$. This includes the parameter selected from the preparation family below. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-60"></a>
#### Preparation, the cone, and a macroscopic mean

Choose $m$ fixed scalar tests $F_1,\ldots,F_m$ from the potential class defining $\mathcal X$ whose gradient projections onto the slow space form an invertible matrix. Such tests exist by density. Replace them by fixed linear combinations so that the limiting matrix is the identity. Their gradients have uniformly bounded pointwise Euclidean norm, and the functions have polynomial supremum bounds. For a unit output coefficient $u\in\mathbb R^m$, the terminal gradient $d(\sum_j u_jF_j)$ consequently satisfies <a id="eq:cutoff-terminal-cone"></a>$$|A_T|\ge c_0,\qquad N_T\le K_0|A_T|
 \label{eq:cutoff-terminal-cone}$$ uniformly on typically initialized trajectories, after the recipe accuracy is sufficiently small.

The preparation must have a common Poincaré bound even when the slow recipes are refined. We establish this uniformity before making the final approximation choices. For any fixed smooth bounded scaled recipe matrix $\widetilde E$ and any $0<\alpha<1/2$, set $$R_n=n^{1/2-\alpha},\qquad
 g^z(x)=\widetilde E(x)z,\qquad |z|<R_n.$$ Let $T_s^z$ be the rate-one refresh dynamics whose target mean at the old configuration is $$m_i^z(x)=\tanh((Jx)_i+g_i^z(x)).$$ The target may depend on the spin being refreshed, so this process need not be reversible. Its generator is nevertheless exactly <a id="eq:cutoff-preparation-generator"></a>$$L^z f=\sum_i(m_i^z-x_i)d_if.
 \label{eq:cutoff-preparation-generator}$$

<a id="stmt-lem-cutoff-preparation"></a>
<div id="lem:cutoff-preparation" class="lemma">

**Lemma 66** (Common preparation bounds). *For each fixed recipe matrix and all sufficiently large $n$, uniformly for $|z|<R_n$ and $0<h\le1$, the law $\nu_z=\mu T_h^z$ satisfies <a id="eq:cutoff-preparation-density"></a><a id="eq:cutoff-preparation-poincare"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \log\left\lVert \,\mathrm d\nu_z/\,\mathrm d\mu\right\rVert_\infty
   &\le nh(e^{2\varepsilon_n}-1)=O(n^{1-\alpha}),
   &\varepsilon_n&=\sup_{z,x,i}|g_i^z(x)|=O(n^{-\alpha}),
   \label{eq:cutoff-preparation-density}\\
 \mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\nu_z}f
   &\le\left[C_\mu e^{C_*h}
         +4\frac{e^{C_*h}-1}{C_*}\right]\nu_z\left\lVert df\right\rVert^2.
   \label{eq:cutoff-preparation-poincare}
\end{aligned}$$ Here $C_\mu$ can be the inverse equilibrium gap, and $C_*$ is a common constant depending on the original interaction bounds, not on the fixed recipe. A finer recipe changes the sufficiently large dimension threshold, but not this common constant.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cutoff-preparation"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cutoff-preparation</summary>

*Proof.* Both the added field and its difference matrix are small. Scaled recipe calculus gives <a id="eq:cutoff-small-perturbation"></a>$$\sup_{z,x}\left\lVert g^z(x)\right\rVert_\infty+
 \sup_{z,x}\left\lVert (d_i g_j^z(x))_{ij}\right\rVert_\mathrm{op}
 \le C_{\widetilde E}n^{-\alpha}.
 \label{eq:cutoff-small-perturbation}$$ At each refresh attempt, including an attempt that leaves the spin unchanged, the ratio of the perturbed outcome probability to the ordinary outcome probability is at most $e^{2\varepsilon_n}$. On the common attempt construction the path likelihood is therefore at most $e^{2\varepsilon_n N_h}$, with $N_h\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(nh)$ under the ordinary process. Started at $\mu$, the ordinary endpoint has law $\mu$ conditional on $N_h=k$, because its embedded update kernel preserves $\mu$. Thus $X_h$ and $N_h$ are independent under this stationary reference law, and for every endpoint $y$, $$\frac{\mu T_h^z(y)}{\mu(y)}
 \le\mathbb E_\mu[e^{2\varepsilon_n N_h}\mid X_h=y]
 =\exp\{nh(e^{2\varepsilon_n}-1)\}.$$ Averaging the attempt likelihood therefore proves the endpoint density bound [eq:cutoff-preparation-density](#eq:cutoff-preparation-density).

For the variance estimate, we use gradients of the perturbed semigroup. Differentiate [eq:cutoff-preparation-generator](#eq:cutoff-preparation-generator). The exact gradient extension has coefficients $a_{ij}^z=d_im_j^z$, including the diagonal $a_{ii}^z$. Its formula is $$(L^z-I)p_i-2x_i\sum_j a_{ij}^z d_jp_i+\sum_j a_{ij}^z p_j.$$ The diagonal $a_{ii}^z p_i$ is an $o(1)$ zero-order term; the own-spin derivative of an exact gradient is zero. Taylor expansion of $\tanh$, with [eq:cutoff-small-perturbation](#eq:cutoff-small-perturbation) and the bounded row and column square sums, gives common bounds $$\left\lVert a^z\right\rVert_\mathrm{op}\le C,\qquad
 \max_i\sum_j\frac{|a_{ij}^z|^2}{w_j^z}\le C,
 \qquad w_j^z=1-x_jm_j^z.$$ For example the leading matrix is the field-difference matrix times the diagonal variance; $v_j^z\le2w_j^z$ controls the displayed weighted row sum. The quadratic Taylor remainders are bounded Schur products of matrices with bounded row and column square sums. Once the right side of [eq:cutoff-small-perturbation](#eq:cutoff-small-perturbation) is at most one, the square-evolution proof of [prop:path-rough](#prop:path-rough) therefore has a common constant $C_*$. In particular <a id="eq:cutoff-preparation-gradient"></a>$$\left\lVert dT_s^zf\right\rVert^2\le e^{C_*s}T_s^z\left\lVert df\right\rVert^2.
 \label{eq:cutoff-preparation-gradient}$$ Thus the gradient estimate remains valid for this possibly nonreversible preparation: it was derived from the stated generator and its exact gradients, without requiring a Gibbs invariant law.

Its jump bracket is at most $4\left\lVert dT_{h-s}^zf\right\rVert^2$. The conditional martingale variance formula and [eq:cutoff-preparation-gradient](#eq:cutoff-preparation-gradient) give $$\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_x(f(X_h))
 \le4\frac{e^{C_*h}-1}{C_*}\,T_h^z\left\lVert df\right\rVert^2(x).$$ The other term in total variance is $$\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\mu(T_h^zf)
 \le C_\mu\mu\left\lVert dT_h^zf\right\rVert^2
 \le C_\mu e^{C_*h}\mu T_h^z\left\lVert df\right\rVert^2.$$ Their sum is [eq:cutoff-preparation-poincare](#eq:cutoff-preparation-poincare). ◻

</details>

We now fix the remaining parameters in an order that preserves the common constants. First freeze the moderate rate $\rho_0=\lambda/2$ and its propagation constants in [eq:cutoff-propagation](#eq:cutoff-propagation). Use [lem:cutoff-preparation](#lem:cutoff-preparation) with $h\le1$ in [eq:cutoff-trajectory-poincare](#eq:cutoff-trajectory-poincare); this gives a common $C_P$ for every prepared ordinary trajectory, independent of later recipe refinements. Next fix the output tests, choose $K>\max\{K_0,2C_E+2\}$, and choose $\eta$ small in terms of $K$ and the desired rate slack. Choose the coarse coefficient recipes, then the alignment block $D$, and then the finer reporting and preparation recipes, in exactly the order in the proof of [prop:cutoff-coefficients](#prop:cutoff-coefficients). Finally choose a positive $h\le1$ for these fine recipes. Shrinking $h$ cannot increase the common Poincaré constant; larger fine-recipe derivative constants change the dimension threshold in [lem:cutoff-preparation](#lem:cutoff-preparation) and the choice of $h$, not the previously fixed coefficient fluctuation bound or $D$.

<a id="stmt-lem-cutoff-cone"></a>
<div id="lem:cutoff-cone" class="lemma">

**Lemma 67** (Iteration inside the slow cone). *Given $\xi_1>0$ and $\epsilon_0>0$, the preceding choices can be made so that, for $t$ an integer multiple of $D$, the gradient $p_0=dS_t(\sum_j u_jF_j)$ under any prepared law satisfies <a id="eq:cutoff-cone-output"></a>$$|A_0|\ge c e^{-(\lambda+\xi_1)t},\qquad
 \bigl(\mathbb E_{\nu_z}\left\lVert p_0-\widetilde E A_0\right\rVert^2\bigr)^{1/2}
       \le\epsilon_0|A_0|,
 \label{eq:cutoff-cone-output}$$ uniformly for $|u|=1$, $|z|<R_n$, and positive times $D\le t\le A\log n$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cutoff-cone"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cutoff-cone</summary>

*Proof.* The cone compares the full gradient norm with its mean slow coefficient. Assume $N_b\le K|A_b|$ at the end of a block. [eq:cutoff-alignment](#eq:cutoff-alignment) gives $$\begin{aligned}
 |A_a|&\ge(1-K\eta)e^{-\lambda D}|A_b|,\\
 N_a&\le C_E'|A_a|+\eta e^{-\lambda D}N_b
       \le\left(C_E'+\frac{K\eta}{1-K\eta}\right)|A_a|,
\end{aligned}$$ where $C_E'$ is arbitrarily close to $C_E$ after fine approximation. Choose $K\eta<1/4$ and then $\eta$ small enough that the last coefficient is at most $K$, and $K\eta/(1-K\eta)\le\epsilon_0$. Thus the cone is preserved. At the terminal time it holds by [eq:cutoff-terminal-cone](#eq:cutoff-terminal-cone). At each step, apply the fixed-interval restart in the proof of [prop:cutoff-coefficients](#prop:cutoff-coefficients) to the ordinary trajectory with initial block law $\nu_zS_a$. Its upper density bound follows from [eq:cutoff-preparation-density](#eq:cutoff-preparation-density), [eq:cutoff-restart-density](#eq:cutoff-restart-density), and its common Poincaré bound is the one fixed above. This restarts only the ordinary part of the evolution, leaving the preparation $T_h^z$ unchanged. At subsequent blocks the required forward norm ratio follows from the preceding cone step: $$\frac{N_{b+D}}{N_b}
 \le\frac{K C_Ae^{\lambda D}}{1-K\eta},
 \qquad |A_b|\le C_A N_b.$$ This ratio is finite for the already chosen block $D$. Its only role in [prop:cutoff-coefficients](#prop:cutoff-coefficients) is to establish exactness at the block endpoint, so its dependence on $D$ does not create a circular choice.

After $k=t/D$ steps, $$|A_0|\ge c_0(1-K\eta)^k e^{-\lambda t}
 =c_0e^{-[\lambda-D^{-1}\log(1-K\eta)]t}.$$ Take $D\ge1$ and $\eta\le\xi_1/(2K)$, so that the extra exponent is at most $\xi_1$. To verify the inverse-power cutoff throughout the iteration, choose $$Q>A(\lambda+\xi_1)+2.$$ The lower bound for $|A|$, and $|A|\le C_A N$, then keep $N$ above $n^{-Q}$ for all the $O(\log n)$ blocks. Choose the inverse-power accuracies used in the supporting Poincaré estimates larger than $2Q+H+2$. No new union bound over fixed-time limiting errors is needed: [eq:cutoff-alignment](#eq:cutoff-alignment) holds on one event uniformly over the functions, parameter values, and comparison times in question. The residual estimate in [eq:cutoff-cone-output](#eq:cutoff-cone-output) follows from the final cone step. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-cutoff-jacobian"></a>
<div id="lem:cutoff-jacobian" class="lemma">

**Lemma 68** (Preparation creates a ball of final means). *For sufficiently small fixed $h>0$ chosen after the fine recipes, the smooth map $$\mathcal M_t(z)=\bigl(\mu T_h^z S_tF_j\bigr)_{j=1}^m,
 \qquad |z|<R_n,$$ has Jacobian with smallest singular value at least <a id="eq:cutoff-jacobian"></a>$$\sigma_{\min}(D\mathcal M_t(z))
       \ge c h e^{-(\lambda+\xi_1)t}=:a_t.
 \label{eq:cutoff-jacobian}$$ Its image therefore contains the open Euclidean ball of radius $a_tR_n$ centered at $(\mu F_j)_{j=1}^m$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cutoff-jacobian"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cutoff-jacobian</summary>

*Proof.* We estimate the Jacobian in each unit output direction. For $|u|=1$, put $F=\sum_j u_jF_j$ and apply [eq:cutoff-cone-output](#eq:cutoff-cone-output) at the exit from preparation. Differentiation on the finite state space and Duhamel’s formula give the row vector <a id="eq:cutoff-duhamel-jacobian"></a>$$u^tD\mathcal M_t(z)
 =\int_0^h\mathbb E_{\mu T_s^z}
   \left[(dT_{h-s}^zS_tF)^tD_{v^z}\widetilde E\right]\,\mathrm ds,
 \qquad v_i^z=1-(m_i^z)^2.
 \label{eq:cutoff-duhamel-jacobian}$$ Indeed $\partial_{z_k}L^zf=
\sum_i v_i^z\widetilde E_{ik}d_if$, also when the target depends on the old spin.

Write $p_0=\widetilde E A_0+r$ under $\nu_z$. The rough vector extension behind [eq:cutoff-preparation-gradient](#eq:cutoff-preparation-gradient) propagates $r$ back through preparation at cost at most $e^{C_*h/2}$ in mean square. Its contribution to [eq:cutoff-duhamel-jacobian](#eq:cutoff-duhamel-jacobian) is therefore $O(h\epsilon_0|A_0|)$.

For the main vector, uniformly over $0\le s\le h$, <a id="eq:cutoff-short-continuity"></a>$$\left(\mathbb E_{\mu T_s^z}
   \left\lVert K_{h-s}^z\widetilde E-\widetilde E\right\rVert^2\right)^{1/2}
       \le\omega_{\widetilde E}(h)+o_n(1),
 \qquad \omega_{\widetilde E}(h)\longrightarrow0.
 \label{eq:cutoff-short-continuity}$$ Here the norm is the sum over the fixed number of columns. To verify this estimate, the diagonal likelihood representation has row moments bounded by $e^{C h}$, and its likelihood difference from one has squared mean $O(h)$, by the likelihood martingale bracket and the bounded row square sums. The entries of a fixed scaled recipe are bounded by $C/\sqrt n$, so this diagonal error costs $O(h)$ after summation. The part with at least one inserted coefficient matrix costs $O(h)$ in norm by its Duhamel expansion and the common rough bound. Finally the ordinary recipe value changes by $o_h(1)$ in spatial mean square along the short path: its smooth Euclidean extension has Lipschitz constant $C_{\widetilde E}/\sqrt n$, while the expected number of changed spins is at most $nh$. These estimates also apply to the perturbed rates, using [eq:cutoff-small-perturbation](#eq:cutoff-small-perturbation); the own-spin zero-order correction is $o_n(1)$. They prove [eq:cutoff-short-continuity](#eq:cutoff-short-continuity) without a regularity assertion for the exact eigenvectors.

By [eq:cutoff-preparation-density](#eq:cutoff-preparation-density), every marginal in this calculation has upper relative log-density $o(n)$. The one-state typicality comparisons, the chosen fine accuracy, and $\left\lVert v^z-v\right\rVert_\infty=o(1)$ therefore give $$\mathbb E_{\mu T_s^z}[\widetilde E^tD_{v^z}\widetilde E]
       =I+O(\delta_{\rm fine})+o_n(1)$$ uniformly in $s,z$. Combining this with [eq:cutoff-duhamel-jacobian](#eq:cutoff-duhamel-jacobian), [eq:cutoff-short-continuity](#eq:cutoff-short-continuity) yields $$\left|u^tD\mathcal M_t(z)-hA_0^t\right|
 \le Ch\bigl(\epsilon_0+\delta_{\rm fine}
                   +\omega_{\widetilde E}(h)+o_n(1)\bigr)|A_0|.$$ Choose $\epsilon_0$ and the fine accuracy first, and then choose a positive fixed $h$ so that the factor in parentheses is small. [eq:cutoff-cone-output](#eq:cutoff-cone-output) now proves [eq:cutoff-jacobian](#eq:cutoff-jacobian), uniformly for every unit output vector.

To pass from the Jacobian estimate to a ball of attainable means, we lift straight line segments by the inverse Jacobian. This argument requires only the proved singular-value bound, not global injectivity. For a target vector $v$ with $|v|<a_tR_n$, solve the inverse-Jacobian ordinary differential equation $$z'(r)=(D\mathcal M_t(z(r)))^{-1}v,\qquad z(0)=0,
 \qquad 0\le r\le1.$$ The right side is smooth and $|z'(r)|\le |v|/a_t<R_n$. The solution stays in a compact subball of the parameter ball and therefore exists to time one. Differentiation gives $\mathcal M_t(z(r))=\mathcal M_t(0)+rv$. At $z=0$ the preparation is ordinary stationary evolution, so $\mathcal M_t(0)=(\mu F_j)_j$. This proves the assertion. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-lem-cutoff-visible-lower"></a>
<div id="lem:cutoff-visible-lower" class="lemma">

**Lemma 69** (Lower cutoff for an isolated visible rate). *If $\lambda<\lambda_{\rm sp}$, the lower conclusion of [lem:cutoff-spin-lower](#lem:cutoff-spin-lower) still holds.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-lem-cutoff-visible-lower"><summary>Proof of stmt-lem-cutoff-visible-lower</summary>

*Proof.* Fix $0<\epsilon<1$, take $0<\alpha<\epsilon/8$ and $0<\xi_1<\lambda\epsilon/4$, and round $(1-\epsilon)t_n$ *up* to an integer multiple $t$ of $D$. The radius in [lem:cutoff-jacobian](#lem:cutoff-jacobian) is at least $$c h e^{-(\lambda+\xi_1)D}
 n^{\,1/2-\alpha-(1-\epsilon)(\lambda+\xi_1)/(2\lambda)}.$$ The exponent is positive, so the ball of attainable means has diverging radius. In particular, one may choose a preparation for which the mean of $F_1$ differs from $\mu F_1$ by a quantity tending to infinity. The variances of $F_1$ under $\nu_zS_t$ and $\mu$ are bounded: use the common trajectory Poincaré estimate and its bounded pointwise gradient for the first, and the equilibrium gap for the second. Chebyshev’s inequality implies $\left\lVert \nu_zS_t-\mu\right\rVert_{\mathop{\mathrm{TV}}}\to1$. Since $\nu_z$ is a probability law on starting configurations, convexity bounds this distance by $\sup_x\left\lVert S_t(x,\cdot)-\mu\right\rVert_{\mathop{\mathrm{TV}}}$. Monotonicity then gives the same lower bound at the unrounded, earlier time $(1-\epsilon)t_n$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-thm-cutoff-continuous"></a>
<div id="thm:cutoff-continuous" class="theorem">

**Theorem 70** (Continuous-time cutoff). *For every fixed $0<\beta<1$ and $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, put $t_n=\log n/(2\lambda)$. Then <a id="eq:cutoff-continuous"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \sup_x\left\lVert S_{(1-\epsilon)t_n}(x,\cdot)-\mu\right\rVert_{\mathop{\mathrm{TV}}}
       &\longrightarrow1,\\
 \sup_x\left\lVert S_{(1+\epsilon)t_n}(x,\cdot)-\mu\right\rVert_{\mathop{\mathrm{TV}}}
       &\longrightarrow0,
 \end{aligned}
 \label{eq:cutoff-continuous}$$ in probability over the disorder. The number $\lambda>0$ is given entirely by the dimension-first equilibrium construction in [eq:exact-lambda](#eq:exact-lambda).*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-thm-cutoff-continuous"><summary>Proof of stmt-thm-cutoff-continuous</summary>

*Proof.* The upper bound follows from [lem:cutoff-upper](#lem:cutoff-upper). For the lower bound, [lem:cutoff-spin-lower](#lem:cutoff-spin-lower) applies when $\lambda=\lambda_{\rm sp}$, and [lem:cutoff-visible-lower](#lem:cutoff-visible-lower) applies when $\lambda<\lambda_{\rm sp}$. These cases exhaust the definition of $\lambda$. ◻

</details>

supplies the continuous-time conclusion at $\beta=0$, with $\lambda(0)=1$. It remains to transfer both cases to the discrete update clock.

<a id="pm-h-61"></a>
#### The discrete update clock

<a id="stmt-prop-cutoff-clock"></a>
<div id="prop:cutoff-clock" class="proposition">

**Proposition 71** (Cutoff for single-site update attempts). *Let $P=I+L/n$, so one step selects a uniform site and refreshes its spin, including attempts that leave the state unchanged. For every fixed $0\le\beta<1$, its worst-case total-variation cutoff is at $$\frac{n\log n}{2\lambda(\beta)},$$ in probability over the disorder.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-prop-cutoff-clock"><summary>Proof of stmt-prop-cutoff-clock</summary>

*Proof.* We prove both directions of clock transfer. Write $d_c(t)$ and $d_d(k)$ for the continuous and discrete distances; their kernels satisfy the exact Poissonization identity $S_t=e^{nt(P-I)}$. For $k=\lfloor(1-\epsilon)nt_n\rfloor$ and $T=(1-\epsilon/2)t_n$, convexity and discrete-time contraction give $$d_c(T)\le\mathbb P\{\operatorname{Poisson}(nT)<k\}+d_d(k).$$ The probability is $O((nt_n)^{-1})$, while $d_c(T)\to1$, proving the discrete lower bound.

=3em For the upper bound, a uniform holding probability permits the local Poisson-to-binomial lemma. Restrict to the high-probability event $\left\lVert J\right\rVert_\mathrm{op}\le K$. At every configuration, $n^{-1}\sum_i(Jx)_i^2\le K^2$, so at least half of the fields have absolute value at most $\sqrt2K$. The probability of keeping a selected spin is at least $(1+e^{2|(Jx)_i|})^{-1}$. Consequently

<a id="eq:cutoff-holding"></a>$$P(x,x)\ge h_0:=\frac1{2(1+e^{2\sqrt2K})}>0.
 \label{eq:cutoff-holding}$$ Choose $\vartheta=1-h_0/2\in(0,1)$ and write $$P=(1-\vartheta)I+\vartheta R,
 \qquad S_t=e^{\vartheta nt(R-I)}.$$ Here $R$ is a Markov kernel preserving $\mu$. Set $M=\lceil(1+\epsilon)nt_n\rceil$. For every $x$ and $|f|\le1$, put $u_j=R^jf(x)-\mu f$, so $|u_j|\le2$. For each fixed real $y$, $$\mathbb Eu_{\operatorname{Poisson}(\vartheta M+y\sqrt M)}
 =S_{M/n+y\sqrt M/(\vartheta n)}f(x)-\mu f.$$ The time correction is $O_y(\sqrt{\log n/n})$, and hence this time exceeds $(1+\epsilon/2)t_n$ for large $n$. The absolute value of the display is bounded by $2d_c((1+\epsilon/2)t_n)\to0$, uniformly over $x,f$.

We have verified every shifted Poisson average required by [lem:input-clock](#lem:input-clock), uniformly over starts and tests. Apply that uniform transfer: its assumptions are a fixed $\vartheta\in(0,1)$, $M\to\infty$, bounded arrays, and vanishing Poisson averages for every fixed shift $y$, all just verified. It gives $$\mathbb Eu_{\operatorname{Binomial}(M,\vartheta)}
       =P^Mf(x)-\mu f\longrightarrow0$$ uniformly over the test family. Taking half its supremum proves $d_d(M)\to0$. For convergence in disorder probability, the proof of that lemma uses a fixed finite signed approximation by shifted Gaussian densities; its finitely many Poisson averages are all bounded by the same random quantity $2d_c((1+\epsilon/2)t_n)$. Thus it applies on the present high-probability events without any additional convergence rate. ◻

</details>

<a id="sec:rcut-introduction"></a>
### An independent gradient argument below one half

These appendices prove cutoff for $0\le\beta<1/2$ by following the unweighted gradient along the heat-bath dynamics. The proof places the median mixing time on the logarithmic scale and shows that the total-variation transition has vanishing relative width. The central estimate is pointwise: the gradient dissipates at a fixed positive rate outside a set of exponentially small Gibbs mass. Entropy decay first makes that exceptional set unlikely, and smoothing over a positive logarithmic lag then converts gradient control into the cutoff ratio.

This argument also yields estimates with uses beyond its cutoff conclusion. They include a spectral-gap and covariance bound uniform over external fields and interaction scalings, and the scalar variational bound $0.9969$ with its complete analytic and arithmetic certificate. The proof is independent of the limiting exact-gradient operator used in the full high-temperature argument.

Keep the model, half-differences, and two clock conventions of Section <a href="#sec:model" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:model">2</a>. Write $\mathbb P_J$ for the interaction-matrix law and abbreviate the worst-start total-variation distances by $d_c(t)=d_n(t)$ and $d_d(k)=d_n^{\rm disc}(k)$. We will use the two gradient densities and the median mixing time $$U(f)=\sum_i(d_i f)^2,\qquad
 \Gamma(f)=\sum_iw_i(d_i f)^2,\qquad
 t_n^{\rm med}=\inf\{t\ge0:d_c(t)\le1/2\}.$$ The weights are $w_i=1-x_i\tanh((Jx)_i)$. Expanding the square at each spin flip gives the identity <a id="rcut:eq:variance-density"></a>$$L(f^2)-2fLf=2\Gamma(f)
 \label{rcut:eq:variance-density}$$ For a probability measure $\nu$ and an integrable function $f$, write $\nu f=\int f\,d\nu$. All vector and matrix norms in these appendices are Euclidean and Euclidean operator norms, respectively, unless explicitly specified. We continue to write $\mathbb P_x$ and $\mathbb E_x$ for chain probabilities and expectations after fixing the disorder.

<a id="stmt-rcut-thm-main"></a>
<div id="rcut:thm:main" class="theorem">

**Theorem 72**. *For every fixed $\beta\in[0,1/2)$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, and $\eta>0$, let $$t_{n,\beta,J}(\varepsilon)=\min\{k\ge0:d_d(k)\le\varepsilon\}.$$ Then $$\mathbb P_J\left\{
 \frac{t_{n,\beta,J}(\varepsilon)}
 {t_{n,\beta,J}(1-\varepsilon)}>1+\eta\right\}\longrightarrow0.$$ The denominator is positive for sufficiently large $n$.*

</div>

The denominator is eventually positive because $d_d(0)=1-\min_x\mu(x)\ge1-2^{-n}$. We prove the stated ratio directly; the full-phase theorem is not an input to this appendix argument.

The proof has three stages. Section <a href="#rcut:sec:entropy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:entropy">11</a> starts with a uniform two-spin inequality, obtains the gap under all external fields and interaction scalings, and passes from that gap to entropy decay by Gaussian observations. Section <a href="#rcut:sec:gradient" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:gradient">12</a> expresses the pointwise gradient dissipation as a matrix inequality. The matrix comparison in Section <a href="#rcut:sec:comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:comparison">13</a> and the scalar estimate in Section <a href="#rcut:sec:scalar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:scalar">14</a> establish that inequality outside an exponentially small Gibbs set. Finally, Sections <a href="#rcut:sec:dynamics" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:dynamics">15</a> and <a href="#rcut:sec:cutoff" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:cutoff">16</a> use concentration and positive-lag smoothing to prove the cutoff ratio, invoking the general jump-moment and clock lemmas stated in Section <a href="#sec:model" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:model">2</a>. Section <a href="#rcut:sec:scalar-certificate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:scalar-certificate">17</a> supplies every quadrature and arithmetic enclosure used in the scalar estimate.

The temperature parameter $\beta$ remains fixed throughout, and constants may depend on it. Whenever an estimate is used on a logarithmic time horizon, its times are at most $D_*\log n$, with $D_*<\infty$ chosen before taking $n\to\infty$.

<a id="rcut:sec:entropy"></a>
### Uniform spectral and entropy estimates

The entropy estimate needed for the independent cutoff argument rests on a spectral gap that survives both changes of external field and reductions of the interaction strength. We prove this gap by summing a signed two-spin inequality, then pass to entropy through Gaussian observations. The observation posterior changes both the field and the interaction, which is why both uniformities are needed. Throughout this section, the inverse temperature $\beta<1/2$ is fixed.

<a id="pm-h-64"></a>
#### Gaussian estimates and a good disorder event

We first collect the Gaussian tools used to control the operator norm, the row-square sums, and the largest entry of the interaction matrix. These three controls will make the two-spin error summable on a single disorder event.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-gaussian-facts"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:gaussian-facts" class="lemma">

**Lemma 73** (Gaussian concentration and comparison). *Let $Z$ be a vector of independent standard real Gaussian variables. If $F$ is $D$-Lipschitz in Euclidean distance, then <a id="rcut:eq:gaussian-mgf"></a>$$\mathbb E\exp\bigl(s(F(Z)-\mathbb EF(Z))\bigr)
 \le \exp\left(\frac{\pi^2D^2s^2}{8}\right),
 \qquad s\in\mathbb R.
 \label{rcut:eq:gaussian-mgf}$$ In particular, for $D>0$ and $r>0$, $$\mathbb P\bigl(|F(Z)-\mathbb EF(Z)|\ge r\bigr)
 \le 2\exp\left(-\frac{2r^2}{\pi^2D^2}\right).$$ If $(X_a)_{a\in I}$ and $(Y_a)_{a\in I}$ are centered Gaussian processes on the same finite index set and $$\mathbb E(X_a-X_b)^2\le \mathbb E(Y_a-Y_b)^2
 \quad\text{for all }a,b\in I,$$ then $\mathbb E\max_a X_a\le\mathbb E\max_a Y_a$. The comparison also holds for continuous processes on a compact metric index set when their suprema are integrable.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-gaussian-facts"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-gaussian-facts</summary>

*Proof.* For the concentration estimate, we use the Maurey–Pisier Gaussian rotation and double-Jensen argument; see Giraud (Giraud 2021, Exercise 1.6.7, equation (1.10), parts A–B) <a id="pm-cite-44"></a>[[Giraud2021](#ref-Giraud2021)]. Rotation between two independent Gaussian vectors expresses the increment as an integral of directional derivatives. First take $F$ smooth with $\|\nabla F\|\le D$. Let $Z'$ be an independent copy of $Z$ and define the rotation by $$Z_\theta=Z\cos\theta+Z'\sin\theta,
 \qquad V_\theta=-Z\sin\theta+Z'\cos\theta,
 \qquad 0\le\theta\le\pi/2.$$ For a fixed angle, $Z_\theta$ and $V_\theta$ are independent standard Gaussian vectors. This independence lets us evaluate the exponential moment after applying Jensen’s inequality, first in $Z'$ and then with respect to the uniform measure on $[0,\pi/2]$: $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb Ee^{s(F(Z)-\mathbb EF(Z))}
 &\le \mathbb Ee^{s(F(Z)-F(Z'))}\\
 &\le \frac2\pi\int_0^{\pi/2}
     \mathbb E\exp\left(-\frac{\pi s}{2}
             \nabla F(Z_\theta)\cdot V_\theta\right)\,d\theta
 \le e^{\pi^2D^2s^2/8}.
\end{aligned}$$ To pass to a general Lipschitz $F$, smooth by convolution and use dominated convergence. Linear growth gives the Gaussian exponential integrability required for this passage. Optimization of the exponential Markov bound then gives the tail estimate. The case $D=0$ follows directly because the function is constant.

For the comparison statement, we interpolate independent realizations of the two processes and show that the expected maximum increases along the interpolation. For $\lambda>0$, replace the maximum by the smooth function $$\Phi_\lambda(z)=\lambda^{-1}\log\sum_{a\in I}e^{\lambda z_a}.$$ Gaussian integration by parts gives $$\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E\Phi_\lambda
       \bigl(\sqrt{1-t}\,X+\sqrt t\,Y\bigr)
 =\frac12\sum_{a,b}B_{ab}\,\mathbb E(\partial_{ab}\Phi_\lambda),
 \qquad B=\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}(Y)-\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}(X).$$ The Hessian has zero row sums and nonpositive off-diagonal entries. Consequently the derivative can be expressed using only increment variances. With $\Delta_{ab}=B_{aa}+B_{bb}-2B_{ab}$ denoting their difference, the right side becomes $$-\frac14\sum_{a,b}\Delta_{ab}\,\mathbb E(\partial_{ab}\Phi_\lambda)\ge0.$$ The limit $\lambda\to\infty$ gives the finite-set comparison. Exhausting a dense set by finite subsets and using continuity and dominated convergence gives the compact-set version. In the applications below, every such process is a linear function of a finite Gaussian vector, which ensures integrability of its supremum. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-good-disorder"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:good-disorder" class="proposition">

<a id="rcut:eq:good-disorder"></a>
**Proposition 74** (Good disorder). *There are deterministic numbers $\delta_n\downarrow0$ and events $\mathcal E_n=\mathcal E_n(\beta)$ with $\mathbb P(\mathcal E_n)\to1$ such that on $\mathcal E_n$, $$\|J\|\le2\beta+\delta_n,
 \qquad \max_i\sum_jJ_{ij}^2\le\beta^2+\delta_n,
 \qquad \max_{i,j}|J_{ij}|\le\delta_n.
 \label{rcut:eq:good-disorder}$$ Consequently, on the same events, $$\max_i\sum_j|J_{ij}|^3\longrightarrow0.$$ One may take $\delta_n=n^{-1/4}$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-good-disorder"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-good-disorder</summary>

*Proof.* We prove the operator-norm estimate first and then control the row sums and individual entries. The case $\beta=0$ is deterministic. For $\beta>0$, add independent diagonal entries of variance $2\beta^2/n$ to $J$. The resulting centered Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE) matrix $W$ has a covariance that permits a direct Gaussian comparison: for unit vectors $p,q$, $$\mathbb E[(p^{\mathsf T}Wp)(q^{\mathsf T}Wq)]
 =\frac{2\beta^2}{n}(p^{\mathsf T}q)^2.$$ With $\rho=p^{\mathsf T}q$, the increment variance of $p^{\mathsf T}Wp$ is $4\beta^2(1-\rho^2)/n$. Bound it by $8\beta^2(1-\rho)/n$ and compare with the linear process $(2\beta/\sqrt n)p^{\mathsf T}z$, where $z$ is a standard Gaussian vector. Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gaussian-facts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gaussian-facts">73</a> yields $$\mathbb E\lambda_{\max}(W)
 \le\frac{2\beta}{\sqrt n}\mathbb E\|z\|\le2\beta.$$ In the independent standard Gaussian coordinates defining $W$, the quadratic form $p^{\mathsf T}Wp$ is Lipschitz with constant $\sqrt2\beta/\sqrt n$, uniformly over unit vectors. The supremum inherits this constant. Concentration for $\lambda_{\max}(W)$ and $\lambda_{\max}(-W)$ therefore bounds $\|W\|$ by $2\beta+\delta_n/2$ with probability tending to one. The largest absolute diagonal entry is at most $\delta_n/2$ with probability tending to one as well. Removing that diagonal proves the first estimate in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:good-disorder" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:good-disorder">[rcut:eq:good-disorder]</a>.

For a standard Gaussian $g$, $$\mathbb Ee^{\theta(g^2-1)}=e^{-\theta}(1-2\theta)^{-1/2}
 \le e^{C\theta^2},\qquad |\theta|\le1/4.$$ Apply the exponential Markov bound to the $n-1$ independent squares in one row. The probability that their weighted sum exceeds $\beta^2+\delta_n$ is at most $\exp(-c_\beta n\delta_n^2)$ for large $n$. A union bound over the rows gives the second estimate; Gaussian tails and a union bound over entries give the third. The choice $n\delta_n^2=\sqrt n$ makes all the failure probabilities vanish. The cubic row sums needed for the two-spin remainder are now controlled by the last two estimates together: $$\max_i\sum_j|J_{ij}|^3
 \le \left(\max_{i,j}|J_{ij}|\right)
       \left(\max_i\sum_jJ_{ij}^2\right)
 \le\delta_n(\beta^2+\delta_n).$$ ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-65"></a>
#### A two-spin estimate and a uniform gap

We next prove an inequality for a pair of sites and sum it over the set of site pairs to obtain the gap. The pair estimate must remain uniform when a one-site conditional variance is small. For an Ising law $\nu$ with symmetric, zero-diagonal interaction matrix $A$ and external field $\theta\in\mathbb R^n$, write $$\nu(x)\propto\exp\left(\frac12x^{\mathsf T}Ax+\theta\cdot x\right),
 \qquad m_i=\mathbb E_\nu[X_i\mid X_{-i}],\qquad v_i=1-m_i^2.$$ All notation in this subsection refers to this law. To express the one-site energies as squared projection norms, let $E_i$ be conditional expectation given the spins outside $i$, and put $$\mathsf D_i=I-E_i,\qquad \mathsf D_i f=(x_i-m_i)d_i f.$$ These are orthogonal projections in $L^2(\nu)$, and $$\nu[(\mathsf D_i f)^2]=\nu[v_i(d_i f)^2],
 \qquad -L_\nu=\sum_i\mathsf D_i,$$ where $L_\nu$ is the heat-bath generator with rate one at every site.

The signed two-spin estimate below follows the gap method of Wang (Wang 2026, Theorem 1.2 and Lemma 3.4) <a id="pm-cite-45"></a>[[Wang2026](#ref-Wang2026)]. Keeping the sign of the leading interaction term allows the later summation to use an operator norm. We give the algebra and the remainder estimate that make this summation uniform in the external fields and the interaction scale.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-two-spin"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:two-spin" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:two-spin"></a>
**Lemma 75** (Uniform two-spin inequality). *There are absolute constants $t_0>0$ and $C_0<\infty$ with the following property. For any finite-field Ising law $\nu$, any distinct $i,j$ with $t=\tanh A_{ij}$ satisfying $|t|\le t_0$, and any real function $f$, $$\begin{aligned}
 \nu[\mathsf D_i f\mathsf D_j f]
 &\ge-\nu\bigl[(t+2t^2m_i m_j)v_i v_jd_i f d_j f\bigr]\notag\\
 &\hspace{1cm}-C_0|t|^3\nu\bigl[(\mathsf D_i f)^2+(\mathsf D_j f)^2\bigr].
 \label{rcut:eq:two-spin}
\end{aligned}$$ The constants are independent of all external fields and of the dimension. For example, $t_0=1/100$ and $C_0=22000$ are valid.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-two-spin"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-two-spin</summary>

*Proof.* The proof has three steps: factor out the two conditional variances, identify the nonnegative part of the expansion, and absorb the cubic remainder into the one-site energies. Condition on all spins outside $i,j$, and denote the remaining spins by $x,y$. Their probabilities are $$\frac{(1+ax)(1+by)(1+txy)}{4(1+abt)},
 \qquad |a|,|b|<1,$$ where $a,b$ are the hyperbolic tangents of the external fields left after conditioning. Set $Z_0=1+abt$. The corresponding conditional means and variances take the form $$m_i(y)=\frac{a+ty}{1+aty},\qquad
 v_i(y)=\frac{(1-a^2)(1-t^2)}{(1+aty)^2},$$ and the analogous expressions with $a,x$ and $b,y$ interchanged. There are real numbers $p,q,r$ such that $$d_i f=p+r(y-b),\qquad d_j f=q+r(x-a).$$ Indeed, expand the restriction of $f$ in the basis $1,x,y,xy$ and denote the coefficient of $xy$ by $r$. This isolates the common second-difference coefficient from the two first differences.

<a id="rcut:eq:two-spin-expansion"></a>
Let $\mathbb E_0$ denote uniform expectation over the four pairs $(x,y)$. We now combine the mixed projection energy with the correction term in the claimed inequality. The identities $$x-m_i(y)=\frac{(x-a)(1-txy)}{1+aty},
 \qquad (1+ax)(x-a)=x(1-a^2)$$ and their counterparts for $y$ give the exact factorization $$\begin{aligned}
 &\nu[\mathsf D_i f\mathsf D_j f\mid X_{-\{i,j\}}]
 +\nu[(t+2t^2m_i m_j)v_i v_jd_i f d_j f\mid X_{-\{i,j\}}]
   =P_0Q,\\
 &P_0=\frac{(1-a^2)(1-b^2)(1-t^2)}{Z_0},\qquad
 Q=\mathbb E_0\bigl([p+r(y-b)][q+r(x-a)]C(t;x,y)\bigr),
\end{aligned}$$ where $$\begin{aligned}
 C(t;x,y)
 ={}&\frac{xy-t}{(1+aty)(1+btx)}\\
 &+(t+2t^2m_i(y)m_j(x))
  \frac{(1-t^2)(1+ax)(1+by)(1+txy)}
       {(1+aty)^2(1+btx)^2}.
\end{aligned}$$ Only the expansion through second order will contribute to the leading term. Expanding at $t=0$ and reducing by $x^2=y^2=1$ gives $$C(t;x,y)
 =xy\left[1+ab t+(1-a^2-b^2+2a^2b^2)t^2\right]
   +R(t;x,y).
 \label{rcut:eq:two-spin-expansion}$$ The cancellation can be checked directly: before collecting terms, the coefficient of $t^2$ is $$d+xy(d^2-abxy)+(1+ax)(1+by)(xy-2d+2ab),
 \qquad d=ay+bx.$$ Collecting terms gives the coefficient in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:two-spin-expansion" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:two-spin-expansion">[rcut:eq:two-spin-expansion]</a>, with the coefficients of $1,x,y$ cancelling. Thus the displayed expansion contributes through the following single identity: $$\mathbb E_0\bigl(xy[p+r(y-b)][q+r(x-a)]\bigr)=r^2.$$

It remains to control the remainder without excluding nearly deterministic spins; we therefore allow the limiting values $|a|=|b|=1$ in this estimate. On the complex disk $|t|\le1/2$, the denominators $1+aty$ and $1+btx$ have modulus at least $1/2$, while $|m_i(y)|,|m_j(x)|\le3$. The first term of $C$ is bounded in modulus by $6$. In the second term, $t+2t^2m_i m_j$ is bounded by $5$; including its remaining factors gives a bound of $600$. Hence $|C(t;x,y)|\le606$ throughout the disk, and Cauchy’s coefficient estimate yields $$|R(t;x,y)|\le606\sum_{k\ge3}(2|t|)^k
 \le9696|t|^3,\qquad |t|\le1/4.$$ Since $$|[p+r(y-b)][q+r(x-a)]|\le p^2+q^2+8r^2$$ and $1-a^2-b^2+2a^2b^2=a^2b^2+(1-a^2)(1-b^2)\ge0$, we obtain $$Q\ge\bigl(1-|t|-8\cdot9696|t|^3\bigr)r^2
          -9696|t|^3(p^2+q^2).$$ For $|t|\le1/100$, the coefficient of $r^2$ exceeds $1/2$.

The leading term is now nonnegative. To finish, the negative cubic term must be charged to the conditional energies while retaining the variance factors. Write $A_0=1-a^2$ and $B_0=1-b^2$. Summing over $x$ first gives the exact energy formula $$\nu[v_i(d_i f)^2\mid X_{-\{i,j\}}]
 =\frac{A_0(1-t^2)}{2Z_0}
   \sum_{y=\pm1}\frac{1+by}{1+aty}[p+r(y-b)]^2.$$ For $|t|\le1/4$, the denominators lie between $3/4$ and $5/4$, so $$\begin{aligned}
 \nu[v_i(d_i f)^2\mid X_{-\{i,j\}}]
 &\ge\frac35 A_0(p^2+B_0r^2),\\
 \nu[v_j(d_j f)^2\mid X_{-\{i,j\}}]
 &\ge\frac35 B_0(q^2+A_0r^2),\qquad
 P_0\le\frac43A_0B_0.
\end{aligned}$$ These bounds make $P_0p^2$ and $P_0q^2$ at most $20/9$ times their respective conditional energies. Multiply the estimate for $Q$ by $P_0$ and use $9696\cdot20/9<22000$ to obtain the conditional inequality. Averaging over the spins on which we conditioned gives Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:two-spin" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:two-spin">[rcut:eq:two-spin]</a>. The estimates are homogeneous in $p,q,r$, and throughout the argument neither these coefficients nor the external fields were bounded. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-uniform-gap"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:uniform-gap" class="proposition">

**Proposition 76** (Gap and covariance under scaled interactions and fields). *For all sufficiently large $n$, uniformly over $J\in\mathcal E_n$, $s\in[0,1]$, and $\theta\in\mathbb R^n$, let $$\nu_{s,\theta}(x)\propto
 \exp\left(\frac s2x^{\mathsf T}Jx+\theta\cdot x\right).$$ Its rate-one-per-site heat-bath generator has spectral gap at least $$\kappa_\beta=\frac{1-2\beta}{2}>0.$$ Moreover, <a id="rcut:eq:uniform-gap-covariance"></a>$$\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\nu_{s,\theta}}(f)
 \le\kappa_\beta^{-1}\sum_i
       \nu_{s,\theta}[v_i(d_i f)^2],
 \qquad
 \|\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_{\nu_{s,\theta}}(X)\|\le\kappa_\beta^{-1}.
 \label{rcut:eq:uniform-gap-covariance}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-uniform-gap"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-uniform-gap</summary>

*Proof.* We use the pair estimate to compare the squared generator with its Dirichlet form. Fix $\nu=\nu_{s,\theta}$ and define the zero-diagonal matrix by $T_{ij}=\tanh(sJ_{ij})$. On $\mathcal E_n$, all entries are small enough for Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:two-spin" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:two-spin">75</a> to apply simultaneously. At each configuration put $z_i=v_i d_i f$ and $z'_i=m_i z_i$. Summation over ordered pairs gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \left\|\sum_i\mathsf D_i f\right\|_{L^2(\nu)}^2
 \ge{}&\sum_i\|\mathsf D_i f\|_{L^2(\nu)}^2
       -\nu[z^{\mathsf T}Tz+2(z')^{\mathsf T}(T\circ T)z']\\
 &-2C_0\left(\max_i\sum_j|T_{ij}|^3\right)
               \sum_i\|\mathsf D_i f\|_{L^2(\nu)}^2,
\end{aligned}$$ where $\circ$ denotes entrywise multiplication. The field-dependent factors remain inside the vectors, so the interaction matrices can be bounded by their operator norms. With $M=\max(\|T\|,2\|T\circ T\|)$, the sum of the two quadratic forms is at most $$M\sum_i v_i^2(1+m_i^2)(d_i f)^2
 \le M\sum_i v_i(d_i f)^2,$$ because $v_i^2(1+m_i^2)=v_i(1-m_i^4)\le v_i$.

We next control these operator norms using only the disorder event. The Taylor estimate $|\tanh u-u|\le C|u|^3$, together with the maximum absolute row-sum bound for symmetric matrices, gives $$\|T-sJ\|\le C\max_i\sum_j|J_{ij}|^3=o(1).$$ Also $\|T\circ T\|\le\max_i\sum_jT_{ij}^2\le\beta^2+o(1)$. The error bounds depend only on the deterministic tolerances defining the event; they are uniform over $s,\theta$ and $J\in\mathcal E_n$. The fixed assumption $\beta<1/2$ therefore gives $$M\le\max(2\beta,2\beta^2)+o(1)=2\beta+o(1).$$ Thus, for $A=-L_\nu=\sum_i\mathsf D_i$ and all sufficiently large $n$, $$\|Af\|_2^2\ge\kappa_\beta\langle f,Af\rangle_\nu.$$ To read this as a spectral gap, use that $A$ is self-adjoint and nonnegative. Every one-site conditional law has full support, so $\mathsf D_i f=0$ for all $i$ forces $f$ to be constant along every edge of the cube. Thus the kernel consists exactly of constants. Applied to a nonconstant eigenfunction, the last inequality bounds its eigenvalue below by $\kappa_\beta$. This proves the gap and variance assertions. The covariance conclusion is the linear-function case $f(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x$: $$c^{\mathsf T}\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_\nu(X)c
 \le\kappa_\beta^{-1}\sum_i\nu[v_i]c_i^2
 \le\kappa_\beta^{-1}\|c\|^2.$$ ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-66"></a>
#### Entropy through Gaussian observations

We now turn the uniform covariance estimate into entropy dissipation. For a probability measure $\nu$ and a positive function $f$, the homogeneous entropy functional is $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\nu(f)=\nu[f\log f]-\nu[f]\log\nu[f].$$ The convention $0\log0=0$ extends it to nonnegative functions. Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:entropy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:entropy">77</a> imposes no normalization on $f$. The proof uses the Gaussian observation entropy factorization principle of Chen and Eldan (Y. Chen and Eldan 2025, Theorem 49 in arXiv:2203.04163v2) <a id="pm-cite-46"></a>[[CE2025](#ref-CE2025)]. We include the argument to keep the interaction scaling and the rate-one-per-site clock explicit.

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-entropy"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:entropy" class="proposition">

<a id="rcut:eq:entropy-inequality"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:entropy-decay"></a>
**Proposition 77** (Entropy inequality and reduction from point starts). *There are constants $C_1,C_2<\infty$, depending only on the fixed $\beta<1/2$, such that for all sufficiently large $n$ and $J\in\mathcal E_n$, the zero-field Gibbs measure satisfies $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(f)\le C_1\mu\bigl[f(-L)\log f\bigr],
 \qquad f>0.
 \label{rcut:eq:entropy-inequality}$$ For every initial point $x$ and every $t\ge0$, if $\rho_{t,x}=S_t(x,\cdot)$, then $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu\left(\frac{d\rho_{t,x}}{d\mu}\right)
 \le C_2n e^{-t/C_1}.
 \label{rcut:eq:entropy-decay}$$ In particular, the continuous-time worst-start mixing time at every fixed positive accuracy is $O_\beta(\log n)$, uniformly on these events.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-entropy"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-entropy</summary>

<a id="rcut:eq:gaussian-posterior"></a>
*Proof.* We interpolate from the Gibbs measure to product posteriors, compare their expected entropy with the initial entropy, and then remove the observation from the one-site terms. For large $n$, Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:good-disorder" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:good-disorder">[rcut:eq:good-disorder]</a> ensures $\|J\|<1$. Choose $K=J+2I$; then $K$ is positive definite and satisfies $\|K\|<3$. Keep it fixed throughout the argument for the realized disorder. Given $X\sim\mu$ and an independent standard Gaussian vector $z$, use the observation, for $0<u\le1$, $$Y_u=uK^{1/2}X+\sqrt u\,z.$$ The posterior law $\nu_{u,y}=\operatorname{Law}(X\mid Y_u=y)$ is $$\nu_{u,y}(x)\propto\mu(x)
    \exp\left(y^{\mathsf T}K^{1/2}x-\frac u2x^{\mathsf T}Kx\right).
 \label{rcut:eq:gaussian-posterior}$$ Discarding the diagonal term, which is constant on the cube, leaves interaction matrix $(1-u)J$. The observation creates an external field, and a further linear tilt changes only that field. Thus both uniformities in Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:uniform-gap" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:uniform-gap">76</a> apply: every posterior and every such tilt has covariance norm at most $C=\kappa_\beta^{-1}$. At $u=1$, the interaction vanishes and the posterior is a product measure.

<a id="rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-derivative"></a>
*Derivative of the expected posterior entropy.* To quantify the entropy lost to the observation, set $H(u)=\mathbb E[\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\nu_{u,Y_u}}(f)]$. The derivative identity we need is $$H'(u)=-\frac12\mathbb E\left[
       \frac{\|K^{1/2}\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_{\nu_{u,Y_u}}(X,f)\|^2}
            {\nu_{u,Y_u}[f]}\right].
 \label{rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-derivative}$$ The covariance with $f$ here is a vector. We verify the identity using the finite Gaussian mixture defining the observation. Let $\phi_u$ be the centered Gaussian density with covariance $uI$, and define $$\begin{aligned}
 q(u,y)&=\sum_x\mu(x)
       e^{y^{\mathsf T}K^{1/2}x-u x^{\mathsf T}Kx/2},\\
 p(u,y)&=\sum_x\mu(x)f(x)
       e^{y^{\mathsf T}K^{1/2}x-u x^{\mathsf T}Kx/2}.
\end{aligned}$$ These functions give the density of $Y_u$ as $q\phi_u$ and the posterior expectation as $p/q=\nu_{u,y}[f]$. Their finite exponential sums show directly that both $p$ and $q$ solve the backward heat equation: $$(\partial_u+\tfrac12\Delta_y)p=0,\qquad
 (\partial_u+\tfrac12\Delta_y)q=0.$$ Writing $r=p/q$, the chain rule gives the exact identity $$(\partial_u+\tfrac12\Delta_y)\bigl(p\log(p/q)\bigr)
     =\frac12\frac{q\|\nabla_y r\|^2}{r}.$$ Since $\partial_u\phi_u=\tfrac12\Delta_y\phi_u$, differentiation and integration by parts yield $$\frac{d}{du}\int p\log(p/q)\,\phi_u\,dy
   =\frac12\int\frac{q\|\nabla_y r\|^2}{r}\phi_u\,dy.$$ Differentiation and integration by parts are legitimate: the spin sums are finite, $f$ is bounded above and below by positive constants, and the remaining dependence on $y$ grows at most exponentially in $\|y\|$. Gaussian tails therefore control all terms. To identify the derivative as the claimed covariance expression, use $$H(u)=\mu[f\log f]-\int p\log(p/q)\phi_u\,dy,
 \qquad \nabla_y r=K^{1/2}\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_{\nu_{u,y}}(X,f),$$ which proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-derivative" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-derivative">[rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-derivative]</a>. At the initial endpoint $u\downarrow0$, the observations tend to zero in probability and the posterior tends to $\mu$. Since the entropy functional is bounded on this finite space, $H(u)\to\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(f)$, giving the initial value for the comparison.

<a id="rcut:eq:covariance-entropy"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-comparison"></a>
*Covariance controlled by entropy.* We next bound the derivative by the expected entropy itself. Let $\nu$ be any posterior, take a unit vector $a$, and set $Z=a^{\mathsf T}(X-\nu[X])$. The second derivative of the log moment-generating function of $Z$ is the variance of $a^{\mathsf T}X$ under a linear tilt of $\nu$. Applying the uniform covariance estimate to these tilts and integrating twice gives $$\log\nu[e^{\lambda Z}]\le\frac C2\lambda^2,
 \qquad \lambda\in\mathbb R.$$ The change of measure $\widehat\nu=f\nu/\nu[f]$ connects this exponential-moment bound to entropy. Apply Jensen’s inequality to the logarithm under $\widehat\nu$ to obtain $$\lambda\widehat\nu[Z]
 \le\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\nu(f)}{\nu[f]}+
       \log\nu[e^{\lambda Z}]
 \le\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\nu(f)}{\nu[f]}+\frac C2\lambda^2.$$ Optimize in $\lambda$ and take $a$ parallel to $\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_\nu(X,f)$ when this vector is nonzero. This yields $$\|\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}_\nu(X,f)\|^2\le2C\nu[f]\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\nu(f).
 \label{rcut:eq:covariance-entropy}$$ Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-derivative" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-derivative">[rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-derivative]</a> and <a href="#rcut:eq:covariance-entropy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:covariance-entropy">[rcut:eq:covariance-entropy]</a> imply $H'(u)\ge-C\|K\|H(u)$. Integrating from zero to one gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(f)\le e^{C\|K\|}H(1)\le e^{3C}H(1).
 \label{rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-comparison}$$ We have now compared the initial entropy with the entropy at the product endpoint. The comparison used covariance control at every interaction scale: controlling linear tilts only at the original interaction $J$ would leave the quadratic change in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gaussian-posterior" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gaussian-posterior">[rcut:eq:gaussian-posterior]</a> untreated. It remains to express the endpoint entropy in terms of the original one-site energies.

*Removing the observation at the product endpoint.* For a product probability measure $\pi=\bigotimes_i\pi_i$, entropy tensorizes: $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\pi(f)\le\sum_i\pi[\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\pi_i}(f)],$$ where in the $i$th summand the other coordinates are fixed inside the one-coordinate entropy. To prove tensorization, separate one coordinate using the entropy chain rule and apply induction to the remaining product. For a fixed base measure, $f\mapsto\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}(f)$ is convex; hence averaging the separated coordinate can only decrease the remaining one-coordinate entropies. The required convexity follows from joint convexity of $(a,b)\mapsto a\log(a/b)$ with $a=f(x)$ and $b=\pi[f]$.

Apply tensorization to the product posterior at $u=1$. We must then average under the joint law of $(X,Y_1)$, retaining the dependence between the observation and the spins. For this step put $F=f(X)$, $\varphi(z)=z\log z$, $$\mathcal G_i=\sigma(X_{-i}),\qquad
 \mathcal H_i=\sigma(X_{-i},Y_1),\qquad
 e_{\mathcal A}(F)=\mathbb E[\varphi(F)\mid\mathcal A]
                   -\varphi(\mathbb E[F\mid\mathcal A]).$$ Conditional Jensen and the tower property give $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E[e_{\mathcal H_i}(F)\mid\mathcal G_i]
 &=\mathbb E[\varphi(F)\mid\mathcal G_i]
   -\mathbb E[\varphi(\mathbb E[F\mid\mathcal H_i])\mid\mathcal G_i]\\
 &\le\mathbb E[\varphi(F)\mid\mathcal G_i]
       -\varphi(\mathbb E[F\mid\mathcal G_i])
 =e_{\mathcal G_i}(F).
\end{aligned}$$ Thus the additional conditioning on the observation decreases the averaged conditional entropy, even though the observation and the complementary spins are dependent. Combining this fact with the posterior tensorization gives $$H(1)\le\sum_i\mathbb Ee_{\mathcal H_i}(F)
      \le\sum_i\mathbb Ee_{\mathcal G_i}(F)
      =\sum_i\mu\bigl[\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_{\mu(\cdot\mid X_{-i})}(f)\bigr].$$ We can now compare each original one-coordinate entropy with the corresponding heat-bath energy. Concavity of the logarithm gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}(f)\le\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}(f,\log f),$$ because the difference of the right and left sides is $\mathbb Ef\,[\log\mathbb Ef-\mathbb E\log f]\ge0$. Moreover, summing these conditional covariances gives $$\sum_i\mu[\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}(f,\log f\mid X_{-i})]
 =\sum_i\mu[f\mathsf D_i\log f]
 =\mu[f(-L)\log f].$$ The product-endpoint estimate is therefore bounded by the entropy dissipation of the original generator. Substituting into Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-comparison">[rcut:eq:posterior-entropy-comparison]</a> proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:entropy-inequality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:entropy-inequality">[rcut:eq:entropy-inequality]</a>, with the permissible choice $C_1=e^{3/\kappa_\beta}$.

*Entropy decay and mixing.* For a point start, it remains to bound the initial relative entropy $\log(1/\mu(x))$ uniformly in the starting point. The identity $\|x\|^2=n$ gives $$\left|\frac12x^{\mathsf T}Jx\right|\le\frac n2\|J\|,
 \qquad
 \log\frac1{\mu(x)}\le n(\log2+\|J\|)\le n(\log2+1).$$ Reversibility lets us evolve the density $f_t=d\rho_{t,x}/d\mu$ using the same semigroup $S_t$. For $t>0$ the density is strictly positive, so the entropy inequality applies to its derivative: $$\frac{d}{dt}\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(f_t)
   =-\mu[f_t(-L)\log f_t]
   \le-C_1^{-1}\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu(f_t).$$ Integrating this differential inequality and using continuity at zero establishes Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:entropy-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:entropy-decay">[rcut:eq:entropy-decay]</a>, with $C_2=\log2+1$.

To finish, coarsen the measure to an event and its complement; relative entropy then dominates the resulting binary relative entropy. For fixed $q\in(0,1)$, this binary entropy, viewed as a function of $p$, has value and derivative zero at $p=q$ and second derivative $1/[p(1-p)]\ge4$. It is consequently at least $2(p-q)^2$. Choosing an event that attains total variation and using the entropy decay just proved yields $$d_c(t)\le\sqrt{\frac{C_2n}{2}}\,e^{-t/(2C_1)},$$ which proves the stated mixing upper bound. ◻

</details>

<a id="rcut:sec:gradient"></a>
### Dissipation of the unweighted gradient

The next step is a pointwise dissipation bound for the unweighted gradient $U$, with a fixed contraction rate outside a set of exponentially small Gibbs mass. We first perform the deterministic calculation: completing squares removes the second differences and leaves a quadratic form in the first differences. The error estimate retains the variance factors needed when local fields are large. We then apply the probability bounds proved in Sections <a href="#rcut:sec:comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:comparison">13</a> and <a href="#rcut:sec:scalar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:scalar">14</a> to identify the exceptional set.

<a id="rcut:eq:gradient-form"></a>
Two row sums will control, respectively, the quadratic terms and the cubic error. For a symmetric matrix $J$ with zero diagonal, define $$R_2(J)=\max_i\sum_j J_{ij}^2,
 \qquad
 R_3(J)=\max_i\sum_j |J_{ij}|^3.$$ We begin at the all-positive configuration $\mathbf 1$. In the quadratic form below all local quantities are evaluated there: $h_i=(J\mathbf 1)_i$, $m_i=\tanh h_i$, $v_i=1-m_i^2$, and $w_i=1-m_i$. Define $$\begin{split}
 M_J(p)={}&\sum_{i\ne j}J_{ij}p_i v_jp_j
       +2\sum_{i\ne j}J_{ij}^2p_i m_jv_jp_j\\
       &+\sum_{i<j}
          \frac{J_{ij}^2(v_jp_i+v_ip_j)^2}{w_i+w_j},
       \qquad p\in\mathbb R^n.
\end{split}
\label{rcut:eq:gradient-form}$$ For a finite matrix $J$, every denominator is positive. The estimates below remain uniform as any local field tends to infinity, including when these denominators approach zero.

To transfer the calculation to an arbitrary configuration $x$, use the sign change $$J^x=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(x)J\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(x),\qquad
 f^x(y)=f(x_1y_1,\ldots,x_ny_n),\qquad
 p_i^x=x_i d_i f(x).$$ This sign change conjugates the generator for $J$ to the generator for $J^x$. It also gives $d_i f^x(\mathbf 1)=p_i^x$ and $U(f^x)(\mathbf 1)=U(f)(x)$, while preserving the matrix controls: $\|J^x\|=\|J\|$, $R_k(J^x)=R_k(J)$ for $k=2,3$. The calculation at $\mathbf 1$ therefore suffices for every configuration.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-gradient-algebra"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:gradient-algebra" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:gradient-identity"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:gradient-local-bound"></a>
**Lemma 78** (Pointwise gradient calculation). *Let $f_t=S_tf_0$ for the heat-bath generator with a symmetric zero-diagonal interaction matrix $J$. At $\mathbf 1$, write $p_i=d_if_t$, $r_{ij}=d_id_jf_t$, and $a_{ij}=d_im_j$. Then $$\frac12(\partial_t-L)U(f_t)
 =-\|p\|^2
   +\sum_{i\ne j}p_i a_{ij}(p_j-2r_{ij})
   -\sum_{i\ne j}w_jr_{ij}^2.
\label{rcut:eq:gradient-identity}$$ If $\max_{i,j}|J_{ij}|\le1/10$, then, at every configuration $x$, $$\frac12(\partial_t-L)U(f_t)(x)
 \le -U(f_t)(x)+M_{J^x}(p^x)
             +16R_3(J)U(f_t)(x).
\label{rcut:eq:gradient-local-bound}$$ The constants do not depend on the local fields, on $f_0$, or on $t$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-gradient-algebra"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-gradient-algebra</summary>

*Proof.* We first derive the exact evolution identity, then estimate the field differences before completing the squares. The half-difference $d_if$ does not depend on spin $i$. At the all-positive point, the product rule reads $$d_i(ab)=a\,d_ib+b(x^{i,-})\,d_ia.$$ For $j\ne i$, the first difference after a flip is $d_jf(x^{i,-})=p_j-2r_{ij}$. The contribution with $j=i$ to $d_iL f$ is $-p_i$: both $m_i$ and $p_i$ are independent of spin $i$. Separating this term gives $$d_iL f=L(d_if)-p_i
                   +\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}(p_j-2r_{ij}).$$ Apply the square identity $L(g^2)-2gL g=2\Gamma(g)$ with $g=d_if$. The equality $\Gamma(d_if)=\sum_{j\ne i}w_jr_{ij}^2$ then identifies the second-difference energy, proving Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-identity">[rcut:eq:gradient-identity]</a>.

<a id="rcut:eq:gradient-field-difference"></a>
To use the identity uniformly in the local fields, we must keep the conditional variance in the estimate for $a_{ij}$. Set $z=J_{ij}$ and $m=m_j(\mathbf 1)$. Flipping spin $i$ changes the $j$-field by $-2z$. The hyperbolic-tangent subtraction formula therefore gives $$a_{ij}=v_j q(z,m),\qquad
 q(z,m)=\frac{\tanh(2z)}{2(1-m\tanh(2z))}.
\label{rcut:eq:gradient-field-difference}$$ For real arguments with $|z|\le1/10$ and $|m|\le1$, the factor $1-m\tanh(2z)$ is bounded below by $4/5$. The bound is uniform as $m$ approaches either endpoint of $[-1,1]$, so the variance factor can be retained without a field cutoff.

<a id="rcut:eq:gradient-q-bounds"></a>
To track the constants in the cubic remainder, write $T=\tanh(2z)$ and expand the denominator exactly: $$q(z,m)=\frac T2+\frac{mT^2}{2}
                   +\frac{m^2T^3}{2(1-mT)}.$$ The inequalities $|T|\le2|z|$ and $|\tanh u-u|\le |u|^3/3$ imply $$\begin{split}
 |q(z,m)-z-2mz^2|&\le7|z|^3,\\
 |q(z,m)-z|&\le\frac{27}{10}z^2,
 \qquad |q(z,m)|\le\frac54|z|.
 \end{split}
\label{rcut:eq:gradient-q-bounds}$$ For the first estimate, the three terms of this decomposition contribute errors bounded by $(4/3)|z|^3$, $(16/3)|z|^4$, and $5|z|^3$, respectively. Their sum is less than $7|z|^3$. The second estimate is a consequence of the first, while the last is immediate from Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-field-difference" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-field-difference">[rcut:eq:gradient-field-difference]</a>. The hyperbolic-tangent inequality follows by integrating $1-(\tanh u)'=\tanh^2u\le u^2$. Returning to the field difference gives $$a_{ij}=J_{ij}v_j+2J_{ij}^2m_jv_j+e_{ij},
 \qquad |e_{ij}|\le7|J_{ij}|^3v_j,$$ with the variance factor retained in the remainder.

<a id="rcut:eq:gradient-denominator-control"></a>
We can now eliminate the second differences. Since $r_{ij}=r_{ji}$, the terms for one unordered pair in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-identity">[rcut:eq:gradient-identity]</a> combine as $$-2(a_{ij}p_i+a_{ji}p_j)r_{ij}-(w_i+w_j)r_{ij}^2.$$ Completing the square bounds this expression by $(a_{ij}p_i+a_{ji}p_j)^2/(w_i+w_j)$. We compare its numerator with the leading interaction term. For the same pair, write $$A=a_{ij}p_i+a_{ji}p_j,\quad
 B=J_{ij}(v_jp_i+v_ip_j),\quad
 S=v_j|p_i|+v_i|p_j|.$$ Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-q-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-q-bounds">[rcut:eq:gradient-q-bounds]</a> gives $$|A-B|\le\frac{27}{10}|J_{ij}|^2S,
 \qquad |A|+|B|\le\frac94|J_{ij}|S.$$ Hence $|A^2-B^2|\le7|J_{ij}|^3S^2$. The remaining issue is the denominator: it can be small at a nearly saturated field. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz keeps the variance factors attached to the corresponding weights and gives $$\frac{S^2}{w_i+w_j}
 \le\frac{v_j^2}{w_j}p_i^2+\frac{v_i^2}{w_i}p_j^2,
 \qquad
 \frac{v_i^2}{w_i}=(1-m_i)(1+m_i)^2\le\frac{32}{27}.
\label{rcut:eq:gradient-denominator-control}$$ This estimate also describes the limiting fields. As $m_j\uparrow1$, the contribution is at most $4(1-m_j)p_i^2$; as $m_j\downarrow-1$, it is at most $2(1+m_j)^2p_i^2$. Both bounds hold without comparing the coupling size with the distance from saturation.

Only the accumulated replacement errors remain. Replacing $\sum_{i\ne j}p_i a_{ij}p_j$ by the first two terms of $M_J(p)$ costs at most $$7\sum_{i\ne j}|J_{ij}|^3|p_i||p_j|
 \le7R_3(J)\|p\|^2.$$ The last inequality uses symmetry and $2|p_i||p_j|\le p_i^2+p_j^2$. For the completed squares, Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-denominator-control" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-denominator-control">[rcut:eq:gradient-denominator-control]</a> bounds the total replacement error by $$\frac{224}{27}\sum_{i<j}|J_{ij}|^3(p_i^2+p_j^2)
 \le\frac{224}{27}R_3(J)\|p\|^2.$$ Adding the two errors and using $7+224/27<16$ proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-local-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-local-bound">[rcut:eq:gradient-local-bound]</a> at $\mathbf 1$. Sign conjugation then gives the asserted inequality at every $x$. ◻

</details>

<a id="rcut:eq:rough-gradient"></a>
The local calculation reduces dissipation to an upper bound on the quadratic form. We first give a bound valid at every configuration; it will also control possible growth inside the exceptional set. For every symmetric zero-diagonal $J$ and every $p$, $$M_J(p)\le
 \left[\|J\|+
       \left(\frac{4}{3\sqrt3}+\frac{32}{27}\right)R_2(J)
 \right]\|p\|^2.
\label{rcut:eq:rough-gradient}$$ To see this, treat the three terms in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-form">[rcut:eq:gradient-form]</a> separately. The first is bounded by $\|J\|\|p\|^2$ because $0\le v_i\le1$. For the second, the symmetric matrix $J\circ J$, with entries $J_{ij}^2$, has norm at most $R_2(J)$; combine this with $\max_{|m|\le1}|m(1-m^2)|=2/(3\sqrt3)$. For the final term, the weighted Cauchy–Schwarz estimate in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-denominator-control" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-denominator-control">[rcut:eq:gradient-denominator-control]</a> gives $(32/27)R_2(J)\|p\|^2$. This proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:rough-gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:rough-gradient">[rcut:eq:rough-gradient]</a> uniformly in the local fields.

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-typical-gradient"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:typical-gradient" class="proposition">

<a id="rcut:eq:gradient-potential"></a>
**Proposition 79** (Typical-state gradient dissipation). *Fix $0\le\beta<1/2$. There are constants $c>0$ and $C<\infty$, and events of disorder probability tending to one, on which a set $\mathcal B_J\subseteq\{-1,1\}^n$ satisfies $$\mu_J(\mathcal B_J)\le e^{-cn}$$ and, for every $f_0$, every $t\ge0$, and every configuration $x$, $$(\partial_t-L)U(S_tf_0)(x)
 \le[-c+C\mathbf 1_{\mathcal B_J}(x)]\,U(S_tf_0)(x).
\label{rcut:eq:gradient-potential}$$ The constants depend only on the fixed $\beta$. If $0\le\beta\le7/20$, the exceptional set can be empty.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-typical-gradient"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-typical-gradient</summary>

*Proof.* We now combine the deterministic calculation with the disorder estimates. For the smaller temperatures, the rough bound already contracts at every configuration. For the remaining temperatures, the planted comparison will provide contraction outside a small Gibbs set. Begin on the events of Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:good-disorder" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:good-disorder">74</a>, where the deterministic tolerances give $$\begin{gathered}
 \|J\|\le2\beta+o(1),\qquad R_2(J)\le\beta^2+o(1),\\
 R_3(J)\le\max_{i,j}|J_{ij}|\,R_2(J)=o(1).
 \end{gathered}$$ Sign conjugation preserves each bound, so they hold for every $J^x$. The remainder in Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gradient-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gradient-algebra">78</a> consequently tends to zero uniformly over configurations, test functions, and times.

If $\beta\le7/20$, it suffices to substitute the disorder estimates into Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:rough-gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:rough-gradient">[rcut:eq:rough-gradient]</a>. Its coefficient is at most $$2\beta+
 \left(\frac{4}{3\sqrt3}+\frac{32}{27}\right)\beta^2+o(1)
 <\frac{189}{200}+o(1)<1.$$ The rational bound follows from $4/(3\sqrt3)+32/27<2$ at $\beta=7/20$, since both terms increase with nonnegative $\beta$. There is therefore a fixed margin below one. Absorbing the vanishing remainder in Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gradient-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gradient-algebra">78</a> proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-potential" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-potential">[rcut:eq:gradient-potential]</a> with a fixed positive $c$ and $\mathcal B_J=\varnothing$ for all sufficiently large $n$. The endpoint $\beta=0$ can also be read directly from Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-identity">[rcut:eq:gradient-identity]</a>: $a_{ij}=0$, $w_i=1$, and $(\partial_t-L)U\le-2U$. This part of the proof therefore uses no nondegenerate Gaussian field law.

<a id="rcut:eq:gradient-bad-set"></a>
For $7/20<\beta<1/2$, we need a sharper estimate on most configurations. The inputs are proved in Sections <a href="#rcut:sec:comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:comparison">13</a> and <a href="#rcut:sec:scalar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:scalar">14</a>, independently of Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:typical-gradient" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:typical-gradient">79</a>. First, Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:scalar-gap" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:scalar-gap">84</a> bounds the normalized variational expression in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:variational" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:variational">[rcut:eq:variational]</a> by $0.9969$. Choose $\delta=0.0031$ and $\rho=\delta/2$ to retain half this strict margin. Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:planted-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:planted-comparison">80</a> then gives $\kappa>0$ for which the event $$\mathcal A_n=
 \left\{J:\sup_{\|p\|=1}M_J(p)>1-\rho\right\}$$ has planted probability at most $e^{-\kappa n}$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Under the planted law, the entries above the diagonal are independent with mean $\beta^2/n$ and variance $\beta^2/n$; Section <a href="#rcut:sec:comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:comparison">13</a> defines and analyzes this law. To translate the matrix event into a set of spin configurations, define $$\mathcal B_J=\{x:J^x\in\mathcal A_n\}.
\label{rcut:eq:gradient-bad-set}$$ Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:annealed-transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:annealed-transfer">83</a> now yields $\mu_J(\mathcal B_J)\le e^{-\kappa n/2}$ on events whose original disorder probability tends to one. Intersect these with the good disorder events used above. The supremum over all unit vectors in the definition ensures that the set in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-bad-set" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-bad-set">[rcut:eq:gradient-bad-set]</a> depends only on $J$, rather than on the evolving function.

The Gibbs mass estimate is established. To obtain the pointwise dissipation bound, take $n$ large enough that $16R_3(J)\le\rho/2$. For $x\notin\mathcal B_J$, homogeneity of $M_{J^x}$ and Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gradient-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gradient-algebra">78</a> leave the fixed margin $$\frac12(\partial_t-L)U(S_tf_0)(x)
 \le-\frac\rho2 U(S_tf_0)(x).$$ At every configuration, including those in the exceptional set, Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:rough-gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:rough-gradient">[rcut:eq:rough-gradient]</a> and Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gradient-algebra" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gradient-algebra">78</a> give $(\partial_t-L)U\le K U$ for some nonnegative finite $K$ depending only on $\beta$. For instance, the eventual estimates $\|J\|\le2$, $R_2(J)\le1$, and $16R_3(J)\le1$ permit $K=8$. Choose $c=\min\{\rho,\kappa/2\}$ and $C=K+c$ to combine the Gibbs mass and dissipation bounds on the same event. Since the local calculation applies to every function, this event and these constants work simultaneously for all $f_0$, $t$, and $x$. ◻

</details>

<a id="rcut:sec:comparison"></a>
### A planted Gaussian comparison

We seek a bound on the quadratic form in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-form">[rcut:eq:gradient-form]</a> outside a set of configurations of exponentially small Gibbs mass. A bound of the form $M_{J^x}(p)<\|p\|_2^2$ need not hold for every $x$ and every nonzero $p$. We therefore first fix a configuration and weight the disorder by its unnormalized Gibbs weight. Under this planted law, a scalar variational estimate controls the form simultaneously on all unit vectors. The final step transfers the resulting exponential probability bound to Gibbs mass under the original disorder law.

<a id="pm-h-69"></a>
#### The planted law and the variational bound

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-planted-density"></a>
Write $\widehat\mathbb P_n$ for the law under which the entries $J_{ij}$, $i<j$, are independent Gaussians with mean $\beta^2/n$ and variance $\beta^2/n$, with $J_{ji}=J_{ij}$ and $J_{ii}=0$. Relative to the original disorder law $\mathbb P_n$, its density is $$\frac{d\widehat\mathbb P_n}{d\mathbb P_n}(J)
 =\exp\left\{\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}-\frac{\beta^2(n-1)}4\right\}.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-planted-density}$$ The density is the unnormalized Gibbs weight of the all-positive configuration divided by its expectation. Its normalization is therefore deterministic; Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-planted-density" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-planted-density">[rcut:eq:comp-planted-density]</a> contains no random partition function.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels"></a>
For $\beta>0$, let $\mathsf G_\beta=N(\beta^2,\beta^2)$ and write $\langle f\rangle=\int f(h)\,d\mathsf G_\beta(h)$. An asterisk denotes a second argument integrated against the same law. In this Section the scalar functions are <a id="rcut:eq:comp-field-functions"></a>$$m(h)=\tanh h,\qquad v(h)=1-m(h)^2,\qquad w(h)=1-m(h),
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-field-functions}$$ and we put <a id="rcut:eq:comp-kernels"></a>$$D(h)=\beta^2\left\langle
             \frac{v(h_*)^2}{w(h)+w(h_*)}\right\rangle_*,
 \qquad
 K_0(h,h_*)=\frac{v(h)v(h_*)}{w(h)+w(h_*)}.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-kernels}$$ To control large fields uniformly, express the kernels in terms of $w\in[0,2]$, using $v=w(2-w)$ also at the endpoints. The resulting kernels $$F(a,b)=\frac{b^2(2-b)^2}{a+b},\qquad
 K(a,b)=\frac{a(2-a)b(2-b)}{a+b}
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels}$$ extend continuously to $[0,2]^2$ by taking value zero at $(0,0)$. Indeed $F(a,b)\le b(2-b)^2\le32/27$, and $K(a,b)\le4ab/(a+b)\le4\min(a,b)$. Thus the denominators remain harmless after compactifying the field through $w$, including the limit of large positive fields.

The variational parameters describe the part of a unit vector that is constant at a given field and its remaining variation. More precisely, a finite partition into field bins gives a mean $b_a$ of the rescaled coordinates $\sqrt n\,p_i$ and a root-mean-square deviation $r_a\ge0$ in each bin. Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-bin-decomposition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-bin-decomposition">[rcut:eq:comp-bin-decomposition]</a> makes this decomposition precise. With empirical bin proportions as weights, the sum of $b_a^2+r_a^2$ is one. The functional below uses the limiting Gaussian law $\mathsf G_\beta$ instead; the rescaling in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-mass-rescaling" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-mass-rescaling">[rcut:eq:comp-mass-rescaling]</a> will preserve the unit norm when we pass between the two measures. Its final term will bound the conditional Gaussian contribution from the within-bin variation.

<a id="rcut:eq:variational"></a>
For measurable real $b$ and nonnegative $r$ with $\langle b^2+r^2\rangle=1$, define $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal V_\beta(b,r)
 ={}&\langle D(b^2+r^2)\rangle
       +\langle bh\rangle\langle bv\rangle
       +\langle b\rangle\langle bhv\rangle
       -\beta^2\langle b\rangle\langle bv\rangle \notag\\
    &+2\beta^2\langle b\rangle\langle bmv\rangle
       +\beta^2\langle b(h)K_0(h,h_*)b(h_*)\rangle_{h,h_*}
       \notag\\
    &+\beta\left\langle r(h)
       \sqrt{\left\langle(v(h)+v(h_*))^2r(h_*)^2\right\rangle_*
        +\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{h_*}\bigl((v(h)+v(h_*))b(h_*)\bigr)}
       \right\rangle.
 \label{rcut:eq:variational}
\end{aligned}$$ This definition applies to the entire stated $L^2$ class. Boundedness of the kernels and of $m,v$, together with $h,hv\in L^2(\mathsf G_\beta)$, makes the first two lines finite. The last radical is bounded by $\sqrt{4\langle b^2+r^2\rangle}=2$, so its pairing with $r$ is finite as well. In particular, $b$ and $r$ need not be bounded.

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-planted-comparison"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:planted-comparison" class="proposition">

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-exponential-conclusion"></a>
**Proposition 80** (Planted comparison). *Fix $0<\beta\le1/2$. Suppose that, for some $\delta>0$, $$\sup_{\langle b^2+r^2\rangle=1,\ r\ge0}
