       \mathcal V_\beta(b,r)\le1-\delta.$$ There are $\kappa>0$ and $n_0<\infty$ such that for $n\ge n_0$, $$\widehat\mathbb P_n\left(
    \sup_{\|p\|_2=1}M_J(p)>1-\frac\delta2\right)
       \le e^{-\kappa n}.
  \label{rcut:eq:comp-exponential-conclusion}$$ The constants may depend on the fixed $\beta$ and $\delta$.*

</div>

=3em The proof separates the squared interactions from the centered Gaussian matrix. Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:comp-square-replacement" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:comp-square-replacement">81</a> replaces the squares by their means without discarding the dependence between fields and couplings. After this replacement, a finite partition of the fields reduces the matrix term to the conditional comparison in Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:comp-bin-gaussian" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:comp-bin-gaussian">82</a>. A net of the normalized bin parameters then gives simultaneous control of all unit vectors. We choose every approximation accuracy before sending $n$ to infinity, which retains the exponential failure rate required by the proposition.

<a id="pm-h-70"></a>
#### Gaussian squares and the added diagonal

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-square-mgf"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:comp-weighted-square-tail"></a>
The first task is to control weighted sums of interaction squares. We begin with deterministic weights; the later conditioning argument will explain when these estimates also apply to weights depending on the fields. Under $\widehat\mathbb P_n$, $nJ_{ij}^2$ has the same law as $$X_n=(\beta Z+\beta^2/\sqrt n)^2,\qquad Z\sim N(0,1).$$ For $\mu=\beta^2/\sqrt n$ and $|t|<1/(2\beta^2)$, direct Gaussian integration gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \log\mathbb Ee^{t(X_n-\mathbb EX_n)}
  ={}&-\tfrac12\log(1-2\beta^2t)-\beta^2t
      +\frac{2\beta^2\mu^2t^2}{1-2\beta^2t}
      \le C_\beta t^2,
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-square-mgf}
\end{aligned}$$ where the inequality holds for $|t|\le t_\beta$ with a fixed $t_\beta>0$, uniformly in $n$. Consequently, if $X_{n,j}$ are independent copies and $|a_j|\le A$, then exponential Markov inequalities for both signs imply $$\mathbb P\left(\left|\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}
       a_j(X_{n,j}-\mathbb EX_{n,j})\right|>u\right)
 \le 2\exp\{-c_{\beta,A}n\min(u^2,u)\}.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-weighted-square-tail}$$ To see the rate, independence bounds the logarithm of the moment generating function of the unnormalized sum by $C_{\beta,A}nt^2$ on a fixed interval of $t$. In the exponential Markov bound choose $t$ to be a sufficiently small constant multiple of $\min(u,1)$, and repeat with the opposite sign. This argument remains valid after conditioning on a sigma-field that determines the coefficients and is independent of the copies.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-basic-events"></a>
Add independent diagonal entries $\zeta_i\sim N(\beta^2/n,2\beta^2/n)$ to the planted probability space, and set <a id="rcut:eq:comp-goe-coupling"></a>$$\widetilde J=J+\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(\zeta_i)=W+\beta^2ee^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 e=\frac{\boldsymbol 1}{\sqrt n},\quad Q=I-ee^{\mathsf T},\quad
 H=\widetilde J\boldsymbol 1.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-goe-coupling}$$ Here $W$ is a centered GOE with off-diagonal variance $\beta^2/n$ and diagonal variance $2\beta^2/n$. For every fixed $u>0$, Gaussian tails, Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-square-mgf" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-square-mgf">[rcut:eq:comp-square-mgf]</a>, and Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gaussian-facts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gaussian-facts">73</a> give constants $c,C>0$ such that, outside an event of probability at most $Cn^2e^{-cn}$, $$\max_i|\zeta_i|\le u,\quad
 \max_{i<j}|J_{ij}|\le u,\quad
 \max_i\sum_jJ_{ij}^2\le\beta^2+u,\quad
 \|W\|\le2\beta+u.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-basic-events}$$ Each estimate has an exponential rate at fixed $u$. A row sum has mean $(n-1)(\beta^2/n+\beta^4/n^2)$, so Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-weighted-square-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-weighted-square-tail">[rcut:eq:comp-weighted-square-tail]</a> followed by a union over rows gives the third bound. Gaussian tails and finite unions give the first two. For the last, the GOE comparison in the proof of Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:good-disorder" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:good-disorder">74</a> gives $\mathbb E\lambda_{\max}(W)\le2\beta$, with Gaussian Lipschitz constant $\sqrt2\beta/\sqrt n$. Apply Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gaussian-facts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gaussian-facts">73</a> to both $W$ and $-W$. These events also bound the planted norm $\|J\|$ by $2\beta+\beta^2+2u$. Only a fixed bound on that norm is needed in what follows.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-field-decomposition"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:comp-goe-covariance"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:comp-field-law"></a>
The following decomposition is exact: $$\widetilde J
  =QWQ+\frac{He^{\mathsf T}+eH^{\mathsf T}}{\sqrt n}
       -ee^{\mathsf T}\frac{e^{\mathsf T}H}{\sqrt n}.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-field-decomposition}$$ This decomposition separates the field-dependent terms from a matrix that is independent of $H$. Indeed, the GOE covariance identity $$\mathbb E[(a^{\mathsf T}Wb)(c^{\mathsf T}Wd)]
  =\frac{\beta^2}{n}
     \bigl((a^{\mathsf T}c)(b^{\mathsf T}d)
                  +(a^{\mathsf T}d)(b^{\mathsf T}c)\bigr)
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-goe-covariance}$$ makes the covariance of every entry of $QWQ$ with every entry of $We$ equal to zero. Joint Gaussianity then gives independence of $QWQ$ and $H$. The displayed decomposition itself follows by expanding $W$ with $I=Q+ee^{\mathsf T}$. The covariance identity also gives the following representation of the field vector: $$H_i=\beta^2+\beta Z_i+\frac\beta{\sqrt n}Z_0,
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-field-law}$$ where $Z_0,Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ are independent standard Gaussians. Indeed its covariance has diagonal $\beta^2(1+1/n)$ and off-diagonal $\beta^2/n$.

<a id="pm-h-71"></a>
#### Replacing squared entries with their means

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-comp-square-replacement"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:comp-square-replacement" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-square-operator"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:comp-weighted-operator"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:comp-weighted-diagonal"></a>
**Lemma 81** (Weighted square replacement). *On the enlarged planted space, put $w_i=w(H_i)$ and $E_{ij}=J_{ij}^2-\beta^2/n$, including $E_{ii}=-\beta^2/n$. Here $\circ$ denotes entrywise product, and $F$ is defined in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels">[rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels]</a>. For any fixed continuous function $G$ on $[0,2]^2$ and any $u>0$, there are $c>0$ and $n_0$ such that, for $n\ge n_0$, each of the following failures has probability at most $e^{-cn}$: $$\begin{aligned}
  &\left\|J\circ J-\beta^2ee^{\mathsf T}\right\|>u,
    \label{rcut:eq:comp-square-operator}\\
  &\sup_{\|p\|_2=1}
     \left|\sum_{i,j}E_{ij}G(w_i,w_j)p_ip_j\right|>u,
    \label{rcut:eq:comp-weighted-operator}\\
  &\max_i\left|\sum_{j\ne i}
       E_{ij}F(w_i,w_j)\right|>u.
    \label{rcut:eq:comp-weighted-diagonal}
 
\end{aligned}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-comp-square-replacement"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-comp-square-replacement</summary>

*Proof.* We first establish the unweighted operator estimate, then insert the continuous kernel $G$ by approximation. The diagonal estimate will require a separate argument that removes one row from the fields. For the operator estimate, truncate $X_n=nJ_{ij}^2$ at a fixed level $T$. For a sufficiently small fixed $t>0$, $$\sup_n\mathbb Ee^{t(X_n-T)_+}\longrightarrow1
       \quad\text{as }T\longrightarrow\infty.$$ For uniform dominated convergence, use $|\beta Z+\beta^2/\sqrt n|\le\beta|Z|+\beta^2$; the square of the right side has an exponential moment for a sufficiently small parameter. We may therefore choose $T$ so that both the mean tail and the logarithm of the displayed moment are as small as required. Exponential Markov bounds the probability that a row average of $(nJ_{ij}^2-T)_+$ exceeds the prescribed accuracy by $e^{-cn}$. Taking the union over the $n$ rows retains a positive exponential rate. Symmetry and entrywise nonnegativity bound the tail matrix’s operator norm by its largest row sum, and the same estimate controls its expectation.

For a fixed unit vector, the quadratic form of the centered truncated matrix is a sum of independent bounded variables with coefficients $2p_ip_j/n$, $i<j$. To bound its moment generating function, recall that a centered variable whose range has length $a$ has logarithmic moment generating function at most $a^2s^2/8$. The second derivative is a variance under a tilted law and is at most $a^2/4$; integrating twice gives this bound. Since $\sum_{i<j}(2p_ip_j)^2\le2$, the present quadratic form has logarithmic moment generating function at most $CT^2s^2/n^2$, and hence a tail at fixed accuracy bounded by $2e^{-c n^2/T^2}$. To obtain an operator estimate, use a $1/4$-net of the unit sphere with at most $9^n$ points. This cardinality follows by comparing volumes of disjoint balls of radius $1/8$. For a symmetric matrix $A$, twice the maximum of $|p^{\mathsf T}Ap|$ on this net bounds $\|A\|$. The union bound is therefore absorbed by the quadratic exponential rate. It remains to restore the mean and diagonal: $$\mathbb EJ_{ij}^2=\frac{\beta^2}{n}+\frac{\beta^4}{n^2}
       \quad(i\ne j),$$ so the resulting mean correction and missing diagonal have norm $O_\beta(1/n)$. Together with the truncation and net bounds, this proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-square-operator" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-square-operator">[rcut:eq:comp-square-operator]</a>.

We now insert $G$. Uniform continuity gives an approximation on a finite rectangular partition of $[0,2]^2$, of the form $\sum_{a,d}g_{ad}\mathbf 1_{I_a}(w_i)\mathbf 1_{I_d}(w_j)$. Multiplication of $p$ by the corresponding coordinate masks reduces each summand to Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-square-operator" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-square-operator">[rcut:eq:comp-square-operator]</a>. The number of summands and their coefficients are fixed. For the remaining kernel error $R_{ij}$, use $$\left|\sum_{i,j}E_{ij}R_{ij}p_ip_j\right|
   \le\max_{i,j}|R_{ij}|\,
          |p|^{\mathsf T}|E|\,|p|
   \le\max_{i,j}|R_{ij}|\max_i\sum_j|E_{ij}|.$$ The row-sum bound in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-basic-events" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-basic-events">[rcut:eq:comp-basic-events]</a> controls this error, since $\sum_j|E_{ij}|\le\sum_jJ_{ij}^2+\beta^2$. This proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-weighted-operator" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-weighted-operator">[rcut:eq:comp-weighted-operator]</a>. On the operator and row-sum events, the argument is deterministic for every choice of masks and residual coefficients. Thus these weights may depend on the whole interaction matrix.

For the diagonal estimate we must recover independence before applying the weighted tail bound. Fix a row $i$ and condition on $$\mathcal F_i=\sigma\bigl(J_{kl}:k,l\ne i;\ \zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_n\bigr).$$ This sigma-field leaves the entries of the off-diagonal row $(J_{ij})_{j\ne i}$ independent. Remove that row from the other fields by defining $$H_j^{(-i)}=\zeta_j+\sum_{k\ne i,j}J_{jk},\qquad j\ne i.$$ The fields so obtained are $\mathcal F_i$-measurable, with $H_j-H_j^{(-i)}=J_{ij}$. Keep $a\in[0,2]$ deterministic for now and set $c_j(a)=F(a,w(H_j^{(-i)}))$. Under the conditioning these weights are fixed and lie in $[0,32/27]$, so Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-weighted-square-tail" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-weighted-square-tail">[rcut:eq:comp-weighted-square-tail]</a> gives a bound $e^{-cn}$ for the event $$\left|\sum_{j\ne i}c_j(a)
      \left(J_{ij}^2-\frac{\beta^2}{n}\right)\right|>u,$$ for all large $n$, uniformly in $\mathcal F_i$ and $a$; the mean correction is at most $(32/27)\beta^4/n$. Take a union first over a fixed finite mesh of $a$ values and then over the $n$ rows. Uniform continuity of $F$ and the bound on $\sum_j|E_{ij}|$ extend the estimate to all $a\in[0,2]$. Next restore the original fields. On the maximum-entry event, $|H_j-H_j^{(-i)}|$ is uniformly small. The Lipschitz property of $w$ and uniform continuity of $F$ bound the resulting error by a small multiple of the same row sum. Only after these simultaneous estimates do we set $a=w_i$. Conditioning on $w_i$ at the outset would condition on a row sum and destroy the independence used above. The mesh, continuity tolerances and entry bound are chosen before $n$; their failures therefore retain positive exponential rates. This completes Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-weighted-diagonal" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-weighted-diagonal">[rcut:eq:comp-weighted-diagonal]</a>. ◻

</details>

We can now simplify the quadratic form. Before applying the replacement lemma, change the fields in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-form">[rcut:eq:gradient-form]</a> from $J\boldsymbol1$ to $H$. Each coordinate changes by $\zeta_i$. For the squared-entry terms, uniform continuity of the compact kernels in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels">[rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels]</a> and the bounded row sums make the error uniformly small on the unit sphere. The unsquared term has error at most $\|J\|\max_i|v((J\boldsymbol1)_i)-v(H_i)|$; adding its diagonal costs at most $\max_i|\zeta_i|$. We then apply Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:comp-square-replacement" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:comp-square-replacement">81</a> to the squared entries.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-reduced-error"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:comp-reduced-form"></a>
Put $A=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(v(H_i))$, $\overline H=n^{-1}\sum_iH_i$, and $$D_n(t)=\frac{\beta^2}{n}\sum_j
       \frac{v(H_j)^2}{w(t)+w(H_j)}.$$ For every fixed accuracy $u>0$, the preceding estimates show that, outside probability $e^{-cn}$, $$\sup_{\|p\|_2=1}|M_J(p)-\widehat M(p)|\le u,
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-reduced-error}$$ where $$\begin{aligned}
 \widehat M(p)={}&p^{\mathsf T}QWQAp
 +\frac{p^{\mathsf T}H}{\sqrt n}(e^{\mathsf T}Ap)
 +(p^{\mathsf T}e)\frac{H^{\mathsf T}Ap}{\sqrt n}
 -\overline H(p^{\mathsf T}e)(e^{\mathsf T}Ap)\notag\\
 &+2\beta^2(p^{\mathsf T}e)
       \bigl(e^{\mathsf T}\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(m(H_i)v(H_i))p\bigr)
 +\sum_iD_n(H_i)p_i^2
 +\frac{\beta^2}{n}\sum_{i,j}K_0(H_i,H_j)p_ip_j.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-reduced-form}
\end{aligned}$$ Here the two weighted replacement estimates have different roles. Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-weighted-diagonal" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-weighted-diagonal">[rcut:eq:comp-weighted-diagonal]</a> treats the diagonal part of the last square in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-form">[rcut:eq:gradient-form]</a>; Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-weighted-operator" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-weighted-operator">[rcut:eq:comp-weighted-operator]</a> treats its cross part and the other squared-entry term. The added terms with $i=j$ in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-reduced-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-reduced-form">[rcut:eq:comp-reduced-form]</a> contribute only $O_\beta(1/n)$ on the unit sphere. To check the coefficient of the kernel term, expand the square over $i<j$: the cross part is exactly the ordered off-diagonal sum with coefficient $\beta^2/n$.

<a id="pm-h-72"></a>
#### Finite field bins and normalized parameters

The reduced form still depends on all $n$ field values. We next replace them by a fixed finite collection while retaining uniformity over every unit vector. Choose a finite partition $\mathcal I=(I_1,\ldots,I_k)$ of the real line into intervals, with the two extreme intervals unbounded, and choose a representative $h_a\in I_a$ for each interval. Write $$h^{\mathcal I}(h)=h_a\quad(h\in I_a),\qquad
 m_a=m(h_a),\quad v_a=v(h_a),\quad w_a=w(h_a).$$ For every prescribed accuracy, the partition and representatives can be chosen so that $\|h-h^{\mathcal I}\|_{L^2(\mathsf G_\beta)}$ is small, and so that $m,v$ and the kernels in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels">[rcut:eq:comp-compact-kernels]</a> change uniformly by a small amount on replacing each field by its representative. Construct the partition by first choosing $R$ so that the Gaussian square tails outside $[-R,R]$ are small. In each tail take a representative far enough out that $\tanh$ is uniformly close to its endpoint; uniform continuity on the compactified $w$-square then controls both kernels. A fine mesh of $[-R,R]$ gives the remaining approximations. Choose every interval to have positive $\mathsf G_\beta$-probability.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-empirical-events"></a>
Let $$\pi_a=\mathsf G_\beta(I_a),\qquad
 \widehat\pi_a=\frac1n|\{i:H_i\in I_a\}|.$$ The following properties hold with exponentially small failure at any fixed accuracy: $$\max_a|\widehat\pi_a-\pi_a|\ \text{is small},\qquad
 \frac1n\sum_i|H_i-h^{\mathcal I}(H_i)|^2\ \text{is small},
 \qquad |\overline H-\beta^2|\ \text{is small}.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-empirical-events}$$ We verify the exponential rates because the final comparison needs more than convergence in probability. In the representation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-field-law" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-field-law">[rcut:eq:comp-field-law]</a>, the common shift lies in any prescribed small fixed interval except with probability $e^{-cn}$. For the independent fields $Y_i=\beta^2+\beta Z_i$, the bounded-variable moment generating function estimate from the square-replacement proof gives exponential concentration of each bin count. A common shift of magnitude at most $a$ can move a field to a different bin only when $Y_i$ is within $a$ of a boundary. There are finitely many boundaries. Choose $a$ so that their neighborhoods have small total probability, and concentrate their empirical count by the same estimate. For the empirical square error, the mesh, common shift and boundary counts control the bounded middle interval. The tail contribution is at most a constant times the empirical average of $(1+Y_i^2)\mathbf 1_{\{|Y_i|>R-a\}}$. These variables possess an exponential moment at a small fixed parameter. Increasing $R$ makes its logarithm arbitrarily small, by the same domination argument used for Gaussian square tails. Exponential Markov therefore makes the tail average small with probability $1-e^{-cn}$. The remaining assertion follows from $\overline H-\beta^2\sim N(0,2\beta^2/n)$. Thus every tolerance in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-empirical-events" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-empirical-events">[rcut:eq:comp-empirical-events]</a> has a fixed positive exponential rate. These events also bound the empirical second moment of $H$ and ensure, for large $n$, at least two sites in every bin.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-bin-decomposition"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:comp-normalized-parameters"></a>
For a unit vector $p$, let $p_c$ be its orthogonal projection onto vectors constant on every bin and write $p=p_c+u$. On bin $a$ put $$(p_c)_i=\frac{b_a}{\sqrt n},\qquad
 \sum_{i:H_i\in I_a}u_i=0,\qquad
 \|u_a\|_2^2=\widehat\pi_a r_a^2,
 \quad r_a\ge0.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-bin-decomposition}$$ Then $\sum_a\widehat\pi_a(b_a^2+r_a^2)=1$. It is useful to use the normalized coordinates $$B_a=\sqrt{\widehat\pi_a}\,b_a,
 \qquad R_a=\sqrt{\widehat\pi_a}\,r_a,
 \qquad \sum_a(B_a^2+R_a^2)=1.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-normalized-parameters}$$ These coordinates place all bin parameters in a compact subset of a unit sphere of fixed dimension. They also accommodate vectors concentrated on very few sites. For example, if $p$ is one coordinate vector in a bin of $m=n\widehat\pi_a$ sites, then $$B_a=\frac1{\sqrt m},\qquad R_a=\sqrt{1-\frac1m},$$ and all other coordinates vanish. If instead $p$ is constant and normalized on that bin, then $b_a=\widehat\pi_a^{-1/2}$, but $B_a=1$ and $R_a=0$.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error"></a>
For any probability measure $\nu$ with finite second moment, denote by $\mathcal V_{\beta,\nu}$ the expression in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:variational" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:variational">[rcut:eq:variational]</a> with every bracket and variance taken under $\nu$, and with $D$ defined using that same measure. Write $\mathcal A_{\beta,\nu}$ for its first two lines, so that its last line is the remaining Gaussian comparison term. For the empirical bin measure $\widehat\nu_{\mathcal I}=\sum_a\widehat\pi_a\delta_{h_a}$, let $\overline A=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(v_{a(i)})$, where $a(i)$ is the bin of $H_i$. Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-reduced-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-reduced-form">[rcut:eq:comp-reduced-form]</a> and <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-empirical-events" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-empirical-events">[rcut:eq:comp-empirical-events]</a> imply, with any fixed prescribed accuracy and exponentially small failure, $$\sup_{\|p\|_2=1}
 \left|\widehat M(p)-
   \left[p^{\mathsf T}QWQ\overline A p
       +\mathcal A_{\beta,\widehat\nu_{\mathcal I}}(b,r)\right]
 \right|\ \text{is small}.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error}$$

=3em The bin decomposition explains each part of this expression. The diagonal term is $\sum_a\widehat\pi_aD_{\widehat\nu_{\mathcal I}}(h_a)(b_a^2+r_a^2)$, whereas terms bilinear in bin-constant vectors depend only on $b$. The three rank terms in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-field-decomposition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-field-decomposition">[rcut:eq:comp-field-decomposition]</a> give the three $h$-terms of Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:variational" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:variational">[rcut:eq:variational]</a>, after replacing $\overline H$ by $\beta^2$.

Uniformity follows from the unit norm of $p$, without a pointwise bound on $b$. For instance, write $\|f\|_{n,2}^2=n^{-1}\sum_i f_i^2$ and apply Cauchy–Schwarz: $$\frac{|p^{\mathsf T}(H-H^{\mathcal I})|}{\sqrt n}
       \le\|H-H^{\mathcal I}\|_{n,2},$$ and the corresponding error for $Hv$ is at most this error plus $\max_i|v(H_i)-v_{a(i)}|\,\|H^{\mathcal I}\|_{n,2}$. The other factors in the rank products are controlled by $\|p\|_2=1$ and the empirical second moment of the fields. A uniform kernel error contributes at most a constant times $\|p\|^2$ in the diagonal term, and a constant times $(n^{-1/2}\sum_i|p_i|)^2\le1$ in the cross term. Finally, the matrix term changes by at most $\|W\|\max_i|v(H_i)-v_{a(i)}|$. This proves the uniform error estimate in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error">[rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error]</a>.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-mass-rescaling"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:comp-functional-approximation"></a>
We have now reduced the form to finitely many field values. To apply the hypothesis of Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:planted-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:planted-comparison">80</a>, we must also replace empirical bin masses by their Gaussian probabilities. For parameters $b_a,r_a$ normalized under $\widehat\pi$, define functions on the original intervals by $$b^{\mathcal I}(h)=\frac{B_a}{\sqrt{\pi_a}},\qquad
 r^{\mathcal I}(h)=\frac{R_a}{\sqrt{\pi_a}}
       \quad(h\in I_a).
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-mass-rescaling}$$ They satisfy $\langle(b^{\mathcal I})^2+(r^{\mathcal I})^2\rangle=1$. By choosing the partition accurately enough and the proportion tolerance small enough, we have $$\sup_{\sum_a(B_a^2+R_a^2)=1,\ R_a\ge0}
 \left|\mathcal V_{\beta,\widehat\nu_{\mathcal I}}(b,r)
       -\mathcal V_\beta(b^{\mathcal I},r^{\mathcal I})\right|
       \ \text{arbitrarily small}.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-functional-approximation}$$ The only nonpolynomial term requires care when its radical vanishes. For bin probabilities $\pi$, set $t=(\sqrt{\pi_a})_a$ and $c_{ad}=v_a+v_d$. In normalized coordinates, write the $a$th radical as a Euclidean norm: <a id="rcut:eq:comp-normalized-radical"></a>$$\mathsf N_a(t,B,R)=
 \left\|\left(\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(c_{a1},\ldots,c_{ak})R,
       (I-tt^{\mathsf T})\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(c_{a1},\ldots,c_{ak})B\right)\right\|_2
       \le2.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-normalized-radical}$$ If $t$ changes to another unit probability square-root vector $s$, then $|\mathsf N_a(t,B,R)-\mathsf N_a(s,B,R)|\le4\|t-s\|_2$, since $\|tt^{\mathsf T}-ss^{\mathsf T}\|\le2\|t-s\|_2$. Consequently the last line of the functional, which is $\beta\sum_at_aR_a\mathsf N_a(t,B,R)$, changes by at most $6\beta\|t-s\|_2$. The remaining terms are polynomials in $B,R$, the probability square roots and the fixed bin coefficients. Their coefficients are bounded, so their continuity is uniform on the normalized sphere. Since the finitely many $\pi_a$ are positive, we can choose a sufficiently small tolerance for the empirical proportions even when some fixed bins have very small probability.

It remains to replace each representative by the actual field inside its interval. Again use a norm representation for the last line: at outer field $h$, its radical is $$\left\|\left((v(h)+v(\cdot))r(\cdot),
        (I-\mathbb E)((v(h)+v(\cdot))b(\cdot))\right)\right\|_{L^2\oplus L^2}.$$ Changing $v$ uniformly by at most $a$ changes this vector by norm at most $2a\sqrt{\langle b^2+r^2\rangle}=2a$. This estimate is valid also when either radical is zero. The diagonal and kernel terms use uniform errors, and the coherent terms use, for example, $$|\langle b(h-h^{\mathcal I})\rangle|
       \le\|b\|_2\|h-h^{\mathcal I}\|_2,
 \quad
 \|hv-h^{\mathcal I}v^{\mathcal I}\|_2
       \le\|h-h^{\mathcal I}\|_2
             +\|h^{\mathcal I}\|_2\|v-v^{\mathcal I}\|_\infty.$$ The norm estimate and these $L^2$ estimates complete Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-functional-approximation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-functional-approximation">[rcut:eq:comp-functional-approximation]</a>. In particular, the comparison holds on the whole normalized class, including functions whose mass is concentrated on rare bins.

<a id="pm-h-73"></a>
#### The conditional Gaussian comparison

We now bound the remaining Gaussian matrix term. We use the centered expected-supremum comparison recalled by Vitale (Vitale 2000, Equation (3)) <a id="pm-cite-47"></a>[[Vitale2000](#ref-Vitale2000)]; the proof below verifies the increment inequality for the present constraints.

Condition on $H$ and on the chosen bin partition. Independence in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-field-decomposition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-field-decomposition">[rcut:eq:comp-field-decomposition]</a> leaves the law of $QWQ$ unchanged. For this conditional calculation, represent it with a fresh GOE independent of $H$ and continue to call that matrix $W$. Fix also the empirical proportions and $b_a,r_a$. We optimize only over the residual vectors $u_a$, subject to the zero-sum and norm conditions in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-bin-decomposition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-bin-decomposition">[rcut:eq:comp-bin-decomposition]</a>.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-comp-bin-gaussian"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:comp-bin-gaussian" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-bin-gaussian-bound"></a>
**Lemma 82** (Comparison within fixed bins). *With this conditioning and these fixed parameters, $$\begin{aligned}
 &\mathbb E\left[\sup_u
       p^{\mathsf T}QWQ\overline A p\,\middle|\,H\right]
 \notag\\[-2pt]
 &\qquad\le\beta\sum_a\widehat\pi_a r_a
    \sqrt{\sum_d\widehat\pi_d(v_a+v_d)^2r_d^2
           +\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{d\sim\widehat\pi}((v_a+v_d)b_d)}.
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-bin-gaussian-bound}
 
\end{aligned}$$ The full supremum on the left has Gaussian Lipschitz constant at most $\sqrt2\beta/\sqrt n$, uniformly in the normalized parameters.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-comp-bin-gaussian"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-comp-bin-gaussian</summary>

*Proof.* Separate the bin-constant space $\mathcal C$ from the zero-sum space $\mathcal U_a$ in each bin. Then $\mathcal C$ is orthogonal to $\bigoplus_a\mathcal U_a$, and $\overline A$ preserves each space. Since $Qu=u$ and $Q\overline A u=\overline A u$, the process expands as $$\begin{aligned}
 p^{\mathsf T}QWQ\overline A p
  ={}&C_{b}+
       \sum_a u_a^{\mathsf T}WQ(v_aI+\overline A)p_c
       +u^{\mathsf T}W\overline A u,\\
 C_b={}&p_c^{\mathsf T}QWQ\overline A p_c.
 
\end{aligned}$$ For these fixed bin parameters, $C_b$ is constant in the residual index and has conditional mean zero. The linear residual term uses the $\mathcal U$–$\mathcal C$ block of the GOE, while the quadratic term uses the $\mathcal U$–$\mathcal U$ block. Their independence follows from Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-goe-covariance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-goe-covariance">[rcut:eq:comp-goe-covariance]</a>.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-linear-covariance"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:comp-quadratic-covariance"></a>
For two indices $u,u'$, set $$s_a=\widehat\pi_a r_a^2,
  \qquad q_a=u_a^{\mathsf T}u'_a,
  \qquad V_a=\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{d\sim\widehat\pi}((v_a+v_d)b_d).$$ The linear residual covariance is $$\frac{\beta^2}{n}\sum_a q_a V_a.
  \label{rcut:eq:comp-linear-covariance}$$ Here $Q(v_aI+\overline A)p_c$ lies in $\mathcal C$ and has squared norm $V_a$. Orthogonality to the residual spaces makes the other covariance contraction vanish. Applying the same covariance identity to the quadratic residual term gives $$\frac{\beta^2}{2n}\sum_{a,d}(v_a+v_d)^2q_aq_d.
  \label{rcut:eq:comp-quadratic-covariance}$$ This follows from $$\frac{\beta^2}{n}
   \bigl((u^{\mathsf T}u')
          ((\overline A u)^{\mathsf T}\overline A u')
       +(u^{\mathsf T}\overline A u')
          ((\overline A u)^{\mathsf T}u')\bigr)$$ and symmetrization in the bin indices.

Cauchy–Schwarz gives $-s_a\le q_a\le s_a$, and hence <a id="rcut:eq:comp-overlap-inequality"></a>$$s_as_d-q_aq_d
       \le s_a(s_d-q_d)+s_d(s_a-q_a),
  \label{rcut:eq:comp-overlap-inequality}$$ because the right side minus the left side is $(s_a-q_a)(s_d-q_d)\ge0$. The inequality therefore holds also for negative overlaps. Combining it with Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-linear-covariance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-linear-covariance">[rcut:eq:comp-linear-covariance]</a> and <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-quadratic-covariance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-quadratic-covariance">[rcut:eq:comp-quadratic-covariance]</a> bounds the increment variance of the residual process by $$\frac{2\beta^2}{n}\sum_a(s_a-q_a)
       \left(V_a+\sum_d(v_a+v_d)^2s_d\right).$$ This is exactly the increment variance of the linear process $$\frac\beta{\sqrt n}\sum_a
       \sqrt{V_a+\sum_d(v_a+v_d)^2s_d}\ z_a^{\mathsf T}u_a,$$ with independent standard Gaussian vectors $z_a$ in $\mathcal U_a$. Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gaussian-facts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gaussian-facts">73</a> therefore bounds the expected supremum of the residual process by that of the linear process. We can maximize the latter separately in each residual space: each maximum is the corresponding Gaussian norm multiplied by $\sqrt{s_a}$. Using $\mathbb E\|z_a\|\le\sqrt{\dim\mathcal U_a}
                     \le\sqrt{n\widehat\pi_a}$, we obtain Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-bin-gaussian-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-bin-gaussian-bound">[rcut:eq:comp-bin-gaussian-bound]</a>. Adding $C_b$ leaves this expectation unchanged because its conditional mean is zero and the bin parameters remain fixed.

Concentration must, however, include $C_b$. For a unit vector $p$, the full GOE functional has symmetric coefficient matrix $$\tfrac12\bigl((Qp)(Q\overline A p)^{\mathsf T}
                +(Q\overline A p)(Qp)^{\mathsf T}\bigr),$$ whose Frobenius norm is at most one. Consequently its coefficient norm in independent standard Gaussian coordinates is at most $\sqrt2\beta/\sqrt n$. The supremum inherits this Lipschitz constant, proving the assertion for the full process, including $C_b$. ◻

</details>

The comparison so far fixes $b$ and $r$. We must now make it simultaneous over these parameters. Although $C_b$ has mean zero for each fixed $b$, optimizing $b$ need not preserve that property. We therefore use concentration for the full supremum just proved, and pass through a finite net of the normalized parameters.

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-net-bound"></a>
Fix a mesh size $\eta>0$. The feasible set in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-normalized-parameters" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-normalized-parameters">[rcut:eq:comp-normalized-parameters]</a> has an $\eta$-net inside that set of size at most $(1+2/\eta)^{2k}$, with an inessential enlargement of this bound if necessary. Conditional on $H$, this net is fixed independently of $W$. At each net point, adding the deterministic $\mathcal A$ to the full supremum and applying Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gaussian-facts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gaussian-facts">73</a> gives an upper bound $$\mathcal V_{\beta,\widehat\nu_{\mathcal I}}(b,r)+a
 \label{rcut:eq:comp-net-bound}$$ outside probability $2\exp(-c_\beta n a^2)$, for every fixed $a>0$. A union over the fixed net makes this estimate simultaneous at all its points.

To pass from the net to every parameter, use the quadratic form in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error">[rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error]</a>. Whenever $\|W\|$ and the empirical field second moment are bounded, its operator norm is at most a fixed $K_{\rm form}$. Indeed, $\|W\|$ controls the random term, the coherent terms are bounded rank forms, and the remaining kernels are bounded. The estimates above give exponentially small probability for the complement of this event. For any residual directions, changing $(B,R)$ to $(B',R')$ while keeping the same unit direction in each residual space changes the vector $p$ by exactly $\|(B,R)-(B',R')\|_2$. Hence the form changes by at most $2K_{\rm form}\|(B,R)-(B',R')\|_2$. If a residual norm is zero, choose any direction in its residual space for this comparison. The event giving at least two sites per bin ensures that every such space is nonzero for large $n$. Thus the maximum of the net bounds, enlarged by $2K_{\rm form}\eta$, controls the supremum over all normalized parameters.

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-comp-bin-gaussian-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-comp-bin-gaussian</summary>

*Proof of Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:planted-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:planted-comparison">80</a>.* We assemble the estimates with five fixed error allowances. Given $\delta$ from the hypothesis, put $a=\delta/10$. First require an error at most $a$ in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-reduced-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-reduced-error">[rcut:eq:comp-reduced-error]</a>. Next choose the field partition and tolerances to make each error in Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error">[rcut:eq:comp-bin-form-error]</a> and <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-functional-approximation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-functional-approximation">[rcut:eq:comp-functional-approximation]</a> at most $a$. Take concentration error $a$ in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-net-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-net-bound">[rcut:eq:comp-net-bound]</a> and choose $\eta$ so that $2K_{\rm form}\eta\le a$. Every choice precedes the limit in $n$. The rescaling in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-mass-rescaling" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-mass-rescaling">[rcut:eq:comp-mass-rescaling]</a> makes the limiting functions admissible for the hypothesis. Functional approximation and concentration therefore bound each net value by $1-\delta+2a$. The two form errors and extension from the net add the remaining $3a$, giving, for every unit vector, $$M_J(p)\le1-\delta+5a=1-\frac\delta2.$$

To verify that this simultaneous assertion retains an exponential rate, collect the failure probabilities after fixing all parameters. Their sum has the form $$\begin{aligned}
  &C n^2e^{-c_1n}+2nN_we^{-c_2n}
      +Ck e^{-c_3n}+2N_{\rm par}e^{-c_4n}
      +2\,9^ne^{-c_5n^2},\\
  &\hspace{25mm}N_w<\infty,\qquad
      N_{\rm par}\le(1+2/\eta)^{2k}.
 
\end{aligned}$$ Each $c_i$ is positive and depends only on $\beta$ and the fixed choices. The initial terms account for the entry, diagonal, norm, empirical-tail and common-shift events; $N_w$ counts the deterministic row-parameter mesh. Only the last term uses an exponentially large sphere net, and its rate quadratic in $n$ absorbs $9^n$. The other prefactors are fixed or polynomial in $n$. Hence the sum is at most $e^{-\kappa n}$ for some $\kappa>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. Finally the event in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-exponential-conclusion" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-exponential-conclusion">[rcut:eq:comp-exponential-conclusion]</a> does not involve the auxiliary diagonals, so its probability on the enlarged space equals that on the planted marginal. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-74"></a>
#### From planted probability to Gibbs mass

The planted estimate controls a disorder event for one configuration. Sign conjugation turns it into a bound on the expected unnormalized weight of all exceptional configurations. To obtain Gibbs mass, we also need the partition function to remain near its annealed value on the exponential scale.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-annealed-transfer"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:annealed-transfer" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-gibbs-small"></a>
**Lemma 83** (Annealed transfer). *Fix $0<\beta<1$. Let $\mathcal A_n$ be a measurable event for symmetric zero-diagonal interaction matrices, and suppose that $\widehat\mathbb P_n(\mathcal A_n)\le e^{-\kappa n}$ for all large $n$, with a fixed $\kappa>0$. For $x\in\{-1,1\}^n$, write $J^x=\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(x)J\mathop{\mathrm{diag}}(x)$ and define $$\mathcal B_J=\{x:J^x\in\mathcal A_n\}.$$ There are events whose original disorder probabilities tend to one on which $$\mu_J(\mathcal B_J)\le e^{-\kappa n/2}.
  \label{rcut:eq:comp-gibbs-small}$$ In fact the complementary probabilities can be bounded by $e^{-c n}$ for a fixed $c>0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-annealed-transfer"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-annealed-transfer</summary>

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-annealed-numerator"></a>
*Proof.* Let $Z_J$ be the original partition function and $$Z_{\mathcal B,J}=\sum_x e^{x^{\mathsf T}Jx/2}\mathbf 1_{\{J^x\in\mathcal A_n\}}.$$ The original disorder law is invariant under sign conjugation. Each summand therefore reduces to the all-positive configuration, and the planted density in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-planted-density" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-planted-density">[rcut:eq:comp-planted-density]</a> gives $$\mathbb EZ_{\mathcal B,J}
    =2^n\mathbb E\left[e^{\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal A_n}\right]
    =\mathbb EZ_J\,\widehat\mathbb P_n(\mathcal A_n)
    \le e^{-\kappa n}\mathbb EZ_J.
  \label{rcut:eq:comp-annealed-numerator}$$ Here $\mathbb EZ_J=2^n\exp(\beta^2(n-1)/4)$.

We next bound the denominator $Z_J$ from below on the exponential scale. Gaussian integration, with an independent uniform sign vector $(\varepsilon_i)_{i=1}^n$, gives the exact second-moment identity <a id="rcut:eq:comp-partition-second-moment"></a>$$\frac{\mathbb EZ_J^2}{(\mathbb EZ_J)^2}
    =e^{-\beta^2/2}\mathbb E_{\varepsilon}
       \exp\left\{\frac{\beta^2}{2n}
                    \left(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\right)^2\right\}
    \le\frac{e^{-\beta^2/2}}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}=:C_\beta.
  \label{rcut:eq:comp-partition-second-moment}$$ For the inequality, introduce a standard Gaussian $Z$ to linearize the square. The sign average becomes $\cosh(\beta Z/\sqrt n)^n\le e^{\beta^2Z^2/2}$, with expectation $(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$. Separate the event $\{Z_J\ge\mathbb EZ_J/2\}$ and apply Cauchy–Schwarz to obtain $$\mathbb P_n(Z_J\ge\mathbb EZ_J/2)\ge\frac1{4C_\beta}.$$

<a id="rcut:eq:comp-partition-lower"></a>
We upgrade this fixed positive probability using concentration. Each derivative of $\log Z_J$ in an independent standard disorder Gaussian has magnitude at most $\beta/\sqrt n$, giving Lipschitz constant at most $\beta\sqrt{(n-1)/2}$. The preceding lower event and Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:gaussian-facts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:gaussian-facts">73</a> force $$\mathbb E\log Z_J\ge\log\mathbb EZ_J-C\sqrt n.$$ Otherwise $\log\mathbb EZ_J-\log2$ would exceed the mean by a sufficiently large multiple of $\sqrt n$, and upper-tail concentration would make the preceding event less likely than its fixed lower bound. Lower-tail concentration now gives, for all large $n$, $$\mathbb P_n\left(\log Z_J<\log\mathbb EZ_J-\frac{\kappa n}4\right)
      \le e^{-c n}.
  \label{rcut:eq:comp-partition-lower}$$ Constants here may depend on the fixed $\beta$ and $\kappa$.

By Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-annealed-numerator" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-annealed-numerator">[rcut:eq:comp-annealed-numerator]</a> and Markov’s inequality, $$\mathbb P_n\left(Z_{\mathcal B,J}>
          e^{-3\kappa n/4}\mathbb EZ_J\right)\le e^{-\kappa n/4}.$$ On the complement of this event and the event in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-partition-lower" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-partition-lower">[rcut:eq:comp-partition-lower]</a>, divide the numerator bound by the partition-function lower bound to obtain Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:comp-gibbs-small" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:comp-gibbs-small">[rcut:eq:comp-gibbs-small]</a>. A smaller positive exponent absorbs the sum of the two failure probabilities. ◻

</details>

<a id="rcut:sec:scalar"></a>
### A uniform bound on the variational expression

This appendix supplies the variational gap required by the planted comparison. We use the notation of Section <a href="#rcut:sec:comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:comparison">13</a>: $h\sim N(\beta^2,\beta^2)$, brackets denote expectation under this law, and $m=\tanh h$, $v=1-m^2$, $w=1-m$. The bound below has one numerical margin for the entire stated temperature interval and for all admissible functions.

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-scalar-gap"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:scalar-gap" class="proposition">

**Proposition 84** (Uniform scalar gap). *For every $\beta\in[0.35,0.5]$, every real measurable $b\in L^2$, and every measurable $r\geq0$ in $L^2$ satisfying $\langle b^2+r^2\rangle=1$, the expression in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:variational" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:variational">[rcut:eq:variational]</a> satisfies $$\mathcal V_\beta(b,r)\leq 0.9969.$$*

</div>

Every terminating decimal in the proof denotes an exact rational number. We will apply Young’s inequality with a positive field-dependent multiplier to separate the square-root term into quadratic terms in $b$ and $r$. The multiplier has two jobs: the total diagonal coefficient must stay below $.9789$, and its cost on $b^2$ must absorb the remaining quadratic form, with an excess of at most $.018\langle b^2\rangle$. Normalization will then give $.9789+.018=.9969$. The functional reductions are proved here. The scalar enclosures on which they rely, including quadrature and arithmetic errors, are proved in Appendix <a href="#rcut:sec:scalar-certificate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:scalar-certificate">17</a>.

<a id="rcut:sec:scalar-identities"></a>
#### Identities and the positive kernel remainder

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-sign-identity"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-integration-parts"></a>
We begin with two identities that simplify the scalar coefficients. Conditioned on $|h|=t$, the sign of the field has weights proportional to $e^t$ and $e^{-t}$, and hence mean $\tanh t$. Multiplying by an even function of the field gives, for every $q$ for which the expectations exist, $$\langle m q(m^2)\rangle=\langle m^2 q(m^2)\rangle.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-sign-identity}$$ In particular, $\langle m\rangle=\langle m^2\rangle$ and $\langle mv\rangle=\langle m^2v\rangle$. The second identity follows by Gaussian integration by parts with $v'=-2mv$: $$\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}(h,v)=-2\beta^2\langle mv\rangle,
 \qquad
 \langle(h-\beta^2+2\beta^2m)v\rangle=0.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-integration-parts}$$

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-multiplier"></a>
Choose the following positive multiplier for Young’s inequality. Its associated cost $k$ will combine with $D$ in the diagonal estimate: $$\begin{split}
 \Lambda{}(h)&=0.45+0.25m(h)^2-0.06m(h),\\
 k(y)&=\frac{\beta^2}{4}
       \left\langle\frac{(1-y^2+v)^2}{\Lambda{}}\right\rangle,
       \qquad -1\leq y\leq1,\\
 a&=\langle v\rangle,
 \qquad l=\langle \Lambda{}\rangle=0.64-0.19a.
 \end{split}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-multiplier}$$ Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-sign-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-sign-identity">[rcut:eq:scalar-sign-identity]</a> gives the expression for $l$ in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-multiplier">[rcut:eq:scalar-multiplier]</a>; since $a\leq1$, we have $l\geq0.45$. Completing the square also gives $\Lambda{}=0.4464+0.25(m-0.12)^2\geq0.4464$. These positive bounds justify the divisions below. To bound the kernel term, define $$g=\frac{v}{w+3/4},\qquad G=\langle g\rangle,
 \qquad
 R=\left\langle\frac{(1+m)v}{2}-\frac32 g^2\right\rangle.$$

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-kernel"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:scalar-kernel" class="lemma">

**Lemma 85** (Kernel remainder). *The quantity $R$ is nonnegative. For every real $b\in L^2$, <a id="rcut:eq:scalar-kernel-bound"></a>$$\langle b(h)K_0(h,h_*)b(h_*)\rangle_{h,h_*}
 \leq \frac32\langle bg\rangle^2+R\langle b^2\rangle.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-kernel-bound}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-kernel"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-kernel</summary>

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-residual-diagonal"></a>
*Proof.* We separate one rank-one term from the kernel and bound the remainder by its diagonal. Put $q=(w-3/4)/(w+3/4)$. A finite field has $w>0$ and $|q|<1$, so expansion as a geometric series gives $$K_0(h,h_*)=\frac32 g(h)g(h_*)\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q(h)^j q(h_*)^j.$$ The $j=0$ term will give $\frac32\langle bg\rangle^2$. For the remaining terms set $\phi_j=\sqrt{3/2}\,gq^j$, $j\geq1$. Their diagonal sum is $$\rho:=\sum_{j\geq1}\phi_j^2
 =\frac{(1+m)v}{2}\,q^2
 =\frac{(1+m)v}{2}-\frac32g^2\geq0.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-residual-diagonal}$$ The bound $(1+m)v=(1-m)(1+m)^2\leq32/27$ implies $\rho\leq16/27$. Moreover $\langle\rho\rangle=R$, proving that $R\geq0$. To justify the series for an arbitrary signed $b\in L^2$, apply Cauchy–Schwarz: $$\sum_{j\geq1}\langle|b\phi_j|\rangle^2
 \leq\langle b^2\rangle\sum_{j\geq1}\langle\phi_j^2\rangle
 =R\langle b^2\rangle.$$ This proves absolute summability of the signed double-integral series, so its sum equals $\sum_{j\geq1}\langle b\phi_j\rangle^2$. The same estimate bounds that sum by $R\langle b^2\rangle$. Restoring the $j=0$ term proves the kernel bound. ◻

</details>

<a id="rcut:sec:scalar-data"></a>
#### The scalar data

Write $s_f=\langle(f-\langle f\rangle)^2\rangle^{1/2}$ for the standard deviation of a real function $f$. Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-data" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-data">[rcut:lem:scalar-data]</a> provides the numerical inputs for both parts of the argument. Its five endpoint enclosures control the diagonal coefficient. To treat the remaining quadratic form, we will write $b=\langle b\rangle+b_0$, with $\langle b_0\rangle=0$, and bound the constant, centered, and mixed terms using the moment table. Appendix <a href="#rcut:sec:scalar-certificate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:scalar-certificate">17</a> proves all these enclosures.

<a id="stmt-rcut-tab-scalar-moments"></a>
<div id="rcut:tab:scalar-moments" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-five-enclosures"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-F"></a>
**Lemma 86** (Certified scalar enclosures). *<span id="rcut:lem:scalar-data" label="rcut:lem:scalar-data"></span> At $\beta=1/2$, define $$d(y)=\frac14\left\langle\frac{v^2}{2-y-m}\right\rangle,
 \qquad -1\leq y\leq1,$$ where at $y=1$ the integrand is interpreted as $v(1+m)$. Then $$\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
 \text{quantity}& k(0)&k(1)&d(0)&d'(0)&d(1)\\ \hline
 \text{lower bound}&.4276&.0898&.0925&.0522&.2288\\
 \text{upper bound}&.4278&.0900&.0927&.0524&.2290
 \end{array}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-five-enclosures}$$ All bounds in this display are strict. For every $\beta\in[7/20,1/2]$, define $$F=(v+a)h+2\beta^2mv+
       \left(0.50-\frac{\beta^2a}{l}\right)v
       +0.12m+3\beta^2Gg.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-F}$$ At the five exact values of $\beta$ displayed in Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-moments">86</a>, each of the eight entries after the first column differs from its corresponding expectation or standard deviation under $N(\beta^2,\beta^2)$ by less than $0.001$.*

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-envelope"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:scalar-envelope" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-envelope"></a>
**Lemma 87** (Diagonal envelope). *For $0.35\leq\beta\leq0.5$ and every real field $h$, $$\Lambda{}(h)+D(h)+k(m(h))\leq0.9789.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-envelope}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-envelope"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-envelope</summary>

*Proof.* We first reduce the temperature interval to its upper endpoint and then bound the dependence on the field. The Gaussian field has density $$p_\beta(h)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}\beta}
   \exp\left(-\frac{\beta^2}{2}+h-\frac{h^2}{2\beta^2}\right).$$ The logarithmic derivative of $\beta^2p_\beta(h)$ is $\beta^{-1}-\beta+h^2\beta^{-3}>0$ for $\beta<1$. Thus, for fixed $y$, positivity of the integrands bounds the corresponding integrals in $D$ and $k$ by those at $\beta=1/2$. At that endpoint, $D(h)=d(m(h))$.

It remains to bound the endpoint expression uniformly in $-1\leq y\leq1$. Convexity of $k$ as a function of $y^2$ gives $k(y)\leq k(0)+(k(1)-k(0))y^2$. To treat $d$, take $A=2-m>1$ and use the identity $$\frac1{A-y}=\frac1A+\frac{y}{A^2}
             +\frac{y^2}{A^2(A-y)}$$ which, together with $A-y\geq A-1$, gives, for every $-1\leq y\leq1$, $$d(y)\leq d(0)+d'(0)y+
               y^2\bigl(d(1)-d(0)-d'(0)\bigr).$$ After adding $\Lambda{}$, the quadratic bounds give the following upper bound for $\Lambda{}+d+k$: <a id="rcut:eq:scalar-envelope-arithmetic"></a>$$\max\{.45+d(0)+k(0),\ .70+k(1)+d(1)-d'(0)\}
       +|d'(0)-.06|.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-envelope-arithmetic}$$ We evaluate this bound using slightly enlarged intervals: replace the enclosures in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-five-enclosures" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-five-enclosures">[rcut:eq:scalar-five-enclosures]</a> by radius $.0003$ about the respective centers $$.4277,\quad .0899,\quad .0926,\quad .0523,\quad .2289.$$ The two entries of the maximum are then at most $.9709$ and $.9674$, and the absolute-value term is at most $.0080$. Their sum proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-envelope">[rcut:eq:scalar-envelope]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="rcut:sec:scalar-reduction"></a>
#### Young’s inequality and the centered coherent form

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-coherent"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-young"></a>
The diagonal envelope is now available. We next convert the radical in the variational expression into quadratic terms, retaining its negative square produced by expanding the variance. Set $A=\langle b\rangle$ and $B=\langle bv\rangle$. Apply $\beta r\sqrt{T}\leq \Lambda{}r^2+\beta^2T/(4\Lambda{})$ to the last term of Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:variational" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:variational">[rcut:eq:variational]</a>. Interchanging the two expectations in the resulting quadratic terms gives $$\langle(\Lambda{}+k(m))r^2\rangle
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \langle k(m)b^2\rangle
   -\frac{\beta^2}{4}\left\langle\frac{(B+vA)^2}{\Lambda{}}\right\rangle.$$ Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the negative term from above by $-\beta^2(B+aA)^2/(4l)$. Collect it with the products of expectations and the kernel term, defining the coherent form $$\begin{split}
 \mathcal C_\beta(b)={}&\langle bh\rangle B
 +A\langle b(h-\beta^2+2\beta^2m)v\rangle\\
 &+\beta^2\langle bK_0b_*\rangle
 -\frac{\beta^2}{4l}(B+aA)^2,
 \end{split}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-coherent}$$ and $$\mathcal V_\beta(b,r)
 \leq\langle(D+k(m))(b^2+r^2)\rangle
       +\langle \Lambda{}r^2\rangle+\mathcal C_\beta(b).
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-young}$$

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-coherent"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:scalar-coherent" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-coherent-bound"></a>
**Lemma 88** (Coherent form bound). *For every $0.35\leq\beta\leq0.5$ and every real $b\in L^2$, $$\mathcal C_\beta(b)\leq\langle(\Lambda{}+.018)b^2\rangle.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-coherent-bound}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-coherent"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-coherent</summary>

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-full-expansion"></a>
*Proof.* We reduce the inequality to a quadratic form in the constant and centered parts of $b$. Write $b=A+b_0$, with $\langle b_0\rangle=0$, and set $H_0=\langle b_0h\rangle$, $B_0=\langle b_0v\rangle$, $G_0=\langle b_0g\rangle$. Replace the kernel term by Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-kernel">85</a>, and call the resulting upper form $\mathcal C_\beta^+$. Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-integration-parts" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-integration-parts">[rcut:eq:scalar-integration-parts]</a> makes its purely constant part $\beta^2(a+\tfrac32G^2+R-a^2/l)A^2$. Define the two slacks <a id="rcut:eq:scalar-slacks"></a>$$\begin{split}
 U_0&=l+.018+\beta^2\left(\frac{a^2}{l}-a-\frac32G^2\right)
                -\beta^2R,\\
 U_1&=.4644-\frac{\beta s_v}{2}+\beta^2\langle mv\rangle
                -\beta^2\left(\frac32s_g^2+R\right).
 \end{split}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-slacks}$$ Expanding the upper form around $A+b_0$ and subtracting the desired upper bound gives $$\begin{split}
 \mathcal C_\beta^+(b)-\langle(\Lambda{}+.018)b^2\rangle
 ={}&-U_0A^2+A\langle b_0F\rangle+H_0B_0
       +\frac32\beta^2G_0^2\\
 &+\beta^2R\langle b_0^2\rangle
       -\frac{\beta^2B_0^2}{4l}
       -\langle(\Lambda{}+.018)b_0^2\rangle.
 \end{split}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-full-expansion}$$ The coefficient of the mixed term can be checked directly. The first two terms in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-coherent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-coherent">[rcut:eq:scalar-coherent]</a> give $(v+a)h+2\beta^2mv$; the negative square gives $-\beta^2av/l$; and the kernel bound gives $3\beta^2Gg$. Subtracting $2\langle \Lambda{}b_0\rangle$ contributes $.50v+.12m$, up to a constant whose pairing with $b_0$ vanishes. These contributions sum to $F$ from Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-F" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-F">[rcut:eq:scalar-F]</a>.

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-two-dimensional"></a>
We next bound the terms quadratic in $b_0$. On the centered space, $$H_0B_0\leq\frac{\beta s_v+\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}(h,v)}2\langle b_0^2\rangle
 =\left(\frac{\beta s_v}{2}-\beta^2\langle mv\rangle\right)
       \langle b_0^2\rangle.$$ For this inequality, the symmetric rank-two operator associated with $u=h-\langle h\rangle$ and $z=v-a$ has largest eigenvalue $(\|u\|_2\|z\|_2+\langle uz\rangle)/2$. Together with $G_0^2\leq s_g^2\langle b_0^2\rangle$ and $\Lambda{}+.018\geq.4644$, this controls all centered quadratic terms. Discarding the negative $B_0^2$ term from Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-full-expansion" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-full-expansion">[rcut:eq:scalar-full-expansion]</a> yields $$\mathcal C_\beta(b)-\langle(\Lambda{}+.018)b^2\rangle
 \leq-U_0A^2-U_1\langle b_0^2\rangle+A\langle b_0F\rangle.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-two-dimensional}$$ By Cauchy–Schwarz, the mixed term is at most $s_F|A|\|b_0\|_2$. Thus positivity of $U_0,U_1$ and the bound $s_F<2\sqrt{U_0U_1}$ will finish the proof. We verify these inequalities on the entire temperature interval, using the full radius $.001$ of Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-moments">86</a>.

First we establish the monotonicities needed between table entries. The density of $|h|$ is proportional to $\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta^2/2-h^2/(2\beta^2)}\cosh h$ on $h\geq0$; its ratio at a larger and a smaller $\beta$ is increasing in $h$. To see the implication for expectations, let $\ell$ be this ratio and $f$ a decreasing function. For independent $X,X'$ under the smaller-$\beta$ law, $$\mathop{\mathrm{Cov}}(f(X),\ell(X))
 =\frac12\mathbb E[(f(X)-f(X'))(\ell(X)-\ell(X'))]\leq0.$$ Since $\mathbb E\ell(X)=1$, the expectation of $f$ decreases as $\beta$ increases. In particular $a$ decreases. For $G$, average $g$ over the conditional signs and write $u=\tanh^2|h|$; the resulting function is $$\frac{(1-u)(1.75+u)}{1.75^2-u}.$$ Its derivative, $4(64u^2-392u-35)/(16u-49)^2<0$ for $0\leq u\leq1$, proves that $G$ decreases as well. The pointwise increase of $\beta^2p_\beta$ from Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-envelope" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-envelope">87</a> gives the other needed monotonicities: both $\beta^2\langle mv\rangle=\beta^2\langle m^2v\rangle$ and $\beta^2R$ increase. For $\beta^2s_v^2$ and $\beta^2s_g^2$, write each weighted variance as the infimum over constant centers of the integral of a nonnegative squared function against $\beta^2p_\beta$. Each such integral increases, so the infimum does too.

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-interval-slacks"></a>
Now take successive temperatures $j<z$ from Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-moments">86</a>. Enclose $a$ on this interval by taking $a_-$ to be the center at $z$ minus $.001$, and $a_+$ the center at $j$ plus $.001$. Define $G_-,G_+$ in the same way, and set $l_-=.64-.19a_+$, $l_+=.64-.19a_-$. For any endpoint quantity $X_t$, write $X_t^+$ and $X_t^-$ for its table center plus and minus $.001$. The monotonicities above give the following lower bounds for the slacks throughout $[j,z]$: $$\begin{split}
 \underline U_0={}&l_-+.018
   +j^2\left(\frac{a_-^2}{l_+}-a_--\frac32G_+^2\right)-z^2R_z^+,\\
 \underline U_1={}&.4644-\frac{z(s_v)_z^+}{2}
   +j^2\langle mv\rangle_j^-
   -z^2\left(\frac32((s_g)_z^+)^2+R_z^+\right).
 \end{split}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-interval-slacks}$$ For the first bound, use that $a^2/l-a$ increases in $a$ and decreases in $l$ on $.795\leq a\leq.891$, $.45\leq l\leq.489$. The parenthesized coefficient in that line is positive on each interval; its explicit lower bounds are given below.

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-interval-cross"></a>
To control the mixed coefficient, compare its standard deviation to the value at the right endpoint. For $j\leq\beta\leq z$, the density ratio satisfies $$\sup_h\frac{p_\beta(h)}{p_z(h)}
 =\frac z\beta\exp\left(\frac{z^2-\beta^2}{2}\right)
 \leq\frac zj\exp\left(\frac{z^2-j^2}{2}\right).$$ Choose a constant center before changing measure. This bounds the standard deviation of any function by its standard deviation under $p_z$ times the square root of the displayed factor. Next compare the coefficients of $F$ at $\beta$ and $z$, and apply the triangle inequality for the centered $L^2(p_z)$ seminorm. With $s_h=z$ under $p_z$, this gives $$\begin{split}
 \overline s_F={}&
 \sqrt{\frac zj\exp\left(\frac{z^2-j^2}{2}\right)}
 \biggl[(s_F)_z^++(a_+-a_-)z
       +2(z^2-j^2)(s_{mv})_z^+\\
 &\hspace{15mm}
       +\left(\frac{z^2a_+}{l_-}-\frac{j^2a_-}{l_+}\right)(s_v)_z^+
       +3(z^2G_+-j^2G_-)(s_g)_z^+\biggr].
 \end{split}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-interval-cross}$$ Substituting the full enclosures from Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-moments">86</a> gives the interval bounds in Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-intervals" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-intervals">2</a>. Appendix <a href="#rcut:sec:scalar-certificate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:scalar-certificate">17</a> specifies their directed-arithmetic verification. In the same interval order, the parenthesized coefficients in the first line of Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-interval-slacks" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-interval-slacks">[rcut:eq:scalar-interval-slacks]</a> exceed $.229787,.152558,.111290,.074675$, confirming the positivity used above.

<div id="rcut:tab:scalar-intervals">

|:-------------:|:-----------------:|:-----------------:|:---------------------------------------:|:----------------:|
| $[.350,.400]$ |      .513818      |      .437638      |                 .948403                 |     .842935      |
