The table therefore provides uniform margins $U_0>.513$, $U_1>.426$, $s_F<.920$, and $2\sqrt{U_0U_1}>.930$. These margins absorb the mixed term: $$s_F|A|\|b_0\|_2
 \leq\frac{92}{93}\bigl(U_0A^2+U_1\|b_0\|_2^2\bigr).$$ Substitution in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-two-dimensional" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-two-dimensional">[rcut:eq:scalar-two-dimensional]</a> makes its right side at most $-(.426/93)\|b\|_2^2$, and in particular nonpositive. This proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-coherent-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-coherent-bound">[rcut:eq:scalar-coherent-bound]</a> for every $b\in L^2$. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-coherent-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-coherent</summary>

*Proof of Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:scalar-gap" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:scalar-gap">84</a>.* We can now assemble the two bounds. Insert the coherent-form estimate of Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-coherent" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-coherent">88</a> into Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-young" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-young">[rcut:eq:scalar-young]</a>, and then apply the diagonal envelope of Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-envelope" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-envelope">87</a>: $$\mathcal V_\beta(b,r)
 \leq\langle(D+k(m)+\Lambda{})(b^2+r^2)\rangle+.018\langle b^2\rangle
 \leq.9789+.018=.9969.$$ The argument applies to the full function class in the proposition. The coefficients $h,hv$ belong to $L^2$, all other coefficient functions are bounded, and Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-kernel">85</a> already justifies the kernel integral for signed, unbounded $b$. The quantity under the last radical in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:variational" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:variational">[rcut:eq:variational]</a> is at most $4\langle b^2+r^2\rangle=4$, making its pairing with $r$ finite. Thus Fubini for the nonnegative quadratic integrals and every use of Cauchy–Schwarz are valid without an infinity-norm bound on either function. The estimate consequently also covers concentration on arbitrarily rare field sets. ◻

</details>

<a id="rcut:sec:dynamics"></a>
### Avoiding exceptional states and the mixing scale

The gradient estimate contracts outside an exceptional set of small Gibbs mass. To use it from an arbitrary initial configuration, we must also control the time the chain spends in that set. We first obtain this control after a constant burn-in, then propagate gradients over logarithmic times. The resulting concentration bounds will locate the median mixing time on that same scale.

<a id="rcut:eq:dyn-entropy-input"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:dyn-gradient-input"></a>
Fix $\beta\in[0,1/2)$. Intersect the good-disorder events in Propositions <a href="#rcut:prop:good-disorder" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:good-disorder">74</a>, <a href="#rcut:prop:uniform-gap" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:uniform-gap">76</a>, <a href="#rcut:prop:entropy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:entropy">77</a>, and <a href="#rcut:prop:typical-gradient" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:typical-gradient">79</a>, and denote the resulting event by $\mathcal G_n$. Then $\mathbb P_J(\mathcal G_n)\to1$. We collect the inputs on this event before starting the argument. There are constants $K,C_E,C_L,\gamma,\kappa>0$ and $A\ge0$, depending only on the fixed $\beta$, such that the following bounds hold for all sufficiently large $n$ and every realization in $\mathcal G_n$. The interaction satisfies $\|J\|\le K$, the continuous-time gap is at least $\gamma$, and the transition density has the entropy bound $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu\!\left(\frac{S_t(x,\cdot)}{\mu}\right)
 \le C_E n e^{-t/C_L}
 \qquad(x\in\Omega_n,\ t\ge0).
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-entropy-input}$$ Here the quotient denotes the density with respect to $\mu$. There is also a set $\mathcal B=\mathcal B(J)\subseteq\Omega_n$ such that $$\mu(\mathcal B)\le e^{-\kappa n},\qquad
 (\partial_r-L)U(S_r f)
 \le \bigl(-\kappa+A\mathbf 1_{\mathcal B}\bigr)U(S_r f)
 \quad(r\ge0)
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-gradient-input}$$ for every real function $f$ on $\Omega_n$. The same $\kappa$ can be used for the exceptional mass and the contraction rate by shrinking it and enlarging $A$. From now on we work deterministically on $\mathcal G_n$: both the constants and the sufficiently large dimension thresholds are uniform over this event. Suppressing the fixed disorder, we write $\mathbb P_x,\mathbb E_x$ for the law and expectation of the continuous-time chain started at $x$.

<a id="pm-h-80"></a>
#### Gradient propagation and jump concentration

We begin by expressing the gradient bound along a chain trajectory. The exponential weight below records contraction outside the exceptional set and the possible loss during visits to it. A rough bound on this weight will suffice for the initial burn-in.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-feynman-kac"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:feynman-kac" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:dyn-feynman-kac"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:dyn-rough-envelope"></a>
**Lemma 89** (Feynman–Kac comparison). *Put $V=-\kappa+A\mathbf 1_{\mathcal B}$. For every real $f$, every $0\le s\le d$, and every initial configuration $x$, $$U(S_d f)(x)
 \le \mathbb E_x\!\left[
    \exp\!\left(\int_0^s V(X_u)\,du\right)
    U(S_{d-s}f)(X_s)
 \right].
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-feynman-kac}$$ Consequently, $$\|U(S_r f)\|_\infty
 \le e^{Ar}\|U(f)\|_\infty
 \qquad(r\ge0).
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-rough-envelope}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-feynman-kac"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-feynman-kac</summary>

*Proof.* Let $G(r,x)=U(S_r f)(x)$. Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-gradient-input" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-gradient-input">[rcut:eq:dyn-gradient-input]</a> gives $-\partial_rG+L G+VG\ge0$. Following the chain forward while running the semigroup parameter backward therefore gives nonnegative drift for $$\exp\!\left(\int_0^u V(X_v)\,dv\right)G(d-u,X_u),
 \qquad 0\le u\le s,$$ so the finite state space and bounded time interval justify taking expectations. This proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-feynman-kac" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-feynman-kac">[rcut:eq:dyn-feynman-kac]</a>. For the rough envelope, take $s=d=r$ and bound the exponential weight using $V\le A$. This gives Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-rough-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-rough-envelope">[rcut:eq:dyn-rough-envelope]</a>. ◻

</details>

To convert gradient envelopes into fluctuation bounds we use Lemma <a href="#lem:input-mgf" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:input-mgf">3</a>, with $U(f)=\|df\|^2$. Its complete finite-chain proof uses only the heat-bath jump rates, so it applies throughout the present argument without a temperature assumption.

<a id="pm-h-81"></a>
#### Uniform avoidance after a constant burn-in

Small Gibbs mass alone does not control a chain started inside the exceptional set. We first show that entropy dissipation moves a fixed amount of probability a macroscopic Hamming distance away from that set. Concentration of the distance then makes the probability of a visit at any later deterministic time very small.

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-bad-avoidance"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:bad-avoidance" class="proposition">

**Proposition 90**. *There are constants $d_0,c_{\mathrm a}>0$, independent of $n$ and the realization in $\mathcal G_n$, such that, for all sufficiently large $n$, <a id="rcut:eq:dyn-bad-avoidance"></a>$$\sup_{x\in\Omega_n}\mathbb P_x(X_u\in\mathcal B)
 \le q_n:=e^{-c_{\mathrm a}\sqrt n}
 \qquad(u\ge d_0).
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-bad-avoidance}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-bad-avoidance"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-bad-avoidance</summary>

<a id="rcut:eq:dyn-neighborhood"></a>
*Proof.* If $\mathcal B$ is empty there is nothing to prove. Otherwise we first enlarge it by a small fixed fraction of the coordinates and show that the enlargement still has exponentially small Gibbs mass. Let $d_H$ denote Hamming distance and, for $0<\delta<1/2$, set $$\mathcal B^{(\delta)}
 =\{x:d_H(x,\mathcal B)\le\lfloor\delta n\rfloor\}.$$ If $d_H(x,y)\le\delta n$, then $$\left|\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Jx-y^{\mathsf T}Jy}{2}\right|
 =\frac12\left|(x-y)^{\mathsf T}J(x+y)\right|
 \le2K\sqrt\delta\,n.$$ Thus the energy change within the neighborhood is controlled by the operator norm of the interaction. Counting the neighbors of each $y\in\mathcal B$, with multiplicity, gives $$\mu(\mathcal B^{(\delta)})
 \le \mu(\mathcal B)e^{2K\sqrt\delta\,n}
       \sum_{j\le\delta n}\binom nj
 \le \exp\!\left[-n\bigl(\kappa-2K\sqrt\delta-h(\delta)\bigr)\right],
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-neighborhood}$$ where $h(\delta)=-\delta\log\delta-(1-\delta)\log(1-\delta)$. The binomial bound follows by inserting $z=\delta/(1-\delta)<1$ into $(1+z)^n$ and using $z^j\ge z^{\delta n}$ for $j\le\delta n$. Choose a fixed $\delta$ so small that $2K\sqrt\delta+h(\delta)\le\kappa/2$. Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-neighborhood" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-neighborhood">[rcut:eq:dyn-neighborhood]</a> then bounds the neighborhood mass by $e^{-\kappa n/2}$.

We next use this small equilibrium mass to bound the probability of the neighborhood after burn-in. For probability measures $\nu,\mu$ and an event of probabilities $p,q$, respectively, conditioning on the event and its complement gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ent}}_\mu\!\left(\frac{\nu}{\mu}\right)
 \ge p\log\frac pq+(1-p)\log\frac{1-p}{1-q}
 \ge p\log\frac1q-\log2.$$ Apply this inequality to $\nu=S_{d_0}(x,\cdot)$ and the neighborhood, choosing the burn-in time to be $$d_0=1+C_L\log\max\{1,8C_E/\kappa\}.$$ By Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-entropy-input" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-entropy-input">[rcut:eq:dyn-entropy-input]</a>, for sufficiently large $n$, $$\mathbb P_x(X_{d_0}\in\mathcal B^{(\delta)})
 \le\frac{2C_E}{\kappa}e^{-d_0/C_L}
       +\frac{2\log2}{\kappa n}
 \le\frac12.$$

At least half the law is now outside the neighborhood. To strengthen this fact to avoidance of the original set, consider $g(x)=d_H(x,\mathcal B)/\sqrt n$. Its half-differences have magnitude at most $1/(2\sqrt n)$, so $U(g)\le1/4$. Outside $\mathcal B^{(\delta)}$ the distance is greater than $\delta n$. The integer rounding in the neighborhood definition therefore gives $$S_{d_0}g(x)\ge\frac{\delta\sqrt n}{2}.$$ Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-rough-envelope" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-rough-envelope">[rcut:eq:dyn-rough-envelope]</a> permits the envelope $b(r)=e^{Ar}/4$ for $0\le r\le d_0$. Put $Q=e^{Ad_0/2}$. Then $B\le Q^2/4$ and $I\le d_0Q^2/4$ in Lemma <a href="#lem:input-mgf" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:input-mgf">3</a>. Taking $\theta=-1/Q$ in Lemma <a href="#lem:input-mgf" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:input-mgf">3</a> yields $$\mathbb P_x(X_{d_0}\in\mathcal B)
 \le\exp\!\left(\frac{e d_0}{2}
                 -\frac{\delta\sqrt n}{2Q}\right)
 \le e^{-c_{\mathrm a}\sqrt n},
 \qquad c_{\mathrm a}=\frac{\delta}{4Q},$$ after increasing the fixed minimum dimension. The event on the left is exactly $\{g(X_{d_0})=0\}$, so the negative exponential moment controls precisely the required lower tail. This proves avoidance at the burn-in time. To obtain the same bound at every deterministic $u\ge d_0$, apply the Markov property to the last burn-in interval: $$\mathbb P_x(X_u\in\mathcal B)
 =\mathbb E_x\!\left[\mathbb P_{X_{u-d_0}}(X_{d_0}\in\mathcal B)\right]
 \le q_n.$$ Every choice depended only on the constants collected at the start of this section. The estimate is therefore uniform in the starting point and in the disorder on the good event. ◻

</details>

The pointwise-in-time avoidance bound also controls occupation time by integration. We now return to the Feynman–Kac weight: on a logarithmic time horizon, an exceptional occupation larger than one has such small probability that even the rough exponential envelope is harmless.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-dyn-occupation-propagation"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:dyn-occupation-propagation" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:gradient-propagation"></a>
**Lemma 91** (Propagation on a logarithmic time horizon). *Fix $D_*>0$ and set <a id="rcut:eq:dyn-occupation-error"></a>$$T_n=D_*\log n,\qquad
 C_{\mathrm{dyn}}=e^{A(d_0+1)},\qquad
 r_n=T_ne^{AT_n}q_n
     =D_*\log n\,n^{AD_*}e^{-c_{\mathrm a}\sqrt n}.
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-occupation-error}$$ For every $0\le s\le d\le T_n$, every real $f$, and every $x$, $$\begin{split}
 U(S_d f)(x)
 &\le C_{\mathrm{dyn}}e^{-\kappa s}
      S_s\!\left[U(S_{d-s}f)\right](x)\\
 &\quad+r_n\|U(S_{d-s}f)\|_\infty.
 \end{split}
 \label{rcut:eq:gradient-propagation}$$ For every fixed $p>0$, $r_n=o(n^{-p})$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-dyn-occupation-propagation"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-dyn-occupation-propagation</summary>

*Proof.* Measure only the exceptional occupation after burn-in: let $Z_n=\int_{d_0}^{T_n}\mathbf 1_{\mathcal B}(X_u)\,du$ when $T_n\ge d_0$, and put $Z_n=0$ otherwise. Integrating Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:bad-avoidance" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:bad-avoidance">90</a> and applying Markov’s inequality gives $$\mathbb P_x(Z_n>1)\le\mathbb E_x Z_n\le T_nq_n.$$ On $\{Z_n\le1\}$, the total bad-set occupation up to any $s\le T_n$ is at most $d_0+1$. Therefore $$\exp\!\left(\int_0^s V(X_u)\,du\right)
 \le C_{\mathrm{dyn}}e^{-\kappa s}
 \quad\hbox{on }\{Z_n\le1\}.$$ The rough bound $e^{AT_n}$ applies to the exponential weight on the complementary event. Split the expectation in Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:feynman-kac" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:feynman-kac">89</a> accordingly. For occupation at most one, use the displayed weight bound and enlarge the expectation of the nonnegative endpoint quantity to the whole space. For larger occupation, use its supremum and the probability bound above. These two contributions are exactly the terms in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-propagation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-propagation">[rcut:eq:gradient-propagation]</a>; occupation and endpoint gradient need not be independent. This also covers $s<d_0$, since the occupation up to $s$ is then at most $d_0$. Finally, $e^{-c_{\mathrm a}\sqrt n}$ dominates every fixed power of $n$, which proves the stated decay of the error. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-82"></a>
#### Linear observables and the order of the mixing time

The propagated gradient has a bounded time integral for every linear observable with bounded coefficient norm. The jump exponential-moment estimate therefore gives fluctuations of bounded size, uniformly over all such observables and all starts. We will use this uniformity to choose a distinguishing observable after the disorder and the initial configuration have been selected.

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-linear-concentration"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:linear-concentration" class="proposition">

<a id="rcut:eq:dyn-linear-variance"></a>
**Proposition 92** (Uniform concentration for linear observables). *Fix $D_*>0$ and $L\ge0$. For $a\in\mathbb R^n$ write $\ell_a(x)=a^{\mathsf T}x$, and define $$B_L=L^2(C_{\mathrm{dyn}}+1),\qquad
 I_L=L^2\left(\frac{C_{\mathrm{dyn}}}{\kappa}+1\right).$$ For all sufficiently large $n$, every $\|a\|\le L$, every $x$, every $0\le d\le D_*\log n$, and every $\theta\in\mathbb R$, <a id="rcut:eq:dyn-linear-mgf"></a>$$\mathbb E_x\exp\!\left(\theta\bigl(\ell_a(X_d)-S_d\ell_a(x)\bigr)\right)
 \le M_{\theta,L}
 :=\exp\!\left(2\theta^2e^{2|\theta|\sqrt{B_L}}I_L\right),
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-linear-mgf}$$ and $$\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_x(\ell_a(X_d))\le4I_L,\qquad
 \mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\mu(\ell_a)\le\gamma^{-1}L^2,\qquad
 \mu(\ell_a)=0.
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-linear-variance}$$ These bounds hold simultaneously over all the indicated vectors and starting points, and uniformly over $\mathcal G_n$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-linear-concentration"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-linear-concentration</summary>

*Proof.* For a linear observable, $U(\ell_a)=\|a\|^2$, so the endpoint gradient in the propagation estimate is constant. Taking $s=d=r$ in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-propagation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-propagation">[rcut:eq:gradient-propagation]</a> gives the deterministic envelope $$\|U(S_r\ell_a)\|_\infty
 \le b(r):=L^2\bigl(C_{\mathrm{dyn}}e^{-\kappa r}+r_n\bigr),
 \qquad 0\le r\le T_n.$$ For sufficiently large $n$, both $r_n\le1$ and $T_nr_n\le1$. Consequently $\sup b\le B_L$ and $\int_0^{T_n}b(r)\,dr\le I_L$. These are the two quantities needed by Lemma <a href="#lem:input-mgf" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:input-mgf">3</a>, which gives both the transient exponential-moment bound and the variance bound.

The equilibrium variance uses the gap input instead. Applying its Dirichlet-form inequality gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\mu(\ell_a)
 \le\gamma^{-1}\mu\!\left[\ell_a(-L)\ell_a\right]
 =\gamma^{-1}\sum_i a_i^2\mu(v_i)
 \le\gamma^{-1}\|a\|^2.$$ The energy identity follows by conditional expectation: $\mu(x_i m_i)=\mu(m_i^2)$, so the coordinate energy is $\mu(v_i)$. Spin inversion in the zero-field model supplies the zero mean in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-linear-variance" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-linear-variance">[rcut:eq:dyn-linear-variance]</a>. Since the gradient envelope holds on the entire coefficient ball, none of these bounds requires $a$ to be chosen before the disorder or the starting configuration. ◻

</details>

We can now place the mixing time between logarithmic bounds. For the lower bound, a spin correlation will produce a linear observable whose mean is still large while both variances remain bounded. For the upper bound, the entropy estimate already available at the start of the section suffices.

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-mixing-scale"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:mixing-scale" class="proposition">

<a id="rcut:eq:dyn-strong-lower"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:dyn-median-scale"></a>
**Proposition 93** (The median mixing scale). *There is a constant $C<\infty$ such that, uniformly over $\mathcal G_n$ and all sufficiently large $n$, $$d_c\!\left(\frac14\log n\right)
 \ge1-Cn^{-1/2}.
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-strong-lower}$$ The continuous median mixing time $$t_n^{\rm med}=\inf\{t\ge0:d_c(t)\le1/2\}$$ satisfies $d_c(t_n^{\rm med})=1/2$ and, for some constants $0<c<C<\infty$, $$c\log n\le t_n^{\rm med}\le C\log n.
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-median-scale}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-mixing-scale"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-mixing-scale</summary>

*Proof.* Write $\sigma_i(x)=x_i$. Spin inversion gives $\mu(\sigma_i)=0$ and $\mu(\sigma_i^2)=1$, while $$\mu\!\left[\sigma_i(-L)\sigma_i\right]=\mu(v_i)\le1.$$ Use the spectral decomposition of the finite-dimensional self-adjoint operator $-L$. The squared coefficients of $\sigma_i$ form nonnegative weights summing to one, and the preceding energy is their mean eigenvalue. Jensen’s inequality for $\lambda\mapsto
e^{-d\lambda}$ therefore yields <a id="rcut:eq:dyn-spin-correlation"></a>$$\mu\!\left[\sigma_i S_d\sigma_i\right]
 \ge\exp\!\left(-d\mu[\sigma_i(-L)\sigma_i]\right)
 \ge e^{-d}.
 \label{rcut:eq:dyn-spin-correlation}$$ Sum these correlations over $i$. Since their sum is an average over the initial state under $\mu$, some configuration $x=x(d,J)$ satisfies $$S_d\ell_{x/\sqrt n}(x)
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_i x_i S_d\sigma_i(x)
 \ge\sqrt n e^{-d}.$$ The coefficient vector $x/\sqrt n$ has norm one, so Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:linear-concentration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:linear-concentration">92</a>, with $D_*=1$ and $L=1$, applies even to this choice. Let $V_*=4I_1$. The displayed observable has transient variance at most $V_*$, equilibrium mean zero, and equilibrium variance at most $\gamma^{-1}$. Let its transient mean be $m\ge\sqrt n e^{-d}$. The event that the observable exceeds $m/2$ separates the transient law from equilibrium. Applying Chebyshev’s inequality under both laws gives, for $0\le d\le\log n$, $$d_c(d)\ge1-\frac{4(V_*+\gamma^{-1})}{m^2}
 \ge1-\frac{4(V_*+\gamma^{-1})e^{2d}}{n}.$$ Taking $d=(\log n)/4$ proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-strong-lower" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-strong-lower">[rcut:eq:dyn-strong-lower]</a>.

For the upper bound, the entropy-to-total-variation estimate proved in Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:entropy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:entropy">77</a>, applied to Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-entropy-input" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-entropy-input">[rcut:eq:dyn-entropy-input]</a>, gives $$d_c(t)^2\le\frac12 C_E n e^{-t/C_L}.$$ Hence $t_n^{\rm med}\le C_L\log(2C_E n)$ for sufficiently large $n$. Together with Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-strong-lower" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-strong-lower">[rcut:eq:dyn-strong-lower]</a>, this proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:dyn-median-scale" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:dyn-median-scale">[rcut:eq:dyn-median-scale]</a>. It remains to justify the exact median identity. The function $d_c$ is continuous, as a maximum of finitely many continuous transition-law distances, and the entropy bound shows that it tends to zero. Since $d_c(0)=1-\min_x\mu(x)\ge1-2^{-n}>1/2$, its first crossing is attained and satisfies $d_c(t_n^{\rm med})=1/2$. ◻

</details>

<a id="rcut:sec:cutoff"></a>
### Cutoff and the discrete update clock

Section <a href="#rcut:sec:dynamics" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:dynamics">15</a> placed the median mixing time on a logarithmic scale. We now show that, once the chain has a fixed positive amount of common mass with equilibrium, any additional positive logarithmic lag makes its total-variation distance vanish. Applying this implication on either side of the median proves continuous-time cutoff; a comparison of update clocks then gives the discrete-time result.

Fix $\beta\in[0,1/2)$. Throughout this section, the disorder belongs to the simultaneous good events $\mathcal G_n$ from Section <a href="#rcut:sec:dynamics" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:dynamics">15</a>. In particular, $\|J\|\le K$, the spectral gap is at least $\gamma>0$, and the constants in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-propagation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-propagation">[rcut:eq:gradient-propagation]</a> are uniform on these events. We use its notation $\kappa>0$, $C_{\mathrm{dyn}}$, and $r_n$. For each fixed $D_*>0$, Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-propagation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-propagation">[rcut:eq:gradient-propagation]</a> applies whenever $0\le s\le d\le D_*\log n$, and its deterministic remainder satisfies <a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-remainder"></a>$$n^p r_n\longrightarrow0\qquad\text{for every fixed }p>0.
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-remainder}$$ We retain this uniformity throughout: unless stated otherwise, every limit is uniform over $\mathcal G_n$. Constants may depend on the fixed inverse temperature and on the fixed parameters in the relevant statement.

<a id="pm-h-84"></a>
#### Common mass and local fields

If two laws share a fixed positive amount of mass, their means can be separated only to the extent permitted by their variances. The following elementary estimate makes this precise. We first apply it to local fields; later we apply it to bounded test functions after semigroup smoothing.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-common-mass"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:common-mass" class="lemma">

**Lemma 94** (Means under measures with common mass). *Let $\nu$ and $\pi$ be probability measures on a finite set, and suppose $\|\nu-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le1-\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon>0$. For every real function $H$ on that set, <a id="rcut:eq:common-mass-means"></a>$$|\nu H-\pi H|
 \le \frac{\sqrt{\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\nu H}+\sqrt{\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\pi H}}
              {\sqrt{\varepsilon}}.
 \label{rcut:eq:common-mass-means}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-common-mass"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-common-mass</summary>

*Proof.* Take the common part of the measures, $\rho(x)=\min\{\nu(x),\pi(x)\}$, whose mass is $q=1-\|\nu-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\ge\varepsilon$. We compare each mean to the mean under the normalized common part. Since $\rho\le\nu$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $$\left|\nu H-\frac{\rho H}{q}\right|
 =\frac1q\left|\sum_x\rho(x)(H(x)-\nu H)\right|
 \le\sqrt{\frac{\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\nu H}{q}}.$$ The same calculation for $\pi$ bounds the other difference from the common mean. The triangle inequality, followed by the lower bound on the common mass, proves the assertion. ◻

</details>

Write $h_i(x)=(Jx)_i$ for the local field. Its coefficient vector has Euclidean norm at most $K$. Spin inversion gives $\mu h_i=0$ in the zero-field model. Thus the concentration estimate for linear observables applies to every local field. Common mass will also control its transient mean, yielding the following tail bound at each deterministic observation time.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-cutoff-field-tails"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:cutoff-field-tails" class="lemma">

**Lemma 95** (Fields at deterministic observation times). *Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $\delta>0$, and $D_*>0$. Suppose $d_c(t)\le1-\varepsilon$. There is a deterministic sequence $\tau_n=\tau_n(\varepsilon,\delta,D_*)$ such that <a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-field-tails"></a>$$\sup_x\mathbb P_x\left[\max_{1\le i\le n}|h_i(X_z)|>\delta\log n\right]
 \le\tau_n,
 \qquad t\le z\le D_*\log n,
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-field-tails}$$ and $n^p\tau_n\to0$ for every fixed $p>0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-cutoff-field-tails"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-cutoff-field-tails</summary>

<a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-field-means"></a>
*Proof.* First control the means. Contraction of total variation implies that the law $\nu_{x,z}$ of $X_z$ from any point $x$ has common mass at least $\varepsilon$ with $\mu$ for every $z\ge t$. Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:linear-concentration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:linear-concentration">92</a> bounds $\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_{\nu_{x,z}}h_i$ uniformly in $i,x,z$, and the equilibrium variance is at most $K^2/\gamma$. Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:common-mass" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:common-mass">94</a> therefore gives a constant $B_\varepsilon$ such that $$|\mathbb E_x h_i(X_z)|\le B_\varepsilon
 \qquad(t\le z\le D_*\log n).
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-field-means}$$

Next control the deviations from these means. For every fixed $\theta>0$, Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:linear-concentration" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:linear-concentration">92</a> bounds both centered exponential moments by a common constant $M_{\theta,K}$. Apply the exponential bound to both tails of each field and then take a union bound over the coordinates. Together with Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:cutoff-field-means" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:cutoff-field-means">[rcut:eq:cutoff-field-means]</a>, this gives <a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-field-chernoff"></a>$$\mathbb P_x\left[\max_i|h_i(X_z)|>\delta\log n\right]
 \le 2M_{\theta,K}e^{\theta B_\varepsilon}
             n^{1-\theta\delta}.
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-field-chernoff}$$ For a prescribed $p>0$, first fix $\theta$ with $\theta\delta>p+1$, and then let $n$ tend to infinity. Define $\tau_n$ as the supremum of the displayed probabilities over the indicated parameters and good disorders. The same sequence therefore has every asserted inverse-power decay rate. The uniformity is over deterministic times. In the smoothing argument we will integrate the resulting expectation bounds, so a simultaneous field event along the whole sample path is unnecessary. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-85"></a>
#### A positive logarithmic lag finishes mixing

The passage from a nontrivial total-variation overlap to mixing after a positive logarithmic lag is related to the concentration-based cutoff mechanism of Salez (Salez 2024, Theorem 5 and Lemma 9) <a id="pm-cite-48"></a>[[Salez2024](#ref-Salez2024)]. Here we prove the required implication through variances of bounded smoothed tests and their common mass with equilibrium.

We now prove the implication needed for cutoff. The common-mass hypothesis will compare expectations of a smoothed test once its variance is small under both the transient law and equilibrium. The main task is the transient variance: gradient propagation will bound the martingale energy before the observation time by the energy in a later interval of positive logarithmic length.

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-positive-lag"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:positive-lag" class="proposition">

**Proposition 96** (Positive-lag smoothing). *Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, $\alpha>0$, and $D_*>0$, and put $s=\alpha\log n$. Uniformly over all times $t\ge0$ satisfying $$d_c(t)\le1-\varepsilon,
 \qquad t+s\le D_*\log n,$$ one has $d_c(t+s)\to0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-positive-lag"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-positive-lag</summary>

<a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-budget-consequences"></a>
*Proof.* Fix a starting point $x$ and a real test function with $\|f\|_\infty\le1$. We first express the transient variance as an integrated martingale energy. Set $T=t+s$ and $$F_u=S_{T-u}f,\qquad
 G(u)=\mathbb E_x\Gamma(F_u)(X_u),\qquad 0\le u\le T.$$ Here $F_u(X_u)$ is the backward martingale with terminal value $f(X_T)$. Differentiating its second moment and using $(\partial_u+L)F_u=0$ gives the exact identity <a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-variance-budget"></a>$$\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_x(F_r(X_r))=2\int_0^rG(u)\,du,
 \qquad 0\le r\le T.
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-variance-budget}$$ Since $\|F_u\|_\infty\le1$, this implies $$\int_0^T G(u)\,du\le\frac12,
 \qquad
 \mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_x(S_sf(X_t))=2\int_0^tG(u)\,du.
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-budget-consequences}$$

<a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-early-late"></a>
The total energy is thus bounded. To show that little of it lies before the observation time, fix deterministic $u\le t$ and $z\in[t+s/2,t+s]$. Apply Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:gradient-propagation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:gradient-propagation">[rcut:eq:gradient-propagation]</a> starting at $X_u$, with duration $T-u$ and comparison time $z-u$. These parameters lie within the fixed horizon, and the estimate holds for every possible value of $X_u$ with the same constants. Integrating against its law and using the Markov property yields $$\mathbb E_x U(F_u)(X_u)
 \le C_{\mathrm{dyn}}e^{-\kappa(z-u)}
                  \mathbb E_x U(F_z)(X_z)+n r_n.$$ The bound on the remainder uses $U(F_z)\le n$: each half-difference of a function bounded by one has magnitude at most one. Combining this with $\Gamma\le2U$ and the separation $z-u\ge s/2$ gives $$G(u)\le 2C_{\mathrm{dyn}}n^{-\kappa\alpha/2}
                  \mathbb E_x U(F_z)(X_z)+2n r_n.
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-early-late}$$

<a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-field-gradient"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-energy-comparison"></a>
We still need to replace the late unweighted gradient by the late martingale energy. The field-tail estimate supplies the required lower bound on the heat-bath weights. Choose a fixed $\delta$ with $0<\delta<\kappa\alpha/4$, and let $\tau_n$ be the sequence in Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:cutoff-field-tails" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:cutoff-field-tails">95</a>. At every configuration, $$w_i=1-x_i\tanh h_i
 \ge 1-|\tanh h_i|
 =\frac{2}{1+e^{2|h_i|}}\ge e^{-2|h_i|}.$$ On the event $\max_i|h_i(X_z)|\le\delta\log n$ this gives $U(F_z)(X_z)\le n^{2\delta}\Gamma(F_z)(X_z)$. On the complementary event use $U(F_z)\le n$. These are pointwise bounds, so they remain valid even though the fields and $F_z$ depend on the same configuration. Taking expectations gives $$\mathbb E_xU(F_z)(X_z)\le n^{2\delta}G(z)+n\tau_n.
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-field-gradient}$$ Define the positive exponent and the deterministic remainder $$\xi=\frac{\kappa\alpha}{2}-2\delta>0,
 \qquad R_n=2n r_n+2C_{\mathrm{dyn}}n\tau_n.$$ Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:cutoff-early-late" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:cutoff-early-late">[rcut:eq:cutoff-early-late]</a> and <a href="#rcut:eq:cutoff-field-gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:cutoff-field-gradient">[rcut:eq:cutoff-field-gradient]</a> imply $$G(u)\le 2C_{\mathrm{dyn}}n^{-\xi}G(z)+R_n
 \quad\text{for }u\le t,\quad t+s/2\le z\le t+s.
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-energy-comparison}$$ The choice of the field threshold leaves a strictly positive decay exponent, and $R_n$ decreases faster than every inverse power of $n$. We have therefore compared each early energy to every energy in the late interval, with uniform error. Average Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:cutoff-energy-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:cutoff-energy-comparison">[rcut:eq:cutoff-energy-comparison]</a> over the interval of $z$ of length $s/2$, and then integrate over $0\le u\le t$. The total energy budget in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:cutoff-budget-consequences" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:cutoff-budget-consequences">[rcut:eq:cutoff-budget-consequences]</a> gives <a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-late-variance"></a>$$\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_x(S_sf(X_t))
 \le 4C_{\mathrm{dyn}}\frac{t}{s}n^{-\xi}+2tR_n
 \le 4C_{\mathrm{dyn}}\frac{D_*}{\alpha}n^{-\xi}
            +2D_*\log n\,R_n=:V_n.
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-late-variance}$$ Thus $V_n\to0$ uniformly in $f,x,t$ and in the good disorder, proving the required transient variance bound. The integrations concern deterministic expectations of finite-state semigroup expressions; their measurability and nonnegativity justify interchanging the two integrals by Tonelli’s Theorem. No random observation time or union over a continuum of field events enters this step.

It remains to control the equilibrium variance and compare the two means. The uniform spectral gap from Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:uniform-gap" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:uniform-gap">76</a> gives $\frac{d}{dr}\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\mu(S_rf)\le-2\gamma\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\mu(S_rf)$. Integrating yields <a id="rcut:eq:cutoff-equilibrium-smoothing"></a>$$\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\mu(S_sf)\le e^{-2\gamma s}\mathop{\mathrm{Var}}_\mu(f)
                        \le n^{-2\gamma\alpha}.
 \label{rcut:eq:cutoff-equilibrium-smoothing}$$ Both variance bounds now apply to the same observable. Use Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:common-mass" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:common-mass">94</a> for the law of $X_t$ from $x$ and for $\mu$, with observable $S_sf$. The common-mass hypothesis is exactly the assumed distance bound at the observation time, and the two expectations are $S_{t+s}f(x)$ and $\mu f$. Hence $$|S_{t+s}f(x)-\mu f|
 \le \varepsilon^{-1/2}
          \bigl(\sqrt{V_n}+n^{-\gamma\alpha}\bigr).$$ Taking one half of the supremum over $x$ and $\|f\|_\infty\le1$ proves Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:positive-lag" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:positive-lag">96</a>. ◻

</details>

Positive-lag smoothing turns the logarithmic median scale into cutoff. At the median there is enough common mass to apply the proposition. If such common mass appeared a fixed fraction earlier, the same proposition would force mixing before the median, which is impossible.

<a id="stmt-rcut-thm-continuous-cutoff"></a>
<div id="rcut:thm:continuous-cutoff" class="theorem">

**Theorem 97** (Continuous-time cutoff). *Let $t_n^{\rm med}=\inf\{t\ge0:d_c(t)\le1/2\}$ be the continuous-time median mixing time. For every fixed $b\in(0,1)$, <a id="rcut:eq:continuous-cutoff-sides"></a>$$d_c((1-b)t_n^{\rm med})\longrightarrow1,
 \qquad d_c((1+b)t_n^{\rm med})\longrightarrow0,
 \label{rcut:eq:continuous-cutoff-sides}$$ uniformly over $\mathcal G_n$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-thm-continuous-cutoff"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-thm-continuous-cutoff</summary>

*Proof.* Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:mixing-scale" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:mixing-scale">93</a> gives fixed constants $c,C>0$ such that $c\log n\le t_n^{\rm med}\le C\log n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, and $d_c(t_n^{\rm med})=1/2$. Fix $b\in(0,1)$ and set $\alpha=bc/2$. Fix the horizon constant $D_*>(1+b)C$ so that both applications of positive-lag smoothing lie within its range. First apply Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:positive-lag" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:positive-lag">96</a> at $t=t_n^{\rm med}$. This gives $d_c(t_n^{\rm med}+\alpha\log n)\to0$. Since $\alpha\log n\le bt_n^{\rm med}/2$, monotonicity yields the upper conclusion.

For the lower side, argue by contradiction while preserving uniformity in the disorder. If the conclusion failed uniformly, there would be a subsequence of dimensions, a good disorder at each of those dimensions, and a fixed $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that $d_c((1-b)t_n^{\rm med})\le1-\varepsilon_0$. Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:positive-lag" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:positive-lag">96</a> would then give vanishing distance at time $$(1-b)t_n^{\rm med}+\alpha\log n
 \le t_n^{\rm med}-\frac{bc}{2}\log n<t_n^{\rm med}.$$ This contradicts the definition of $t_n^{\rm med}$, since the distance at every time strictly below $t_n^{\rm med}$ exceeds $1/2$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-86"></a>
#### A clock comparison with fixed holding

We next transfer cutoff to the clock that counts individual update attempts. Poisson concentration gives the lower side directly. For the upper side we first extract a fixed holding probability, then apply the uniform Poisson-to-binomial comparison proved in Lemma <a href="#lem:input-clock" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:input-clock">4</a>. This is the same finite-chain comparison used in the main argument; below we verify all its hypotheses for the present median scale.

<a id="stmt-rcut-prop-discrete-cutoff"></a>
<div id="rcut:prop:discrete-cutoff" class="proposition">

<a id="rcut:eq:discrete-cutoff-sides"></a>
**Proposition 98** (Cutoff for single-site update attempts). *For every fixed $b\in(0,1)$, uniformly over $\mathcal G_n$, $$d_d\bigl(\lfloor(1-b)nt_n^{\rm med}\rfloor\bigr)\longrightarrow1,
 \qquad
 d_d\bigl(\lceil(1+b)nt_n^{\rm med}\rceil\bigr)\longrightarrow0.
 \label{rcut:eq:discrete-cutoff-sides}$$ Here each discrete step is one uniformly selected heat-bath update attempt, including attempts that leave the configuration unchanged.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-discrete-cutoff"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-discrete-cutoff</summary>

<a id="rcut:eq:clock-lower-transfer"></a>
*Proof.* The exact clock relation is $S_t=e^{nt(P-I)}$, so continuous time averages discrete update attempts against a Poisson law. For the lower bound, put $k=\lfloor(1-b)nt_n^{\rm med}\rfloor$ and $T=(1-b/2)t_n^{\rm med}$, and let $N\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(nT)$. Convexity of total variation and monotonicity of the discrete distance give $$d_c(T)\le\sum_{j\ge0}\mathbb P(N=j)d_d(j)
                \le\mathbb P(N<k)+d_d(k).
 \label{rcut:eq:clock-lower-transfer}$$ The Poisson mean exceeds $k$ by at least $(b/2)nt_n^{\rm med}$. Chebyshev’s inequality therefore implies $\mathbb P(N<k)=O((nt_n^{\rm med})^{-1})=o(1)$ uniformly. Theorem <a href="#rcut:thm:continuous-cutoff" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:thm:continuous-cutoff">97</a>, with parameter $b/2$, gives $d_c(T)\to1$; Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:clock-lower-transfer" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:clock-lower-transfer">[rcut:eq:clock-lower-transfer]</a> proves the discrete lower bound.

<a id="rcut:eq:clock-thinning"></a>
For the upper bound, we must check the fixed holding condition used by the clock-comparison lemma. The operator-norm bound implies $$\frac1n\sum_i h_i(x)^2=\frac{\|Jx\|^2}{n}\le K^2.$$ At least half the fields have magnitude at most $\sqrt2K$. When spin $i$ is selected, its chance of being retained is $e^{x_ih_i}/(2\cosh h_i)\ge(1+e^{2|h_i|})^{-1}$. Averaging this lower bound over the selected coordinate gives <a id="rcut:eq:clock-uniform-holding"></a>$$P(x,x)\ge h_0:=\frac{1}{2(1+e^{2\sqrt2K})}>0.
 \label{rcut:eq:clock-uniform-holding}$$ Choose $q=1-h_0/2\in(0,1)$ once for all $n$ and all good disorders, and write $$P=(1-q)I+q R,
 \qquad R=\frac{P-(1-q)I}{q}.$$ Subtracting this fixed holding component leaves a Markov kernel $R$ with stationary measure $\mu$. In terms of its powers, the two clocks become $$S_t=e^{q nt(R-I)},\qquad
 P^M=\sum_{j=0}^M\binom Mjq^j(1-q)^{M-j}R^j.
 \label{rcut:eq:clock-thinning}$$

We now verify convergence of every fixed shifted Poisson average, as required by Lemma <a href="#lem:input-clock" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:input-clock">4</a>. Set $M=\lceil(1+b)nt_n^{\rm med}\rceil$. For any $x\in\Omega_n$ and any real function $f$ with $\|f\|_\infty\le1$, define $u_j=(R^jf)(x)-\mu f$, so that $|u_j|\le2$. For fixed $y\in\mathbb R$, Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:clock-thinning" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:clock-thinning">[rcut:eq:clock-thinning]</a> identifies the Poisson average with mean $m=q M+y\sqrt M$ as $$\mathbb E\bigl[u_{\operatorname{Poisson}(m)}\bigr]
 =S_{m/(q n)}f(x)-\mu f.$$ Uniformly over the good disorders, $t_n^{\rm med}$ is between fixed positive multiples of $\log n$. Hence $$\frac{m}{q n}
 =\frac Mn+\frac{y\sqrt M}{q n}
 \ge(1+b/2)t_n^{\rm med}$$ for all sufficiently large $n$: the correction is $O_y(\sqrt{\log n/n})$, whereas $(b/2)t_n^{\rm med}$ is of order $\log n$. Theorem <a href="#rcut:thm:continuous-cutoff" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:thm:continuous-cutoff">97</a> and monotonicity bound this Poisson average in absolute value by $2d_c((1+b/2)t_n^{\rm med})=o(1)$, uniformly over $x$, $f$, and the good disorder. Also $M$ tends uniformly to infinity. All hypotheses of Lemma <a href="#lem:input-clock" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:input-clock">4</a> are now uniform over the indicated family, so its binomial average tends uniformly to zero. Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:clock-thinning" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:clock-thinning">[rcut:eq:clock-thinning]</a> identifies that average with $P^Mf(x)-\mu f$. Taking one half of the supremum over $x\in\Omega_n$ and real $f$ with $\|f\|_\infty\le1$ proves the upper bound in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:discrete-cutoff-sides" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:discrete-cutoff-sides">[rcut:eq:discrete-cutoff-sides]</a>. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-prop-discrete-cutoff-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-prop-discrete-cutoff</summary>

*Completion of the proof of Theorem <a href="#rcut:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:thm:main">72</a>.* It remains to express discrete cutoff as the asserted ratio of mixing times and then return to disorder probability. Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and $\eta>0$. Choose once $$0<b<\frac{\eta}{2+\eta},
 \qquad\text{so that}\qquad
 \frac{1+b}{1-b}<1+\eta.$$ Proposition <a href="#rcut:prop:discrete-cutoff" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:prop:discrete-cutoff">98</a> implies, for all sufficiently large $n$ and every disorder in $\mathcal G_n$, $$t_{n,\beta,J}(1-\varepsilon)>
                \lfloor(1-b)nt_n^{\rm med}\rfloor,
 \qquad
 t_{n,\beta,J}(\varepsilon)\le
                \lceil(1+b)nt_n^{\rm med}\rceil.$$ The first bound ensures a positive denominator and controls the integer rounding in the ratio. Hence $$\frac{t_{n,\beta,J}(\varepsilon)}
      {t_{n,\beta,J}(1-\varepsilon)}
 \le\frac{\lceil(1+b)nt_n^{\rm med}\rceil}
          {\lfloor(1-b)nt_n^{\rm med}\rfloor+1}
 \le\frac{1+b}{1-b}+\frac{1}{(1-b)nt_n^{\rm med}}<1+\eta$$ for all sufficiently large $n$, uniformly on $\mathcal G_n$. The last step uses $t_n^{\rm med}\ge c\log n$. Since $\mathbb P_J(\mathcal G_n)\to1$, the probability of the event in Theorem <a href="#rcut:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:thm:main">72</a> is at most $\mathbb P_J(\mathcal G_n^c)$ for large $n$, and therefore tends to zero. This last step uses only the probability of the good event: all preceding estimates hold for each fixed disorder, uniformly over the starting state and the test function. No coupling of disorders across dimensions is needed. ◻

</details>

<a id="rcut:sec:scalar-certificate"></a>
### Certificate for the scalar enclosures

The scalar argument needs certified moments of the field law $N(\beta^2,\beta^2)$, with $\beta\in[7/20,1/2]$. Retain the notation of Section <a href="#rcut:sec:scalar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:scalar">14</a>. We now prove Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-data" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-data">[rcut:lem:scalar-data]</a> and verify the arithmetic in Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-intervals" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-intervals">2</a>.

There are three distinct error estimates. First, a complex-strip bound controls replacement of each integral by a finite quadrature sum. Second, directed integer arithmetic encloses those sums, which use 41 nodes at each of five exact temperatures. Third, normalization, standard deviations, and the two mean parameters in $F$ must be transferred back to the continuous field law. The estimates below keep these steps separate. The interpolation between temperatures remains the analytic argument of Section <a href="#rcut:sec:scalar" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:sec:scalar">14</a>.

<a id="stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-trapezoid"></a>
<div id="rcut:lem:scalar-trapezoid" class="lemma">

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-trapezoid-error"></a>
**Lemma 99** (Whole-line trapezoidal estimate). *Let $t>0$. Suppose $f$ is continuous on $\{z:|\Im z|\leq t\}$, holomorphic in its interior, and satisfies a bound $$|f(x+iy)|\leq C(1+|x|)^p e^{-c x^2},\qquad |y|\leq t,$$ for some $C,c>0$ and $p\geq0$. If both horizontal-edge integrals of $|f|$ are at most $M$, then, for any mesh $\Delta>0$, $$\left|\Delta\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}f(k\Delta)
                  -\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)\,dx\right|
 \leq\frac{2M}{e^{2\pi t/\Delta}-1}.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-trapezoid-error}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-trapezoid"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-trapezoid</summary>

*Proof.* We compare the integral and the infinite quadrature sum through the Fourier coefficients of the periodization. The assumed decay makes $\sum_k f(x+k\Delta)$ uniformly convergent on a period. Its coefficient at integer $j$ is $\Delta^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}f(x)e^{-2\pi ijx/\Delta}\,dx$. To estimate a nonconstant coefficient, shift the contour to height $-t$ when $j>0$, and to height $t$ when $j<0$. The integrals on the vertical sides vanish by the uniform Gaussian decay. One may first shift to an interior line and then pass to the boundary by dominated convergence, so the stated boundary regularity suffices. The resulting bound for the absolute value of the coefficient is $(M/\Delta)e^{-2\pi t|j|/\Delta}$. These bounds are summable. To identify the Fourier series with the continuous periodization without a further regularity assumption, take arithmetic means of the partial Fourier sums. Relative to normalized measure on a period, their kernels are $N^{-1}|\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}e^{2\pi ijx/\Delta}|^2$. The kernels are nonnegative, have integral one, and concentrate at the origin. Their convolutions therefore converge uniformly to the continuous periodization. Absolute convergence identifies this limit with the Fourier series itself. At zero, the constant coefficient is the integral divided by $\Delta$; summing the bounds for the remaining coefficients proves Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-trapezoid-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-trapezoid-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-trapezoid-error]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-88"></a>
###### A common quadrature error for all moments.

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-strip-bounds"></a>
To apply the trapezoidal estimate uniformly in the temperature, change variables to $x=h/\beta$, whose density is $\varphi(x-\beta)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-(x-\beta)^2/2}$. On $|\Im x|\leq1.5$, we have $|\Im(\beta x)|\leq.75<\pi/4$. The identity $$|\tanh(u+it)|^2
  =\frac{\sinh^2u+\sin^2t}{\sinh^2u+\cos^2t}$$ therefore implies $$|m|\leq1,\qquad |v|\leq2,\qquad |\Lambda{}|\geq.14,
 \qquad |1.75-m|\geq.75,\qquad |2-m|\geq1.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-strip-bounds}$$ For $d(1)$, first cancel the denominator and use the expression $v(1+m)$. The displayed bounds then keep every remaining denominator in the moment integrands away from zero. The integrands are holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed strip and, after multiplication by the Gaussian density, satisfy the uniform decay in Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-trapezoid" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-trapezoid">99</a>.

The function $F$ involves two expectations, so its quadrature uses approximations to those expectations. We need the same analytic bound for every possible pair of means that will arise. Let $a',G'$ be arbitrary constants in $[0,1]$, put $l'=.64-.19a'$, and let $F_{a',G'}$ be the expression in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-F" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-F">[rcut:eq:scalar-F]</a> with these constants. Since $l'\geq.45$, $|.5-\beta^2a'/l'|\leq.5$. Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-strip-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-strip-bounds">[rcut:eq:scalar-strip-bounds]</a> then gives, with $h=\beta x$, <a id="rcut:eq:scalar-strip-F"></a>$$|F_{a',G'}(\beta x)|\leq1.5|x|+4.12.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-strip-F}$$ On either horizontal edge, this is at most $1.5|\Re x|+6.37$. The Gaussian modulus on that edge is $e^{1.125}\varphi(\Re x-\beta)$. Hence its product with $|F_{a',G'}|^2$ has integral at most $$e^{1.125}\bigl(1.5\sqrt{1.25}+6.37\bigr)^2<260.$$ For a simple upper estimate in the last inequality, use $e^{1.125}<4$ and $\sqrt{1.25}<1.12$. We also need the raw moments of $v,g,mv,\rho$, the squares of $v,g,mv$, and the five scaled integrands in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-five-enclosures" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-five-enclosures">[rcut:eq:scalar-five-enclosures]</a>. Their edge integrals satisfy smaller bounds. For example, $|g|\leq8/3$, $|(1+m)v/2-1.5g^2|\leq38/3$, and $|(1+v)^2/(16\Lambda{})|\leq9/(16\cdot.14)$. Consequently $M=1000$ works simultaneously for every first moment, raw second moment, and total-mass integral needed below.

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-tail-error"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-raw-error"></a>
The whole-line estimate leaves a second task: bounding the nodes discarded from the infinite sum. Choose mesh $\Delta=.4$ and retain $|x|\leq8$. At the omitted nodes $|x|\geq8.4$, every relevant real moment integrand is bounded by $(1.5|x|+4.12)^2$. Since $|\beta|\leq.5$, the sum of the two tails is bounded by twice the series with terms $$\frac{.4}{\sqrt{2\pi}}(16.72+.6j)^2
                e^{-(7.9+.4j)^2/2},\qquad j=0,1,\ldots.$$ The ratio of successive terms is at most $$q_*:=e^{-3.24}\left(\frac{17.32}{16.72}\right)^2<.042026.$$ The two omitted tails consequently have total at most $$\frac{.8(16.72)^2 e^{-31.205}}{\sqrt{2\pi}(1-q_*)}
 <2.612\cdot10^{-12}.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-tail-error}$$ Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-trapezoid" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-trapezoid">99</a> bounds the whole-line error by $2000/(e^{7.5\pi}-1)<1.171\cdot10^{-7}$. Together with Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-tail-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-tail-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-tail-error]</a>, this proves the following conservative common bound for each unnormalized raw moment: $$E_{\mathrm{quad}}:=2.3\cdot10^{-7}.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-raw-error}$$ This error includes both the infinite-sum error and the omitted tails; it precedes normalization of the quadrature weights. Each decimal comparison used to obtain it is checkable by the directed recipe below. The coarse enclosure $3.14159<\pi<3.14160$ suffices; it follows, for example, from $\pi=16\arctan(1/5)-4\arctan(1/239)$ and ten terms of the alternating series for each arctangent.

<a id="pm-h-89"></a>
###### The finite quantities to be enclosed.

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-eight-sums"></a>
We next specify the sums exactly, so that their arithmetic verification is a finite calculation with rational inputs. For $-20\leq j\leq20$, put $$\begin{split}
 x_j&=2j/5,\qquad h_j=\beta x_j,
 \qquad c_j=e^{-(x_j-\beta)^2/2},\\
 y_j&=\frac{e^{2h_j}-1}{e^{2h_j}+1},\qquad
 V_j=1-y_j^2,\qquad P_j=\frac{V_j}{7/4-y_j},\\
 N(f)&=\frac{\sum_{j=-20}^{20}c_j f_j}{\sum_{j=-20}^{20}c_j},
 \qquad T(f)=N(f^2)-N(f)^2.
 \end{split}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums}$$ Define $a_N=N(V)$, $G_N=N(P)$, and $$f_j=(V_j+a_N)h_j+2\beta^2y_jV_j+
       \left(.5-\frac{\beta^2a_N}{.64-.19a_N}\right)V_j
       +.12y_j+3\beta^2G_NP_j.$$ In the order of the columns of Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-moments">86</a>, the eight quantities computed from these weights are $$N(V),\ N(P),\ \sqrt{T(V)},\ \sqrt{T(P)},\ N(yV),\
 N\!\left(\frac{V(1+y)}2-1.5P^2\right),\ \sqrt{T(f)},\
 \sqrt{T(yV)}.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-eight-sums}$$ The directed recipe below encloses each of these quantities within $10^{-6}$ of the corresponding entry in Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-finite-values" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-finite-values">3</a>. The five temperatures in that table are exact. These enclosures in particular place every finite quantity within $.00065$ of the center in Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-moments">86</a>, and place every finite standard deviation above $.08$. The latter lower bound will allow us to transfer variance errors to standard-deviation errors.

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-five-sums"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-five-finite-values"></a>
The five additional endpoint enclosures use the same weights at $\beta=1/2$. Their finite expressions are $$\begin{gathered}
 \frac1{16}N\!\left(\frac{(1+V)^2}{.45+.25y^2-.06y}\right),\qquad
 \frac1{16}N\!\left(\frac{V^2}{.45+.25y^2-.06y}\right),\\
 \frac14N\!\left(\frac{V^2}{2-y}\right),\qquad
 \frac14N\!\left(\frac{V^2}{(2-y)^2}\right),\qquad
 \frac14N\bigl(V(1+y)\bigr).
 \end{gathered}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-five-sums}$$ They lie, respectively, within $10^{-6}$ of $$.427718,\quad .089859,\quad .092577,\quad .052281,\quad .228875.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-five-finite-values}$$

<a id="pm-h-90"></a>
###### Directed integer arithmetic.

We now give the finite recipe that establishes the enclosures just listed. It requires no accuracy assumption for a transcendental library: exponentials and square roots are enclosed using integer arithmetic and explicit remainders. Fix $S=10^{50}$, and represent an interval by integer endpoints $[u,v]$, meaning $[u/S,v/S]$. Represent a rational input by its lower and upper nearest multiples of $S^{-1}$. Addition and subtraction act on endpoints in the usual way. For multiplication, take the minimum and maximum of the four integer endpoint products, then divide by $S$, rounding the minimum down and the maximum up. For an interval not containing zero, its reciprocal is represented by $$\left[\left\lfloor\frac{S^2}{v}\right\rfloor,
        \left\lceil\frac{S^2}{u}\right\rceil\right].$$ The reciprocal rule applies to positive and negative intervals alike; division is multiplication by this reciprocal. For a nonnegative interval, square roots are represented by $[\lfloor\sqrt{uS}\rfloor,\lceil\sqrt{vS}\rceil]$, computed by integer square root and an exact square comparison. Powers use repeated interval multiplication. Every operation preserves inclusion.

All exponential arguments $d$ needed in Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums">[rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums]</a>–<a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-five-sums" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-five-sums">[rcut:eq:scalar-five-sums]</a> satisfy $|d|\leq36.125$. For $z=d/32$, compute $$p_{20}(z)=\sum_{i=0}^{20}\frac{z^i}{i!}$$ with the preceding interval operations, for example by the recursion $t_0=1$, $t_i=t_{i-1}z/i$, followed by summation. Enlarge its interval on both sides by an outward enclosure of $$\frac{4(1.13)^{21}}{21!},$$ and raise this interval to the 32nd power. This encloses $e^d$: $|z|<1.13$, and Taylor’s remainder is at most the displayed quantity because $e^{1.13}<4$. In particular the relative error of $p_{20}(d/32)^{32}$ is bounded by <a id="rcut:eq:scalar-exponential-error"></a>$$\left(1+\frac{16(1.13)^{21}}{21!}\right)^{32}-1<10^{-12}.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-exponential-error}$$ This relative-error estimate concerns the polynomial approximation $p_{20}(d/32)^{32}$. The interval enclosure follows directly from inserting the absolute remainder before taking the 32nd power, together with outward rounding at every operation. With the rational enclosure for $\pi$ given above, the same recipe checks the constants in Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-tail-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-tail-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-tail-error]</a> and <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-raw-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-raw-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-raw-error]</a> and the exponential in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-interval-cross" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-interval-cross">[rcut:eq:scalar-interval-cross]</a>.

Apply these operations to Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums">[rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums]</a>– <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-eight-sums" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-eight-sums">[rcut:eq:scalar-eight-sums]</a> to obtain Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-finite-values" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-finite-values">3</a>; applying them to Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-five-sums" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-five-sums">[rcut:eq:scalar-five-sums]</a> gives Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-five-finite-values" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-five-finite-values">[rcut:eq:scalar-five-finite-values]</a>. Applying the same operations to the rational endpoints in Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-interval-slacks" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-interval-slacks">[rcut:eq:scalar-interval-slacks]</a> and <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-interval-cross" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-interval-cross">[rcut:eq:scalar-interval-cross]</a> gives Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-intervals" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-intervals">2</a>. The loop bounds and remainder estimates therefore reduce the finite verification to integer arithmetic alone. The supplementary files `numerics-interval.py` and `numerics-cross-errors.py` implement these operations and the error transfers below; their use is not needed to specify the certificate.

<a id="pm-h-91"></a>
###### From raw sums to normalized moments.

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error"></a>
The finite arithmetic is now specified. It remains to show that its enclosures imply the continuous-law enclosures used in the scalar proof. Let $Q$ be the unnormalized quadrature with weights $.4\varphi(x_j-\beta)$, so $N(f)=Q(f)/Q(1)$. The common multiplicative factor omitted in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums">[rcut:eq:scalar-finite-sums]</a> cancels in this ratio. For every raw moment under consideration, $|Q(f)-\langle f\rangle|\leq E_{\mathrm{quad}}$ and $|Q(1)-1|\leq E_{\mathrm{quad}}$, with $E_{\mathrm{quad}}$ from Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-raw-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-raw-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-raw-error]</a>. If the true $L^2$ norm of $f$ is at most 4, the normalized first- and second-moment errors are consequently bounded by $$E_1=\frac{5E_{\mathrm{quad}}}{1-E_{\mathrm{quad}}},\qquad
 E_2=\frac{17E_{\mathrm{quad}}}{1-E_{\mathrm{quad}}}.$$ Their variance error is at most <a id="rcut:eq:scalar-variance-error"></a>$$E_{\mathrm{var}}=E_2+E_1(8+E_1)
 <1.312\cdot10^{-5}.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-variance-error}$$ For each of the computed standard deviations, $\sqrt{T(f)}>.08$ by Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-finite-values" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-finite-values">3</a>. The identity for a difference of square roots therefore bounds its fixed-function error by $$E_{\mathrm{sd}}=E_{\mathrm{var}}/.08
 <1.64\cdot10^{-4}.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error}$$ The denominator here comes from the finite computation itself. In particular, this argument does not assume the continuous-law enclosures in Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-moments">86</a>, which are still to be proved.

We verify the $L^2$ hypothesis before applying these transfer bounds. The functions $v,g,mv$ have absolute value at most one on the real line. For the fixed function $F_{a',G'}$, the required bound follows from $$|F_{a',G'}(h)|\leq2|h|+1.87,
 \qquad
 \|F_{a',G'}\|_2
 \leq2\sqrt{\beta^2+\beta^4}+1.87<3<4.$$ The real function $g$ belongs to $[0,1]$, since $1-m^2\leq1.75-m$. Positivity of the quadrature weights gives $a_N,G_N\in[0,1]$. It follows that all preceding strip and moment estimates apply to the fixed function $F_N:=F_{a_N,G_N}$, whose values at the quadrature nodes are the $f_j$ used in Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-eight-sums" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-eight-sums">[rcut:eq:scalar-eight-sums]</a>.

<a id="pm-h-92"></a>
###### Replacing the two means in $F$.

<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-parameter-error"></a>
<a id="rcut:eq:scalar-total-error"></a>
There are two different functions in the remaining comparison. The finite calculation uses $F_N$, whereas the desired continuous standard deviation is that of $F$, with the true means $a,G$. First apply Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error]</a> to the fixed function $F_N$. After this step, both standard deviations to be compared are under the same continuous field law. We may then vary the two parameters from $a_N,G_N$ to $a,G$. Because $v,g$ have absolute values at most one, <a id="rcut:eq:scalar-mean-error"></a>$$|a-a_N|,\ |G-G_N|\leq e_a:=\frac{2E_{\mathrm{quad}}}{1-E_{\mathrm{quad}}}
 <4.61\cdot10^{-7}.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-mean-error}$$ Throughout the parameter rectangle $[0,1]^2$, the derivatives of $F_{a',G'}$ are $$\frac{\partial F_{a',G'}}{\partial a'}
   =h-\frac{.64\beta^2}{(.64-.19a')^2}v,
 \qquad
 \frac{\partial F_{a',G'}}{\partial G'}=3\beta^2g.$$ Their centered $L^2$ norms are at most $\tfrac12+\tfrac14(.64)/(.45)^2$ and $3/4$, respectively. The triangle inequality for the centered seminorm consequently gives $$\begin{split}
 |s_F-s_{F_N}|&\leq E_{\mathrm{par}}
 :=\left(\frac12+\frac{.64}{4(.45)^2}+\frac34\right)e_a\\
 &<10^{-6}.
 \end{split}
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-parameter-error}$$ The parameter $l$ needs no separate perturbation allowance: the derivative above already includes its dependence $l=.64-.19a$. Combining Equations <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error]</a> and <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-parameter-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-parameter-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-parameter-error]</a>, the total error between the computed standard deviation of $f_j$ and the desired $s_F$ is $$E_{\mathrm{sd}}+E_{\mathrm{par}}
 <.000165.
 \label{rcut:eq:scalar-total-error}$$

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-trapezoid-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-trapezoid</summary>

*Proof of Lemma <a href="#rcut:lem:scalar-data" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:lem:scalar-data">[rcut:lem:scalar-data]</a>.* We now combine the finite enclosures with the transfer estimates. Every quantity in Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-finite-values" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-finite-values">3</a> is within $.00065$ of its center in Table <a href="#rcut:tab:scalar-moments" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rcut:tab:scalar-moments">86</a>. Among the standard deviations, the largest transfer error is Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-total-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-total-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-total-error]</a>; the three standard deviations not involving $F$ require only Equation <a href="#rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error">[rcut:eq:scalar-sd-error]</a>. <a id="app:clock-comparison"></a>
### A finite-chain clock comparison

This appendix proves the bounded-array clock lemma stated in Section <a href="#sec:model" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="sec:model">2</a>. Both cutoff arguments use it to pass from shifted Poisson averages to a binomial average after extracting a fixed holding probability from the update kernel. The parameters and arrays below are those of Lemma <a href="#lem:input-clock" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:input-clock">4</a>; the proof uses no property of the SK model. It follows the shifted-clock comparison of Chen and Saloff-Coste (G.-Y. Chen and Saloff-Coste 2013, Theorem 1.1 and Lemmas 3.1–3.2) <a id="pm-cite-49"></a>[[ChenSaloffCoste2013](#ref-ChenSaloffCoste2013)], with the finite approximation fixed before the arrays are tested. The Gaussian approximation below uses signed coefficients: cancellation permits translates of the wider Poisson Gaussian to approximate the narrower binomial Gaussian.

<details id="proof-stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-trapezoid-3"><summary>Proof of stmt-rcut-lem-scalar-trapezoid</summary>

*Proof of Lemma <a href="#lem:input-clock" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="lem:input-clock">4</a>.* The proof has three steps. We approximate the two rescaled clocks in $L^1$ by Gaussian densities, approximate the narrower Gaussian by a finite signed sum of translates of the wider one, and then test this single finite approximation against the bounded arrays. Fixing that approximation before taking the limit will also give the uniform statement.

<a id="eq:inputclock-local-limits"></a>
*Step 1: the two local limits.* For an integer $M$ and $j\in\mathbb Z$, let $$I_{M,j}=\left[\frac{j-q M}{\sqrt M},
                   \frac{j+1-q M}{\sqrt M}\right).$$ The histogram density of an integer-valued random variable $Z$ is $\sqrt M\,\mathbb P(Z=j)$ on $I_{M,j}$. Denote by $p_{M,y}$ the histogram for $\operatorname{Poisson}(q M+y\sqrt M)$ and by $q_M$ the histogram for $\operatorname{Binomial}(M,q)$, assigning zero probability outside their supports. For $v>0$ write $$\varphi_v(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi v}}e^{-x^2/(2v)}.$$ We claim that for every fixed $y$, $$\|p_{M,y}-\varphi_q(\,\cdot-y)\|_1\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \|q_M-\varphi_{q(1-q)}\|_1\longrightarrow0.
 \label{eq:inputclock-local-limits}$$

<a id="eq:inputclock-ratio-expansion"></a>
Here is a proof from probability ratios. Let $\pi_M(j)$ denote the probability mass function of either variable, let $k_M$ be an integer nearest its mean, and put $v=q$ in the Poisson case and $v=q(1-q)$ in the binomial case. Their successive ratios are, respectively, $$\frac{m}{j+1},\qquad
 \frac{(M-j)q}{(j+1)(1-q)},
 \qquad m=q M+y\sqrt M.$$ For every fixed $H<\infty$, expanding their logarithms at $k_M$ gives, uniformly for integers $|\ell|\le H\sqrt M$, $$\log\frac{\pi_M(k_M+\ell+1)}{\pi_M(k_M+\ell)}
 =-\frac{\ell}{vM}+O_H(M^{-1}).$$ The constants here may depend on the fixed $q$ and $y$. Indeed, the deviations of the numerator and denominator from their central values are $O_H(\sqrt M)$, and the remainder in $\log(1+h)=h+O(h^2)$ is $O_H(M^{-1})$; rounding the mean costs the same order. All these indices belong to the supports for large $M$. Summing forward or backward from $k_M$ proves $$\frac{\pi_M(k_M+\ell)}{\pi_M(k_M)}
 =\exp\left(-\frac{\ell^2}{2vM}+O_H(M^{-1/2})\right)
 \qquad(|\ell|\le H\sqrt M).
 \label{eq:inputclock-ratio-expansion}$$

The ratio estimate determines the shape near the mean. Its normalization remains to be identified. Set $A_M=\sqrt M\,\pi_M(k_M)$ and $J_H=\int_{-H}^H e^{-x^2/(2v)}\,dx$. Equation <a href="#eq:inputclock-ratio-expansion" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:inputclock-ratio-expansion">[eq:inputclock-ratio-expansion]</a> and Riemann sums imply $$\mathbb P(|Z-k_M|\le H\sqrt M)=A_M(J_H+o(1)).$$ Taking, for example, $H=1$ shows that $A_M$ is bounded. The variance of $Z$ divided by $M$ tends to $v$, and its mean is within $1/2$ of $k_M$. Chebyshev’s inequality therefore gives $$\limsup_{M\to\infty}\mathbb P(|Z-k_M|>H\sqrt M)\le\frac{v}{H^2}.$$ For fixed $H$ this bounds the limit inferior and limit superior of $A_M$ by $(1-v/H^2)/J_H$ and $1/J_H$, respectively. Letting $H\to\infty$ yields $A_M\to(2\pi v)^{-1/2}$. Equation <a href="#eq:inputclock-ratio-expansion" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:inputclock-ratio-expansion">[eq:inputclock-ratio-expansion]</a> now proves uniform convergence of the histogram densities on every compact interval, with limiting center $y$ in the Poisson case and zero in the binomial case. The same Chebyshev estimate controls their tails; the histogram intervals move an observation by at most $M^{-1/2}$ in the rescaled coordinate. Gaussian tails then give the whole-line $L^1(\mathbb R)$ convergence in Equation <a href="#eq:inputclock-local-limits" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="eq:inputclock-local-limits">[eq:inputclock-local-limits]</a>.

*Step 2: approximation by translates.* We claim that the narrower Gaussian belongs to the closed linear span, in $L^1$, of translates of the wider Gaussian. Every derivative $\varphi_q^{(k)}$ belongs to that closed span: its finite differences are finite linear combinations of translates, and their quotients converge to the derivative in $L^1$. For completeness, iterating the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus expresses the $k$th forward-difference quotient as $$\int_{[0,1]^k}\varphi_q^{(k)}
           (x+h(t_1+\cdots+t_k))\,dt_1\cdots dt_k.$$ Gaussian derivatives are integrable polynomial multiples of a Gaussian, and their translations are continuous in $L^1$ by dominated convergence. This proves the asserted limit. Repeated differentiation also gives $\varphi_q^{(k)}=p_k\varphi_q$, where $p_k$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ with leading coefficient $(-1/q)^k$. The nonzero leading coefficients therefore let us express every polynomial multiple of $\varphi_q$ as a finite linear combination of these derivatives. Such multiples lie in the same closed span.

Put $v=q$ and $w=q(1-q)$. The ratio of the two densities is $$\frac{\varphi_w(x)}{\varphi_v(x)}
 =\sqrt{\frac vw}\,e^{-c x^2},
 \qquad c=\frac12\left(\frac1w-\frac1v\right)>0.$$ If $V$ is centered Gaussian of variance $2c$, then $e^{-cx^2}=\mathbb E\cos(Vx)$. This identity follows directly from Gaussian integration by parts: the characteristic function has value one at zero and derivative $-2cx$ times itself. Truncate the expectation to $|V|\le R$. The omitted contribution has absolute value at most $\mathbb P(|V|>R)$, uniformly in $x$. For fixed $R$, replace cosine by its Taylor polynomials. On $|V|\le R$, their absolute values are bounded by $e^{R|x|}$, which is integrable against $\varphi_v(x)\,dx$. Dominated convergence thus approximates the truncated expectation by polynomials in $L^1(\varphi_v(x)\,dx)$. Sending $R$ to infinity and using the preceding derivative argument proves the claimed closed-span property for $\varphi_w$.

*Step 3: test one finite approximation against the arrays.* Extend $a_{n,j}$ by zero to $j<0$, and let $U_n$ be the function equal to $a_{n,j}$ on $I_{M_n,j}$. If $B=0$ the result is immediate, so assume $B>0$. Given $\epsilon_*>0$, choose one finite signed sum $$F=\sum_{\ell=1}^L a_\ell\varphi_q(\,\cdot-y_\ell),
 \qquad
 \|\varphi_{q(1-q)}-F\|_1
                         <\frac{\epsilon_*}{4B}.$$ The number of terms, the real shifts, and the real coefficients are fixed before $n$ tends to infinity. Set $A_0=\max\{1,\sum_\ell|a_\ell|\}$ and abbreviate $\psi=\varphi_{q(1-q)}$, $\phi_\ell=\varphi_q(\,\cdot-y_\ell)$. Then <a id="eq:inputclock-finite-approximation"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \left|\int q_{M_n}U_n\right|
 &\le B\|q_{M_n}-\psi\|_1+B\|\psi-F\|_1 \notag\\
 &\quad+\sum_{\ell=1}^L|a_\ell|
       \left(\left|\int p_{M_n,y_\ell}U_n\right|
             +B\|p_{M_n,y_\ell}-\phi_\ell\|_1\right).
 \label{eq:inputclock-finite-approximation}
\end{aligned}$$ For large $n$, the first $L^1$ error is below $\epsilon_*/(4B)$, each of the finitely many other $L^1$ errors is below $\epsilon_*/(4BA_0)$, and each of the Poisson averages is below $\epsilon_*/(4A_0)$. The right side is then at most $\epsilon_*$. This proves the result. The same bound proves its uniform version: the finite approximation is common to the family, the local-limit errors depend only on $M$ and the fixed shifts, and the hypothesis controls the finite list of Poisson averages uniformly. ◻

</details>
